Name: Blue Celadon - Choy Blue
Description: Spanish red iron oxide is prefered. I have found that my blue celadon glaze, which is very similar to others given to you, likes all the reduction I can give it. I fire blue celadon pieces in the same firings I go for carbon trapping with my shinos. The extra reduction along with a good thick application of the blue celadon glaze, I think, encourages the bubbles trapped in the glaze which gives it a nice softness to the glossy glaze. I introduce a heavy reduction at cone 010 through to cone 06 then lighten up a bit for the rest of the firing. Also, drips melt out and do not show. Despite the only average amount of clay in the glaze, but high amount of feldspar and flint, the glaze does not run at all at cone 10 EPK helps and use Spanish Red Iron oxide and do not get any speckling. I feel the blue celadon glaze is much nicer on porcelain. You may need to add a suspender, I don't though. I have substituted Strontium Carbonate for half of the Barium and all of the Barium at 1 part Barium to 3/4 parts Strontium and received just as nice results. I have the understanding from talking with other colleagues that the glaze should be safe from Barium poisoning because it is a glossy glaze where enough silica molecules have combined with the Barium molecules to make it stable. But, I have never had it tested. Does anyone know if this is true or not? Please reply. Enjoy, Cone 10 down, submitted by: Steve Loucks e-mail:

Variations: Can add 1/4 % Copper Carbonate for Light Green in Oxidation ^9-10 firing. How long have you been using this glaze? Almost 20 years Where is it used? In my studio Where did this recipe come from? I got this recipe from Kieth Campbell from Ontario, Canada but believe that it is an Alfred Univ. glaze originally What do you like most about this glaze? There are no surprises and I can count on it every time. Its food safe. Is this glaze reliable? Very Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? Crazes if applied TOO THICK. How do different firing temperatures/atmospheres affect the glaze? Electric/Oxidation or Gas fired/Reduction or neutral fire are all equally as good. How does the glaze behave on different clay bodies? On porcelain and white stoneware it is clear white. On buff and or red bodies it goes somewhat grey because of the iron in the clays. Very pleasent on all clays. I have tested and used on all the above clays. What consistency should the glaze be for pouring/dipping? The consistancy of my glazes is like homo milk. The normal consistancy. I dip to the count of 5 - 10. How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? Normal. I spray this glaze as well to 1/16th of an inch or better. How does this glaze interact with other glazes? I like it the way it is for my work. Test your glazes and see what happens. I have sprayed other glazes on rims etc. and all worked fine. What is your kiln type and size? 30 cu.ft. downdraft gas kiln. How do you typically fire? Heating...pilots (4) on over night or at least a 9 hour period. Burners (4) on low over night or till cone 07 is down. Turn up the burners to 1/2 way mid. reduce kiln for 30 to 45 mins. depending on the weather. Cut the reduction (open dampers to almost open and a light reduction till cone 10 falls. Clear kiln, shut off and seal. Slow 36 hour cool before cracking the door and work comes out in about 48 hours. Do you experience problems with the raw glaze? NO....this glaze can be stirred easily even after 8 weeks of non use and stays stirred for long periods of time while glazing. I make a large green garbage pail of my well used glazes and they last me for a yr. or more. No smells etc. What is your water pH? City water. Any other comments? Try this glaze...it will be a main stay in your studio. ;>}}} GlazeBase recipe Submitted by: Peggy Heer / Heer Pottery Ice Cream Flavor: Chocolate -------------------------------------------------------------------- ----

Applied thick. A semi mat with movement in the surface. The glaze looks similar to the original Weathered Bronze where thinnest, but with a better melt and therefore slightly more gloss. However, where thickest, this is the brightest of greens of all of the Pinnell new formulations of Weathered Bronze. It is a strong aqua to grass green, with movement in the surface, showing some minute whitish streaking. It is black and green where thinnest. John Hesselberth has tested this glaze for copper leaching and recommends this glaze for decorative use only. 3% copper + 5 % Ti = more green 5% copper + 5% Ti = more black Variation on Pete Pinnell's Weathered Bronze. Black crystals, breaks black over edges and texture. A bit more matte. See Clay Times Mar/Apr. 2004 for article p.19.
Ingredients: Nepheline Syenite 29.3; Spodumene 27.2; Strontium Carbonate 17.8; Grolleg Kaolin 12; Silica 8; Ferro Frit 3134 4.3; Lithium Carbonate 1.4; Copper Carbonate 5 (additional); Titanium Dioxide 5 (additional)

Name: Chappell Floating Blue, Blue Hare
Description: Source/Alternate names: James Chappell The Potters Complete Book of Clay and Glazes Source/Alternate names: same oxides as Slate Blue With Green Specks, similar to Blue Jean Blue and Cobbled Floating Blue Notes: Candice Roeder: a deep blue-brown background of great depth with lighter mottled blues that seem to float on the surface of the background glaze. with more of the lighter mottled blues where the application is thickest. Watch thickness near the bottom of the pot. It fires best on the light side of cone 6 (standard cone just bending), seems to get greener and more fluid the higher you go. Cone 5 works well, too. The book says to weigh the ingredients very carefully, use distilled water or water that is known to have a low mineral content. Mix then add the CMC solution. The book warns that the glaze is fickle, and recommends against firing this glaze in the same kiln with glazes that contain copper, chrome, nickel or manganese. Mineral content of the water is an important factor. I have noticed an adverse effect as the author noted, and now fire an entire kiln load of this glaze. Notes: Martha Muzychka: not what I expected, mostly green with a few spots of blue. On black stoneware clay, it gives an unusual cloudy effect. Notes: Ivy Glasgow: a popular and beautiful (when done right) glaze. The original Floating Blue pigments have been tested and found to be food safe. When floating blue works, it is lovely. Key seems to be firing to no more than Cone 5-1/2 and cooling quickly. Notes: James Chappell: the colours seem to float on a surface of a darker background of great depth, reminiscent of a deep pool of water. Its colour and opacity vary greatly with thickness so it highlights irregularities in the surface. Phase separation in the translucent matrix makes the colour swirl as small rivulets of more fluid glass flow around more viscous phases. Titanium crystals in the matrix make it sparkle. Calcium-borate boron-blue crystals grow on the surface. Bubbles of escaping gases create pools of lighter coloured glass surrounded by darker rings. Small black speckles are produced by unground particles of iron. Use distilled or low mineral water, force all material through an 80 mesh screen, stir thoroughly before and during use to prevent settling out of the iron content, apply the thickness of a dime, fire to cone 6 oxidation exactly, and cool normally. Do not substitute any other chemicals for those given, it is a fickle glaze. It depends on the Gerstley borate to suspend it. Notes: I substitute Cobalt Carb 2.0. What caught my eye, was the description of it as slate blue, which doesn't fit my results. So, I picked up the original recipe, and it differs from the one Sharon posted. You might try this version in your tests. It is called Floating Blue...from James Chappell's book, Clay and Glazes. This glaze produces a deep blue-brown background of great depth with lighter mottled blues that seem to float on the surface of the background glaze. The glaze has more of the lighter mottled blues where the application is thickest. Watch thickness near the bottom of the pot. The C.M.C. measurement refers to a premixed CMC and water solution. For the Silica, I use 325 mesh Flint. The rutile, is just powdered rutile from the ceramics supply. It fires best on the light side of cone 6 (standard cone just bending), seems to get greener and more fluid the higher you go. Cone 5 works well, too. I do not find a need for bentonite. The book says to weigh the ingredients very carefully, use distilled water or water that is known to have a low mineral content. Mix then add the CMC solution. Sieve two or three times through a 60 to 80 mesh sieve to thoroughly disperse the cobalt, iron, and rutile. The book warns that the glaze is fickle, and recommends against firing this glaze in the same kiln with glazes that contain copper, chrome, nickel or manganese. Mineral content of the water is an important factor. I have noticed an adverse effect as the author noted, and now fire an entire kiln load of this glaze. The glaze should be stirred occasionally during application because the iron has a tendency to settle. Chappell's Suggested variations: Stipple on additional glaze with brush or apply with sponge for an even more mottled effect. Or: lightly sponge a thin wash of 3 grams of chrome oxide to 100 grams of water plus a tablespoon of CMC over the top to produce a floating blue glaze with subtle green tints. Or: Over the glaze, sponge lightly with a rutile wash consisting of 2 grams rutile per 100g of water for a floating blue glaze with slightly tan crystalline tints on the surface. submitted by: Candice Roeder source for original recipe: James Chappell
Ingredients: Nepheline Syenite 47.3; Gerstley Borate 27; Silica 20.3; EP Kaolin 5.4; Rutile 4 (additional); Bentonite 2 (additional); Red Iron Oxide 2 (additional); Cobalt Oxide 1 (additional)

Description: ClayArt Listserv recipe < NOTE that recipe is in parts - not stated whether that's parts by weight or volume This is to LJ in Alexandria and anyone else interested in raku glazes. We have been using these two glazes along with white crackle and copper wash and have gotten VERY NICE results. Apply 1 coat. Stie glaze with each brush stroke to keep rutile in suspension. Our raku kiln is fired between 1830 and 1900 degrees. Reduce in very heavy pine needles, broken pine cones and some sawdust. The surface effect is like a 100 grit sandpaper. Colors range from a silver blue to silver/bronze with flashes of color that can run the full spectrum. Lots of bright teal and purple with halos of fuschia and mustard. Every now and then I get splotches of tomato red! Name: Alisa Butter Base (+3 Copper Carb.)
Description: Author: Alisa Liskin Clausen Comments: Glaze made because I mixed WoDo 40/10 wrong and could remember my mistake. The initial mistake glaze looked semi mat which is a base I have been trying to get. After some changes to get the Silica higher, I made this base. Overall a smooth surface, butter sheen, fattens up with additions of Rutile and Titanium. Can get glossier with some oxide mix addtions. Copper gives some oil spot effects, dark and browns. Good color results with Cobalt and Opacifiers. Must look at edges, and closely overall, as there are many color nunances and changes. Some high fire looks as well.

Name: Dolita Base (Alisa's Glossy Base)
Description: Source/Alternate names: Alisa Clausen I have later used my local boron frit JM 169 with good results. Try with Frit 3134 also for similar results. Can run. Notes: Alisa Clausen: Base: translucent, gloss. With 1 cobalt carbonate, translucent, gloss, medium blue. With 3 cobalt carbonate, translucent, gloss, dark blue, running. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 2 rutile, translucent, gloss dark blue with dark to black pooled areas. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 4.5 rutile, translucent, olive green ground with blue rivulets and streaks. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 6 rutile, gloss, overall and covering medium green, breaking brown with slight bluish streaking. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 2 chrome oxide, gloss, covering medium to dark green. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 2 chrome, gloss, covering dark greenish teal. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 2 copper carbonate and 2 tin dioxide, gloss, covering dark green, slightly lighter than above. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 2 copper carbonate and 10 tin dioxide, gloss, covering teal green. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 2 copper carbonate and 3 titanium dioxide and 2 rutile, semigloss, covering, grey blue ground with greenish brown cast. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 1 red iron oxide, gloss, cover, very dark blue. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 3 red iron oxide, gloss, dark blue with almost black pooling. Very fluid and high edges but did not run, crazed. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 5 ochre, gloss, very dark blue, fluid edges. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 1 tin dioxide, gloss, very dark blue, fluid and ran off tile. With 3 rutile, translucent, gloss, pale yellow, crazed. With 6 rutile, translucent ground, pale yellow, heavily streaked with opalescence. Very fluid but did not run off tile, crazed. With 6 rutile and 6 red iron oxide, semimat, covering medium brown baizes. Appears to have and overall sparkle made up of tiny crystals. With 3 copper carbonate, translucent, gloss, pale green. With 6 copper carbonate, translucent, gloss, medium green with dark green streaking. Very fluid, but did not run, crazed. With 3 copper carbonate and 3 rutile, translucent, gloss, medium green streaking and shell over light brown ground, crazing. With 3 copper carbonate and 6 rutile and 1.5 cobalt carbonate, gloss, covering, very fluid with several streaking colours over a medium green grown, streaking is turquoise, brown and blue, very fluid and ran off tile in one area, breaking brown. With 4 copper carbonate and 6 rutile, almost translucent gloss, very fluid, exaggeration of above, ran off the tile. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 4 rutile and 2 red iron oxide, gloss, covering multi coloured glaze, brown ground and breaking, with streaking blue, green and beige, a lot of movement without running, a good runner up for Floating Blue. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 5 rutile and 0.5 red iron oxide, semigloss, covering and variegated green, dark green ground with lighter green speckling. With 5 red iron oxide, translucent, gloss, medium brown. With 10 red iron oxide, translucent, gloss, dark brown. With 5 tin dioxide, gloss, covering, soft white, slight yellowish cast. With 10 tin dioxide, gloss, covering, white. With 5 zirconia, translucent, cream, badly crazed. With 10 zirconia, gloss, covering, stark white. With 5 titanium dioxide, translucent, pale umber, slight opalescence where pooled. With 10 titanium dioxide, translucent, gloss, light yellow ground, with thick streaking white crystals and blue opalescence, ran off tile. With 5 titanium dioxide and 5 red iron oxide, gloss, covering medium brown with dark blue streaking, red in one of the streaks, a lot of movement, high edge, but did not run. With 1.5 titanium dioxide and 15 red iron oxide, gloss, medium brown ground with a lot of movement streaking, blue and black, ran off tile. With 1 rutile and 12.5 red iron oxide, semigloss, brown and black streaking, darkest where pooled. With 4 manganese dioxide and 6 rutile, gloss, overall beige with blueish pooling. With 4 manganese dioxide and 0.4 cobalt carbonate and 6 rutile, gloss, overall beige with very fluid grey blue streaking and pinkish casts, ran off tile.
Ingredients: EP Kaolin 30; Ferro Frit 3124 30; Dolomite 15; Silica 15; Ball Clay 10

What I hate about it: The glaze settles VERY fast; the yellow color comes only if you’re lucky; it tends to have a greenish hue; if you dip too thin it comes out a washed out stony black color that is very rough to the touch (but I sand it down and it is actually really nice after being sanded!); it is inconsistent as of yet…needs some tweaking.

Name: Janice Hill's Teal from Chrome and Cobalt
Description: With 13% Gerstley borate and a sufficient alumina level, this recipe is versatile enough to go from cone 5-9. It looks fabulous at cone 7. The chrome and cobalt combine make a strong teal blue-green, and the titanium keeps it from looking like a flat commercial glaze. The silica level gives it a pretty gloss that feels good on the mouth and keeps the glaze well encased in the silica matrix. The formula is "robust" as defined by glazy.org's database of articles. The boron level is enough to melt the glaze at cone 5 but not too much to melt it off the sides in a high firing. I have fired it in an electric kiln and in a wood-fired kiln with an atmosphere that shifted between, oxidation, neutral and light-reduction. I haven't fired it to cone 10. One drawback of this version is that it is unforgiving because of the chrome. If you don't wipe the glaze off the wax resist really well, you may find little bits of color in places where you don't want it. Also, if you like a crisp line of wax, you'd better make it really crisp because that line will show. I'm working on a second version with ingredients that flow more. On the other hand, there is no trick to getting the color. I've fired it with both a slow-cool (1800-1400) and crash cool (2230 and off). They are both great, but I like the crash cool best because it reflects light so beautifully--it practically sparkles.
Ingredients: Nepheline Syenite 39; Silica 22; Gerstley Borate 13; Wollastonite 11; Ball Clay 9; Dolomite 6; Titanium Dioxide 3; Bentonite 2; Chrome Oxide 1; Cobalt Carbonate 0.75

Name: Sonoran Crawler
Description: This is a magnesium crawl glaze that contains a lot of clay. This means it can be applied on top of some other glazes and still retain its reticulations. I invented this glaze myself. My goal was to make a crawling glaze that could be applied thick and not flake off. Mix this glaze up thick- preferably in small batches and to the consistency of yogurt. Apply a thin layer of a dark glaze, high in clay such as satin black to leather-hard ware or green ware, or barnard slip, and bisque this lower layer onto the clay. Dark clays also work well. Apply a couple coats of Sonoran Crawler on top of the bisqueware with a brush and cease application once you observe cracking. The glaze will crack in the direction of your brush strokes! The more times you brush over the glaze as it dries, the better it adheres. Under heavy reduction or on top of certain iron bearing bodies it can flash. You can try adding a pinch of soda ash to the glaze in order to make it a little less thick without lowering the water content. Thinning this glaze down with water WILL cause it to peel off the piece, keep that specific gravity REALLY high. One day I may try mixing it to a thick paste and applying with a palette knife, but for now, yogurt consistency with a calligraphy bamboo brush works for me. Test this glaze on top of various glazes. I've not had great luck with it over Temmoku, the fine powdery temmoku glaze prevents it from adhering properly. Shinos on the other hand seem to work well underneath it, and the soda ash from the shinos changes the texture in interesting ways. To adjust the texture, change the ratio of Talc and Spodumene: Decreasing talc, increasing spodumene by 2% results in a smoother, more lumpy surface. Decreasing spodumene and increasing talc by 2% results in a rougher, more papery-bark-like surface. Of course, test adjustments before using. Can you tell I have a bit of an obsession? Thank you Klaes for trying out my glaze, altering it and uploading photos! I'll try it myself. I added Borax to the recipe because I believe it will help it stick to the surface better.

Comenta Gladys Sardella: "Les comparto esta muestrita con la receta correspondiente. Dan Turnidge cono 5 (1180º) Carbonato de Litio 5%, Frita 3110 (yo usé FK10 de Kelper Omar Dominguez) 50%, Cuarzo 22,5, Oxido de Cinc 22,5%, más 3 de bióxido de manganeso. Fue en oxidación en horno eléctrico a 1180º, 3º por min hasta los 400º con meseta de 10min y 4º por minuto hasta los 1180º con meseta de 20 minutos. Si con esta curva dio cristalitos habría que probarlo con una mejor curva." Comenta Fabiana Sacnún: "Para continuar con el hilo de la base Dan Turnidge, que hace mucho circuló por aquí. Estas dos muestritas son producto de un seminario que acabo de dar. La base original que había compartido Gladys Sardella era: Dan Turnidge cono 5(1180º) Carbonato de Litio 5% Frita 3110, 50% Cuarzo 22,5 Oxido de Cinc 22,5% A falta de la frita 3110 y sus sustitutos, en el seminario se trabajó con la 804 de Crecer en igual proporción. Los resultados idénticos! Quema, cono 5, bajada lenta hasta los 900 aproximadamente." ☆Source/Alternate names: Dan Turnidge. also known as MFE crystalline Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 900C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: Gloss, transparent glaze with stark white streaking. White crystals developed around edges of test tile, which is an extruded square tube. Runny. Glaze is crazed. With added 2 nickel: gloss, transparent glaze with softer white and pink streaking. Bright blue crystals along edges of test tile and bottom dipping line. Runny. Glaze is not crazed. Notes: John Sankey: I use this glaze with Fusion 75 frit plus 3 manganese dioxide and 1 cobalt oxide as colorants; it does not craze but it is runny as virtually all crystalline glazes are.

Name: Mason Color Works White Underglaze Base
Description: For years I relied on the internet to find information about ceramics. One of the most useful and reliable sources both then and now is Vince Pitelka's website. There he shares his knowledge on all aspects of the studio, from making your own tools to loading & firing kilns. (Although I have yet to try his Fabulous Top-Secret Extra-Special Spicy Cheesy Black Bean Dip recipe!) For all of Vince Pitelka's Handouts, please visit: https://www.vincepitelka.com/handoutsinformation/ One very useful recipe on his website is for Mason Underglaze, which actually includes three recipes: CMC solution (great on its own as a glaze additive to slow drying and improve brushability), Underglaze Liquid (which can be used with any underglaze to greatly improve brushability), and finally the Mason Underglaze recipe itself. If you do any underglaze decoration, even just to sign your name, I hope you'll try out these recipes! One note: You should be able to purchase "food grade", non-toxic propylene glycol via the internet, DO NOT just buy automobile anti-freeze which may contain other additives. ## Mason Underglaze Recipe https://www.vincepitelka.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/Mason-Underglaze-Recipe.pdf This recipe for an opaque white underglaze base comes from the Mason Color Works of Liverpool, Ohio, manufacturers of Mason ceramic stains. It’s been in use for decades, and seems to give good results for underglaze brushwork. Like most commercial underglazes, it is not appropriate for trailing or other thick-application techniques. #### Dry Materials F-4 Soda Spar -------------- 20 Kaolin ----------------------- 10 Ball Clay --------------------- 5 3124 Frit ---------------------10 Zircopax --------------------- 5 (or any other zircon opacifier) Total Dry Materials ------- 50 Add Underglaze Liquid -- 75 For colors other than white, add: Ceramic stain -------------- 40 Add the stain after everything else is combined, including the underglaze liquid. Vary the amount of stain for a darker or lighter color, and of course if you add a significant amount of stain you will need to add additional water to adjust the consistency of the final mix. To make the underglaze liquid, combine: Non-toxic antifreeze ------ 2 parts Water ----------------------- 2 parts CMC Liquid --------------- 1 parts To make CMC liquid, stir 30 grams of dry CMC in 1 qt. hot water and let it sit for 2 days. Be sure to use non-toxic antifreeze! Normal antifreeze is ethylene-glycol and is toxic. Instead, use non-toxic propylene-glycol antifreeze. It’s available in auto-supply stores and is safe for people and pets. The CMC gum and propylene glycol in this mixture make it thicker and smoother than a slip containing only water, giving a smoother brushing consistency especially when applying underglaze to dry greenware or bisqueware. When making this recipe: Dry-mix all the dry ingredients, add about 3/4 of the underglaze liquid and blend thoroughly, and then blend in more underglaze liquid a little at a time as needed until you achieve the desired brushing consistency. You may not need the full amount of underglaze liquid. Clarification This recipe can be a bit confusing. When a recipe just provides numbers without specifying the weighing increments, the increments can be whatever you wish – grams, ounces, pounds, etc. For the sake of accuracy when mixing glazes or slips, we generally use grams. With any recipe, there is always the question of what factor to multiply the base recipe by in order to get a certain amount of final product. For example, glaze recipes are almost always given in a form where the dry raw materials for the glaze base add up to 100, plus the modifiers, colorants, etc. In a recipe that contains only dry materials, we know from experience that a batch of 12,000 grams of dry material will fill a five-gallon bucket to the rim once combined with water. But this recipe includes underglaze liquid added by weight, and that does confuse matters Since the instructions tell us to make a quart of CMC liquid, a logical starting point is to figure out the whole recipe based on using that full quart of CMC liquid in the underglaze liquid, adjusting all the other amounts proportionally. As explained below, by doing this we end up needing a little over 3000 grams of dry materials, and the recipe produces about a gallon and a half of underglaze base. Here’s how we figured that. Combining one quart of CMC liquid with two quarts of water and two quarts of non-toxic antifreeze as per the recipe gives five quarts of underglaze liquid. A quart of water weighs 946 grams. Multiply that times five (five quarts) to get 4730 grams of underglaze liquid. The recipe specifies 75 measuring units of underglaze liquid, and if we divide 4730 by 75 we get 63.07, rounded off to 63. Thus if we use the whole five quarts of underglaze liquid, in order to get the correct proportional amounts of dry materials we multiply each amount by 63, which gives a total dry materials weight of 3150 grams. Based on these calculations, our recipe is: F-4 spar ----------------- 20x63 = 1260 grams Kaolin -------------------- 10x63 = 630 grams Ball Clay ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams 3124 frit ------------------ 10x63 = 630 grams Zircopax ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams Total weight of dry materials -- 3150 grams Underglaze liquid ------ 75x63 = 4725 grams Total weight of batch ------------ 7875 grams Since 12,000 grams of dry glaze materials yields a full five-gallon bucket of glaze, we can extrapolate and estimate that since the dry materials weigh 3180 grams (including the CMC gum), this recipe should make about six quarts, which is a lot of underglaze base. If you want more or less underglaze base, just proportionally adjust the number of grams of everything, and adjust the quantity of CMC liquid and underglaze liquid that you prepare.

This glaze is the best result I found for a "celadon-like" clear at cone 6. It is derived from an Si:Al biaxial test with R2O fixed at 0.2 and B2O3 fixed at 0.18: http://www.derekau.net/2018/07/15/orton-cone-6-r2o-0-2-b2o3-0-18-regions/ This test was inspired by Sue's Clear: https://glazy.org/recipes/10997 This glaze has fairly low expansion and seems to have a good fit for the clay bodies I tested. It takes colorants quite well. A very small addition of stain, cobalt, and/or copper can yield results very similar to a high-fire reduction celadon glaze.

Name: Song Dynasty Inspired Tianmu/Tenmoku Glaze
Description: This glaze was inspired by analyses of Song Dynasty dark iron glazes in Nigel Wood's "Chinese Glazes". I find this glaze superior to typical Tenmoku glazes like Leach Tenmoku due in part to the inclusion of magnesium. The minor additions of titania and manganese add to the depth. Rather than a slightly translucent dark brown typical of recipes like Leach, my glaze is an opaque, rich, and almost black. (If you wanted an even deeper black, you could add a small percentage of cobalt oxide, say 0.5%.) I've paired this glaze with Kaki Biaxial D4 (8% Bone Ash, 13% RIO) This glaze was developed with a series of line and biaxial tests, unfortunately I cannot find the original images. ALWAYS STORE YOUR IMAGES IN GLAZY DEREK! I've posted here the firing schedule i developed for iron saturate glazes, it is based on ideas from Carol Marians. This black iron glaze probably doesn't even need a hold at 1700F. I'd just try it in a normal cone 10 oxidation firing with natural cooling and see what happens. Original Firing Schedule (used by Kaki glazes): 150°F/hr to 250°F 400°F/hr to 2050°F 120°F/hr to 2250°F 60°F/hr to 2290°F 40°F/hr to 2310°F Hold of 10 minutes at 2310°F 400°F to 1700°F (Down fire) Hold 2 hours at 1700°F Adjusted Firing Schedule: 150°F/hr to 250°F 375°F/hr to 2050°F 120°F/hr to 2250°F 60°F/hr to 2290°F 40°F/hr to 2310°F Hold of 15 minutes at 2315°F 400°F to 1700°F (Down fire) Hold 1 hour at 1700°F Original firing schedule was 2 hour hold. One hour seems just as good. Perfect cone 10 firing.
Ingredients: Mahavir Potash Feldspar 31.6; Silica 23.5; EP Kaolin 19.1; Wollastonite 19; Talc 6.8; Red Iron Oxide 10.9 (additional); Titanium Dioxide 0.8 (additional); Manganese Dioxide 0.3 (additional)

Name: Anita’s Green Crackle /Yellow Matte
Atmospheres: Reduction; Salt & Soda; Wood; Oxidation; Neutral
Description: Simple 3 ingredient glaze developed from a Triaxial under the direction of John Britt. Applied very thick will pool in recesses to a Green Crackle Celadon on B-mix and where thin on iron-bearing stoneware (like studio pug that has some brown clay but mostly light stoneware) will give a light yellow matte that lets the speckles in the clay shine through. Poured will give lots of variation due to thick/thin application areas and gives a wood fired look to the surface. Designed to run so leave room at the bottom, will crackle if thick and green, won’t crackle if thin and yellow matte. No colorants needed as the iron in Alberta Slip is sufficient. If you use or make any changes to this glaze please give me credit (Anita Ries) by keeping the original name and add the word “modified.” TIPS Add 2% bentonite if making large batches as the high neph sy content will cause this glaze to hardpan Use less water to get the green crackle effect and thin the mixture down using teaspoon or so of Darvan 7 or Sodium Silicate. If you add too much water, this will give you a thin application no matter how many times you dip, resulting in a more yellow/tan matte surface. Play w/ the application to create visual interest in your piece and get green crackle and yellow/tan matte areas. This glaze does well substituting Redart or local clay high in iron. Leave room at the bottom in case it runs Do not apply too thick a coat on the inside of functional vessels, the glaze will be green and pool nicely but may allow liquids to slowly leak at the bottom. For functional items that will hold liquids, it’s better to be judicious with the application. Thank you to the following artists for their feedback by testing the glaze and/or submitting images of their results: Paula Weiss Ginger Lukas Robyn Irene Vicki Chamberlain Maureen Cullen

Name: Snowflake TRI1
Description: Precisa cono 7 (foto 1) para desarrollar correctamente, quizá 8. A cono 6 casi no se aprecian las escamas (foto 2 y 3) He probado muchas recetas de escarchados. Casi todas de buen resultado, pero presentan un problema: Nodulizado (crawling). Se puede solucionar con reesmaltado, pero queda una cicatriz a veces indistinguible, a veces notoria. También se puede evitar con múltiples esmaltados, sumando una capa de esmalte en cada bizcochado. Excelente resultado, pero muy trabajoso. Por casualidad y sin buscarlo expresamente, en un triaxial, encontré una receta que no noduliza, por más grueso que se aplique el esmalte. El problema es la aplicación de un esmalte ultra-defloculado, pero revolviendo con paciencia se soluciona. También calcinar la cuarta parte del carbonato de calcio soluciona la ultradefloculación, y lo vuelve más manejable. Se aprecian muchas pequeñas burbujas (foto 4) Thick. No crawling, but little bubbles. See all the pictures, at cone 7 and 6. Needs full cone 7, maybe 8. Picture 1: cone 7 Picture 2 and 3: cone 6 Picture 4: bubbles, cone 7

Description: Mismo análisis que Aventurine C6 OR1, Van Gilder' Red, Bailey Red... A cono 6, ox y retención en bajada a 960°C, sólido rojo naranjoso flotando sobre marrón opaco oscuro. Formación de cristales, más notorio sobre pasta blanca. A cono 5, en reducción, con mis materiales, forma cristales claros flotando sobre fondo oscuro. No hay naranja, ni rojo, ni aventurina. Ciertamente faltó temperatura, pero es muy bonito igual Same chemistry as Aventurine C6 OR1, Van Gilder' Red, Bailey Red... At cone 6, ox, controlled cooling cycle with a hold at 960°C, and the right thickness, orange/red crystals over a dark brown background. Better crystals on white clay. At cone 5, reduction, with my raw materials, I got light crystals floating on a shiny dark, almost black, background. No orange, red or aventurine. Needs more temperature, but really nice anyway. Nota que acompaña el esmalte original Original notes in Glazy: Glaze Type: Iron saturate rio 11-17% source: Michael Bailey, Glazes Cone 6 This is a "kaki" (plum) saturated iron red. It can be a brilliant red-orange with just the right amount of iron. It does better if you do a controlled cooling as it is a crystalline glaze and needs the slow cool for the crystals to grow (fast cool will yield a chocolate brown gloss).You have to do a line blend on this one to get it right as iron oxides are never the same. I use Spanish red iron oxide. Generally increments of 1% RIO will be fine. But, you really need to do the line blend to get the best red and to fully appreciate the range of colors in that small range of RIO additions. From Bill Buckner https://glazy.org/recipes/1431

I'd seen Pieter Mostert's cone 4 oil spots ages ago, of course (for example https://glazy.org/recipes/10570), but stupidly assumed there was some magic in the earthenware he used. I also knew that a biaxial on Ron Roy's cone 6 Licorice, but stupidly assumed that the Cobalt had something to do with it. They work in mush the same way that cone 10 oil spots work. The effect is more robust (works over a wider range of parameters) at cone 10 but it still works at cone 6. They are legit oil spots, not really any smaller or worse in any way than similar cone 10 glazes. Test one is this recipe with 6-10 RIO. All produced spots. Test two is this recipe with all wollastonite going to all talc. Only the all talc end produced spots. The divisions were 0,3,6,9,12 talc. I should zoom in on the 9-12 talc end. Unlike at cone 10, because of the inherent calcium content of the frit, I can't easily increase the magnesium more, though I could make the glaze less alkaline in order do so. Jake Glaze (https://glazy.org/recipes/36081) seems to have a less alkaline cone 6 oil spot. It looks like he was instructed and inspired by Matt Katz's Ceramics Materials Workshop. At any rate if cone 10 is anything to go by, the spots quickly become too dense and too big with increased magnesia. Test three is an alumina/Silica biaxial. Most glazes didn't finish bubbling, a few did and produced nice spots. There's a sweet spot around the mid silica range of the lower alumina glazes. Fortunately, for the line blends that I did at the end of a very long day, I chose a glaze that's in that sweet spot. I assume adding 1-2% cobalt will result in black spots, and bigger spots, in which case you may want to dial down something - either the talc or the iron. All the tiles were fired vertically, leaning on posts.

Name: Minspar & NZK Porcelain
Description: I've left this porcelain body recipe as "test" because all though I've done some light testing with cold & boiling water, I haven't yet tested absorption and didn't even measure shrinkage. (It seems to shrink a lot though!) This recipe is quite similar in chemistry to Tom Coleman Midfire Porcelain (https://glazy.org/recipes/24523), which uses Neph Sye and Grolleg. It's also a little similar to the chemistry of Jeff Campana's revised cone 6 clay body (https://glazy.org/recipes/46324). The New Zealand Halloysite fires whiter than Grolleg, and is in fact cheaper in cost based on Laguna's 2019 prices. (I actually think EPK fires whiter than Grolleg, see my "English" Porcelain Kaolin tests here: https://glazy.org/posts/80714) This porcelain fires quite white, rivaling Laguna's cone 5 Frost, but it is not as vitrified and glassy as the Frost. btw the "NZK" stands for New Zealand Kaolin (Halloysite). Also, Velvacast isn't on sale any more. I included it because I wanted a good mix of kaolins. You can substitute directly with Opticast, or use a different high-purity kaolin like Grolleg, or you can just leave it out which would make the recipe: Minspar 40.6 NZK 39.6 Silica 19.8 Add Veegum T 1.5 Total: 101.5

Name: Marc's Clear
Description: A high gloss clear glaze with a smooth surface and very few bubbles. It was designed to be used with ceramic stains on cone six porcelain slip-casting bodies.Additions of copper, cobalt, rutile, etc., will often cause pinholes as the glaze has a low melt fluidity. It is at its best when applied thin to medium and fired to a full cone 6. It has a fairly low CTE so tends not to craze on most clays. This glaze is fairly high in alumina and silica and gets its fluxing power through diversifying both the R2O and RO fluxes. Replace the talc with zinc for tan/brown stains based on chrome-iron-zinc system. It will cloud a little on iron stoneware clays. For better clarity drop the silica down to 16 -18%. The CTE will still be ok and likely not craze on most stoneware bodies even with the lower silica. For optimum results sieve through 100 mesh or 80 at least twice. Tends to settle in the bucket at low SG so maybe add 1-2 % bentonite.

Name: Ravenscrag Gloop tests
Description: Here is a simple starting point using a single material for anyone wanting to explore clay/glaze "gloop" effects. Alone it is a thixotropic clay-like material (used as a major component of slip glazes at cone 6 and up). With additions of ball clay and a little epsom salts in the water to counteract its tendency to delocculation it can be shaped - coiled, pinched, rolled, etc., into various forms. The ball clay stops it from "glooping" but small additions of wollastonite bring it back (additions of frit 3124 will do the same but I think the wollastonite makes it a more viscous melt). Here are some tests using: 100g Ravenscrag Slip 20g OM#4 ball clay 5-25g Wollastonite increasing by 5g increments from left to right and a pure Ravenscrag test at the far right. All tests have 2g mazerine blue stain added. The beige button is pure Ravenscrag, no stain. Traces of an "R" scratched into the button at leatherhard remain visible. Ravenscrag is a product of Plainsman Clays, Medicine Hat, Alberta and was developed by Tony Hansen, I believe. I have no idea if this product is available outside N. America so might not be of use to everybody. Ravenscrag.com

Name: Crude Oil
Description: This glaze only makes sense looking at the extended UMF calculations. This glaze is intended to mimic Jian ware using Matt Fiske's "Faux Eosin" glazes as a jumping off point. I had seen some manganese saturate glazes but none had the iridescence in oxidation that I was looking for. I was tipped off that the secret to iridescence lays in the usage of multiple alkaline earth fluxes. This particular glaze uses a ratio of 1:4 calcium to manganese. This test came from a line blend between two glazes with the same base and chemistry one with manganese and one with calcium. Tests in the range of of 1:9 to 4:6 all produced some form of iridescence. The tests below 1:4 had a rougher surface which may have been an error in application. A line blend using zinc and manganese with the same base was also done. Zinc results had a interesting texture in the same range as the calcium blend but produced no iridescence. One direction for further research will be a finer grained line blend in the 1:9 to 2:7 ratio with calcium and manganese. A second direction will be trying to change the dark brown color of the underlying glass matrix using opacifiers. A third and final direction will be additional testing with other fluxes particularly iron.

Description: My community studio basically drinks Stroke and Coats by Mayco.. we do a lot of paint nights and kid stuff, so they're perfect. Mix the recipe and then add the cmc afterwards to make it brushable (or not). Flocculate however you want. I don't really ever touch bentonite anymore unless i'm making a mud mask. Note about CMC - if you are mixing it from powder, use hot water, let it stand for a few minutes, and before you mix it up add .02 copper to it (way less than a pinch) to keep it from rotting over the long term. Note about Zircopax, from TH: Suppliers of encapsulated stains recommend a zircon addition, but are often unclear about why. Here is the reason, it is a "fining agent". If you are using this as a lowfire glaze, the zircopax isn't as big a deal. It really counts when you get to cone 6 temps, then it keeps the stain from gassing out, which you definitely have to worry about in quantities more than 8%.

Description: I took a typical Redart Gold Metallic recipe and matched the chemistry without the Redart. The iron and cobalt can be omitted but they were in the test tiles so I've left them in here. Name: Moon-White Glaze

With increasing of the SiC content, C was formed so that Fe2O3 reduced while the rations of Fe2+ to Fe3+ in glazes increased. The SEM microstructure showed that the discrete droplet phase separation structures were developed in glazes and their sizes were less than 100 nm, so the structural color was formed owing to the Rayleigh scattering. A dual coloring changing mechanism with the increasing of the SiC content was in effect for the moon-white glaze, covering the carbothermic reduction and the varying size of phase separa- tion droplets. Name: Jun glaze
Description: Recipe used in "Effects of microstructure on the sky-green color in imitating ancient Jun glazes" Jianfeng ZHU,3 Pei SHI,33 Fen WANG, Longlong DONG and Ting ZHAO School of Materials Science and Engineering, Shaanxi University of Science & Technology, Xi’an 710021, China > The sky-green glaze of ancient Jun ware was successfully imitated with the addition of 4 wt % calcium phosphate for introducing the phosphorus (P) to the composition. Effects of the calcium phosphate contents on the chromaticity, precipitated phase and microstructure of sky-green glaze were investigated. Based on the analysis of colorimeter, XRD, FT-IR, XPS and SEM, a possible coloring mechanism was proposed to explain the variation of glaze colors with the increasing of calcium phosphate content. The results indicated that the addition of calcium phosphate contributed to increasing the content of calcium iron phosphate [Ca19Fe2(PO4)14] and the size of phase separation droplets in glazes. The formation of Ca19Fe2(PO4)14 decreased the ratio of Fe2+ to Fe3+ and the increased size of phase separation droplets weakened the structural color, which increased the L and b value of glazes. Therefore, the color of sky-green glaze got more green and white gradually.

That glaze in question was Charle’s Titanium with copper carbonate (3%) and rutile (2%). I noticed some flaws with that test. It crazes, there wasn’t enough silica and alumina which made it way too fluid, and the R2O:RO flux ratio didn’t meet an ideal ratio of 3:7. After going through the recipe I readjusted the ingredients. I met the minimum amount of silica and alumina that is required for a “stable glaze” in Ron Roy and John Hesselberth’s book ,MC6, while also lowering the thermal expansion at the same time which makes the glaze less likely to craze. Then finally I took in account for the colorants which also influence the flux ratio in the extended UMF, so I added 2% zinc which helped me meet the ideal ratio for a stable glaze. I strongly recommend the book to those interested in making durable and functional cone 6 glazes. Substitution for wollastonite by using whiting. https://glazy.org/recipes/101138

This version has the most silica and least alumina with average iron and calcium and the least magnesium of the 3 glazes listed in the book. This recipe compares to the position on the Alumina/Silica graph, but it is off in other areas. Hare's fur color may be created by the following: Reduction: greyish streaks of ferrous oxide Neutral: silvery streaks of magnetic oxide oxidation: foxy red or yellowish-brown streaks of ferric oxide within black glaze. Oil spot affect is helped when this glaze is coated over an iron rich slip or wash. Possibly a magnetic iron may have been used in China. Glaze never got hot enough to show oil spots, but at cone 8 glaze was reddish brown with large crawling where cracks from application did not heal. Almost a tomato red/brown coloration where underfired. Wood ash added yellow color in nice flecking. Must get hotter than cone 8 to work properly. Most likely, cone 10 is needed for oil spot.

Name: GPT-2 Rising Sun Chang
Description: This glaze recipe did not exist. It was generated by GPT-2, a machine learning language model. Released early last year, GPT-2 is a large language model with 1.5 billion parameters trained on a dataset of 8 million web pages. The model can be "fine-tuned" with custom data sets, for example collections of poetry or cooking recipes. After training, these custom-tuned models can generate "fake" texts, e.g. poetry or recipes. I fine-tuned the GPT-2 355M model using over 10,000 public Glazy recipes as training data. Although the loss was still going down after 6,000 steps, I stopped training at that point as I noticed more duplicates being generated and I was afraid of overfitting my relatively small dataset. I then generated a couple thousand "fake" recipes using two different "temperature" settings, which controls the "creativity" of the output. The results for both sets were surprisingly good: At first glance the recipes seemed "real" with proportional mixes of feldspars, clays, silica, fluxes and colorants/opacifiers. Even the total ingredient amounts added up to a reasonable number, usually in the range of 90-110%. The duplication rate was about 5% for t=0.7 and 4.5% for t=0.9. After removing duplicates, I imported these fake recipes into Glazy in order to see their resulting analyses and visualize them on the Stull Chart. I was surprised to find that, as with "real" glaze recipes, most of these generated recipes fell comfortably within the major Stull regions of Bright, Matte, and Semi-Matte. The set with temperature setting of 0.9 seemed to generate more variation. This recipe, "Rising Sun Chang", is one of the recipes GPT-2 created (including the name). Other GPT-2 generated recipes are here: GPT-2 Three's Company GPT-2 Yellow Textured For more information about this and other ceramics-related machine learning projects, please visit: https://thisvesseldoesnotexist.com/#/about Direct links to fake recipes: Temperature 0.7 Generated Recipes Temperature 0.9 Generated Recipes Related Post: https://glazy.org/posts/145568

Realmente é um esmalte Robusto! com muita sílica, muito alumínio, cálcio suficiente, etc...! Está todo dentro dos limites e lindamente no meio do Stull!!! Foi recalculado com outros ingredientes tendo em vista que a Frita 3195 aqui é cara e de difícil acesso. 70% de água + 30% de CMC. É tão transparente, tem tanto brilho que qualquer 3% de corante dá cores fortes. Não deu bons resultados com óxido de cobre e não pode ser trabalhado com cromo porque contém zinco. Com óxido de cobalto não deu bom resultado acredito eu que por causa da granulometria. Apresentou grãos e outras partes sem nada. Não se misturou bem. Teria que moer o óxido, e como a granulometria dos corantes é em torno de 400 é melhor usar com corantes. É muito transparente e tudo aparece! Para outros corantes como os verdes alface, por exemplo teria que usar mesmo uma quantidade maior. Acredito que em torno de 8% ou até mesmo talvez anexar um Zircopax ou algo para contrastar. Devem ser feitas novas experiências. Isso é só um começo. Vou investir em um estudo maior em cima desse esmalte. Qualquer expansão acima dessa craquela. Se retirar um pouquinho de magnésio para dar para o cálcio: craquela. Craquelou com 5,6 deixando no mesmo lugar.

Name: Black Small Crawl
Description: Shout out to Ceramic Materials Workshop. A Cu-Zn black crawl glaze. This will produce very small metallic black beads of glaze. This needs to be mixed with more water than normal. I used 150:100 water to dry ingredients for the batch pictured. It's not a fun glaze to mix. Even with the extra water it's thick. The application is key for this one. I have found that if it is too thick I don't get the nice beads, instead I get rectangles that tend to have upward pointing edges. Not a pleasant texture. Too thin an application and the glaze becomes more green than black. The picture posted was a 5 second dip. If you try this glaze just know what too thick and too thin looks like, then adjust your water content accordingly. I do not recommend using Darvan or anything else to alter the glaze even though it is difficult to mix. Dispersants will alter the behavior of the glaze. I use this regularly (love the texture on handles), I have had no studio issues with the glaze. I have never had problems with Zn based crawls flaking or becoming powdery. In my experience, Zn based crawl glazes are well behaved. This one is no exception. Because I am using Cu as the AM flux, the areas of clay the glaze leaves exposed has a green tint. I find it pleasant. Your mileage may vary. I have not tested this in reduction. I also have no reason to believe that it would misbehave in reduction.

Name: Mason Color Works White Underglaze Base Australian Version
Description: NB: aussies - propylene glycol = buy on ebay. For years I relied on the internet to find information about ceramics. One of the most useful and reliable sources both then and now is Vince Pitelka's website. There he shares his knowledge on all aspects of the studio, from making your own tools to loading & firing kilns. (Although I have yet to try his Fabulous Top-Secret Extra-Special Spicy Cheesy Black Bean Dip recipe!) For all of Vince Pitelka's Handouts, please visit: https://www.vincepitelka.com/handoutsinformation/ One very useful recipe on his website is for Mason Underglaze, which actually includes three recipes: CMC solution (great on its own as a glaze additive to slow drying and improve brushability), Underglaze Liquid (which can be used with any underglaze to greatly improve brushability), and finally the Mason Underglaze recipe itself. If you do any underglaze decoration, even just to sign your name, I hope you'll try out these recipes! One note: You should be able to purchase "food grade", non-toxic propylene glycol via the internet, DO NOT just buy automobile anti-freeze which may contain other additives. ## Mason Underglaze Recipe https://www.vincepitelka.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/Mason-Underglaze-Recipe.pdf This recipe for an opaque white underglaze base comes from the Mason Color Works of Liverpool, Ohio, manufacturers of Mason ceramic stains. It’s been in use for decades, and seems to give good results for underglaze brushwork. Like most commercial underglazes, it is not appropriate for trailing or other thick-application techniques. #### Dry Materials F-4 Soda Spar -------------- 20 Kaolin ----------------------- 10 Ball Clay --------------------- 5 3124 Frit ---------------------10 Zircopax --------------------- 5 (or any other zircon opacifier) Total Dry Materials ------- 50 Add Underglaze Liquid -- 75 For colors other than white, add: Ceramic stain -------------- 40 Add the stain after everything else is combined, including the underglaze liquid. Vary the amount of stain for a darker or lighter color, and of course if you add a significant amount of stain you will need to add additional water to adjust the consistency of the final mix. To make the underglaze liquid, combine: Non-toxic antifreeze ------ 2 parts Water ----------------------- 2 parts CMC Liquid --------------- 1 parts To make CMC liquid, stir 30 grams of dry CMC in 1 qt. hot water and let it sit for 2 days. Be sure to use non-toxic antifreeze! Normal antifreeze is ethylene-glycol and is toxic. Instead, use non-toxic propylene-glycol antifreeze. It’s available in auto-supply stores and is safe for people and pets. The CMC gum and propylene glycol in this mixture make it thicker and smoother than a slip containing only water, giving a smoother brushing consistency especially when applying underglaze to dry greenware or bisqueware. When making this recipe: Dry-mix all the dry ingredients, add about 3/4 of the underglaze liquid and blend thoroughly, and then blend in more underglaze liquid a little at a time as needed until you achieve the desired brushing consistency. You may not need the full amount of underglaze liquid. Clarification This recipe can be a bit confusing. When a recipe just provides numbers without specifying the weighing increments, the increments can be whatever you wish – grams, ounces, pounds, etc. For the sake of accuracy when mixing glazes or slips, we generally use grams. With any recipe, there is always the question of what factor to multiply the base recipe by in order to get a certain amount of final product. For example, glaze recipes are almost always given in a form where the dry raw materials for the glaze base add up to 100, plus the modifiers, colorants, etc. In a recipe that contains only dry materials, we know from experience that a batch of 12,000 grams of dry material will fill a five-gallon bucket to the rim once combined with water. But this recipe includes underglaze liquid added by weight, and that does confuse matters Since the instructions tell us to make a quart of CMC liquid, a logical starting point is to figure out the whole recipe based on using that full quart of CMC liquid in the underglaze liquid, adjusting all the other amounts proportionally. As explained below, by doing this we end up needing a little over 3000 grams of dry materials, and the recipe produces about a gallon and a half of underglaze base. Here’s how we figured that. Combining one quart of CMC liquid with two quarts of water and two quarts of non-toxic antifreeze as per the recipe gives five quarts of underglaze liquid. A quart of water weighs 946 grams. Multiply that times five (five quarts) to get 4730 grams of underglaze liquid. The recipe specifies 75 measuring units of underglaze liquid, and if we divide 4730 by 75 we get 63.07, rounded off to 63. Thus if we use the whole five quarts of underglaze liquid, in order to get the correct proportional amounts of dry materials we multiply each amount by 63, which gives a total dry materials weight of 3150 grams. Based on these calculations, our recipe is: F-4 spar ----------------- 20x63 = 1260 grams Kaolin -------------------- 10x63 = 630 grams Ball Clay ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams 3124 frit ------------------ 10x63 = 630 grams Zircopax ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams Total weight of dry materials -- 3150 grams Underglaze liquid ------ 75x63 = 4725 grams Total weight of batch ------------ 7875 grams Since 12,000 grams of dry glaze materials yields a full five-gallon bucket of glaze, we can extrapolate and estimate that since the dry materials weigh 3180 grams (including the CMC gum), this recipe should make about six quarts, which is a lot of underglaze base. If you want more or less underglaze base, just proportionally adjust the number of grams of everything, and adjust the quantity of CMC liquid and underglaze liquid that you prepare.

You can experiment with smaller amounts of cobalt too. 0.5-1% has worked well for some other potters who have tried this. I do not roast/calcine any of the Alberta Slip as Tony recommends - I find the glaze is fine without it and will only crack on drying if applied thickly - and even then, the cracks smooth out beautifully in my firings. If it is really thick, it will crawl, so be careful of that. I keep it at 1.45 SG and do a 2 second dip on Plainsman m390 and m350 clay. The glaze does settle quickly so make sure to stir it every few minutes. Calcining half the Alberta Slip does help the settling issues a little bit. I'm now able to get blue without cobalt so I'm using Tony's original recipe now, but adding cobalt was an excellent helper for me when I first started. This is a perfect replacement for Amaco Blue Rutile. - Stiina From the Alberta Slip Rutile description: "The original recipe can be found here: https://digitalfire.com/4sight/recipes/albertasliprutilebluecone631.html The article above suggests calcining part of the Alberta Slip, I have found that to be unnecessary. Description: This is one of a selection of straightforward recipes that use the same 5 base ingredients, to give an easy starting point to buying ingredients and mixing glazes: https://www.oldforgecreations.co.uk/blog/first-five-ingredients-where-to-start-with-glaze-making I cheated slightly here by including Zinc as an addition rather than in the base recipe, but it makes it easier to treat it as a variable. Adjusting the zinc between 5-10% should allow a degree of control over the number of microcrystals in the glaze. Crystalline glazes are a complicated mess of variables though. That said, if it's running too much and not forming crystals, try incrementally swapping the frit in the base for zinc. Name: OldForge FirstFive Oil Spot
Description: This is one of a selection of straightforward recipes that use the same 5 base ingredients, to give an easy starting point to buying ingredients and mixing glazes: https://www.oldforgecreations.co.uk/blog/first-five-ingredients-where-to-start-with-glaze-making Oil Spot glazes have a lot of Red Iron Oxide in them, which releases its oxygen as gas during the firing and causes the glaze to bubble up and mix. This is less obvious on its own, especially with a recipe like this that has less variation within the base glaze, but it becomes very obvious with a contrasting opaque cover glaze. The base will bubble up through it and produce spots. The Red Iron Oxide is also helping the glaze melt sufficiently and balancing out the fluxes, so this glaze requires it to work. Other colourants can be used in combination though, adding 1% Cobalt and/or 1% Chromium will give a black base. The Glossy Base with 10% Zirconium makes a good cover glaze.

Name: XD red
Description: I stumbled upon this in a biaxial two weeks ago. XD because of Xuande (William Chau set the tone of that line of inquiry) but it might as well have been YL (Yongle). I wasn't trying to replicate the chemistry but I am struck by the visual effect. Not as "eye popping" as a modern copper red but a wonderful satin/lower gloss surface with depth and interest, and definitely reminds me of visits to museums where I'd see Ming dynasty copper reds. ^8 - ^10 because the top of the kiln was less than ^9 (maybe 8.5) but the red still came out from there. The middle and bottom of the kiln were more than ^9. Trying to make it pinker by going to Mg was a fool's hope. Also, More alkaline is not better. Zinc seems to be needed, to an extent. Tin, 0.6-0.8 and no more. A bit of iron shifts the colour nicely. There's also a definite potential for a satin celadon here. Edit: William Chau points out that this is closest to the Qianlong red analysis as it appears in Nigel Wood's book on Chinese glazes.

Name: Speckled Fat Turquoise Matte
Description: passed down from Michael Bailey's Glazes Cone 6, base ASM1 (alumina Satin Matte). The original recipe contains 5% zinc oxide, and no lithium carb. Changes have been made by people over time. From my latest tests, it is an absolute favourite! Performed exactly as described. I tested at SG of 1.46, it was very thick, yet applied well. I fired on white, buff, red and dark brown mid-range stoneware clay bodies bisque fired to ^04. Specific gravity was 1:46 and the mixture was pretty thick but I did not deflocculate. I fired them to ^6 with a 15 minute hold on the controlled cool cycle. All four test tiles are just beautiful. Aqua, turquoise and teal variegation with white and brown flecks. Some hare's fur effects, especially on the dark clays, and breaking a lovely crystally copper rust on texture and edges. The surface has a lovely fat, silky texture (even over the rusty edges) with a metallic sheen. Though very expensive with 5% lithium carb. and 10% tin oxide , it's a keeper! Not meant for functional surfaces so suitable for decorative surfaces only. Might be better suited to ^8 firing, but works for me at ^6.

Recipe also informed by Taylor 1990: Mg expands Al/Si range for phase separation, P encourages separation, K suppresses phase separation. Sutherland: at higher temps, Juns should have Si:Al around 12:1. what should it be at lower temps? How much alkaline is too much? Fired with John Britt’s E3 schedule, fast fire to ^6, slow cool to 1400. The results overall have a nice almost metallic shine to the surface, likely because they’re undermelted, which I believe a Jun needs to be to maintain its opalescence? curious to see how much melt can be achieved while maintaining a Jun effect and the quality of this shiny surface. Macro crystals forming, not sure what that’s about, looks like possibly a Si-rich phase? Spot 11 has lowest Al and Si in the test.

Needs iron in the body or a slip for the blue. On white clay, it's pinkish. Also I don't get much blue when firing in oxidation - it is cream flecked with blue. Reduction (not too heavy) produces a strong blue. Too heavy redux, though and it goes a rich brown and blue. Is stable (no running) at cone 7. Huge 'pinholes' at cone 8. I do find it a bit hit and miss with so many variables that can affect getting the blue. NOTE: The gerstley borate makes it gel up when sitting and can make you think it has a higher specific gravity than it does in reality (thixatropic). (It thins down again when mixed.) Test the SG to be sure it's not too weak a glaze.

Name: Aubrey’s White Slip Base Cones 022-12
Atmospheres: Oxidation; Neutral; Reduction; Salt & Soda; Raku; Wood
Description: Originally based on a white slip base recipe in the book Ceramics: The Indispensable Guide by Duncan Hobson & Anthony Quinn (also published under the name The Workshop Guide to Ceramics) but with specific kaolin and ball clays, and using flint 325 mesh for silica, and the biggest change, using neph sye instead of a potash feldspar. Can add colorants using either metal oxides or stains, I prefer Mason stains from about 10-15% (sometimes more) to get bright enough colors. To make the base slip even more white add 2-5% Zirconium Silicate (I use Superpax), but that is rarely necessary, the ball clay used is extremely white and so is the kaolin and neph sye. This slip should work on all clay bodies from cones 06-12, but of course recommend testing beforehand. Mix dry ingredients with water to your preferred thickness, when about the thickness of regular (i.e. not Greek) yogurt it is thick enough for opaque coverage with one coat. I substituted EPK and Spinks Champion Ball Clay for the clays recently due to a supply chain issue with Grolleg and OM4 and and the Spink’s clay (my supplier just has Champion instead of C & C, Champion is one of the blend in the C & C, and I preferred it to the OM4, made the slip a lot whiter. EPK is ok but Grolleg is definitely whiter as well for the slip. It does go down to lower cones as it works well in raku, but I don’t know up past cone 12, I haven’t tested that myself since I don’t have access to firing that high yet so please write in the comments if you use it and it works at a different cone. I have not used it in wood, salt, or soda but do not see a reason why they wouldn’t work, as below I prefer my porcelain slips for soda- which is based on a similar recipe with the amounts of Grolleg and Champion Ball Clay reversed, as well as always 5% ferro frit 3124. It works great in raku, even down to about cone 014 or 015 and in pitfires and saggar firing which can range even lower so I have altered the cones, it actually goes a bit below cone 022 since many of the tinfoil saggers I have used only reach about 1000F or 1100F before disintegrating, I always bisque those pieces at cone 04 first with this slip on. It does well under most glazes including lowfire raku glazes and cone 6 or 8 mid/high fire glazes. Note that the neph sye deflocculates the slip a bit, which is preferred in a slip, so when I want it thicker, say for slip trailing, I use a little vinegar or a few drops of diluted Epsom salts solution in a small amount of slip, which work just as great as they do with glazes, maybe better, and if it starts to get too thick or dry out in a slip bulb just add a little water! Google “Stick up Slip” for an official version of how to make this into a very thick decorating or joining slip. I believe based on some recipes with similar ingredients but different ratios that this may be able to be used as a bisque slip with a thin application as is, but adding 5-10% of Ferro Frit 3124 or Borax definitely makes it workable on bone dry and bisque. If you have any issue with crawling or fit, or using it as a bisque slip, it can help to calcine about half the clay. Please leave a review if you have used it, it would help to know if anyone has had any issues or if it fires above cone 12 or in environments like wood or soda- I prefer to use my porcelain slip in general for awhile now, for colored slips, for white slips, and for soda which is just really white and creamy without the need for any Zircopax, and I use a new version with the ball clay in the porcelain clay replaced by Tile 6 kaolin in soda when I want more flashing and not just a very white creamy slip background or colored slip with very bright colors. This slip is excellent though as a cheaper but still very white slip compared to the porcelain slips.

Description: I want to plug Ceramic Material Workshop (https://www.ceramicmaterialsworkshop.com/). This was the first glaze I made by working backwards from the UMF. This black matte is a true matte. It has an R2O : RO ratio of 0.22 : 0.77. Not ideal but ok. Ca is the primary flux (0.42). The Si and Al levels are good with 2.32 Si and 0.49 Al. The Si:Al ratio is 4.75 making this a true matte. This is also reflected in the position of the glaze on Stull's map. Because it is a cone 6 glaze I wanted to be sure it has 0.15 boron for ideal melt and durability at cone 6, so it has 0.15 boron. Additionally, we have a Bristol reaction with the Zn and Ca. We know the glaze will be fully melted at cone 6. The glaze is well behaved, it does not run for me at all. The glaze is outside the crazed region of Stull and this has not crazed for me yet. I use a slow cool firing cycle, E4 in John Britt's Mid-Range book. But I don't expect this glaze to be impacted by firing cycle. This glaze does appear to have some phase separation going on. It looks like there is a mixture of more matte glass streaking through it. Very hard to photograph and I am just my phone :)

It produced the even, smooth, matte surface expected of a magnesium glaze, and breaks beautifully over texture. More matte than the satin described in the original recipe, due to the firing schedule. I used 6% stain instead of the 5% suggested in the original recipe to deepen the colour, and it is a lovely warm marine grey with subtle flecks that melt nicely into the body of the glaze which adds a streaky, textural depth. The test tile pictures were taken indoors with a cold winter light so they do not do them justice. A new favourite! I now want to try it with just 5% stain to see what a lighter grey would look like.

Name: "Normal" Hard Gloop with soda feldspar
Description: "Normal" Gloop. This is a demonstration of "gloop" at a more normal glaze chemistry with a fixed flux ratio of 0.25:0.75, boron level of 0.15, and Silica:Alumina ratio of 8.0. These tests were created using a line blend, moving from low to high Silica and Alumina. At the low end, the blends are proper glazes, while at the high end the blends act more like self-glazing clays. The middle blends can be classified as "gloops". This recipe is the the top of the line blend with highest Alumina and Silica levels. It's glossy, clay-like and self-glazing. Other tests from this blend: "Normal" Medium Gloop "Normal" Soft Gloop Note: I added Veegum T so that the gloop is more plastic and more easily molded in the wet stage. You could substitute Veegum with Bentonite, or you could just leave it out completely. I added some Mason Stain for color, you could also leave it out for a white gloop. Name: Bill Daley's "Tight" Cone 6 Clay Body
Description: This recipe was posted by Marcia Selsor, one of Bill's former students, in the Ceramic Arts Daily community. I'm not sure if Bill used this clay body exclusively throughout his career (see the section below -- David Wright clears this up); Maria mentioned he used this clay when firing in a brickyard conveyor kiln, but Bill also used an electric kiln in his home studio and might have modified his recipe(s) over time. While being interviewed on Tales of a Red Clay Rambler, Bill mentioned using porcelain grog in many of his pieces to achieve a terrazzo effect on the surface. Bill did not glaze his pieces; instead he spent hours refining the surface (pre and post firing) to achieve the right texture necessary to complement the form. The addition of Barium was likely to help halt the effects of efflorescene (when soluble salts migrate to the surface of the clay body during drying, causing an undesirable mottled look). Recipe Notes: Dissolve Barium in water Update David Wright wrote about developing Bill's clay body on his website, and his recipe uses a 300g batch with 10% grog and 1% Barium. This would mean that a 100g batch should use about 3% grog and .3% Barium. I have only done testing using Marcia Selsor's version, but can attest that even 7% grog felt like more than enough to make the body more workable while providing the terrazzo effect (which is really something, I must say!). I'll post David's words here for posterity, in case his site disappears one day: At the same time, my friend and teacher Bill Daley, was also in search of a red clay. Bill had already developed a red vitrified stoneware using PBX in 1973, as a result of a commission he had received from the Ritz Theater in Philadelphia. He was interested in matching the red brick structure, so he had to develop a red clay body that could withstand the elements, since it would be outdoors. Up to that point, Bill had been using a brown colored clay body that was fired in a reduction atmosphere. He found himself enjoying the new red clay color and also liked the consistency of oxidation firing. At the time, no one else was using a high temperature red stoneware, and it made Bill's pots even more distinctive and original. Unfortunately, as I mentioned before PBX had stopped being mined, so Bill along with many others, had to change his clay formula to something else. I began using the Neuman clay in 1993 and introduced Bill to it soon after. We did a lot of tests and shared our information, developing the D/W body listed below. Bill ultimately refined his own clay body using more Redart clay for greater vitrification and a darker color. DALEY'S BODY C6 This is Bill Daley"s current body based on our original D/W body, it is less red, but as tight as a drum at cone six oxidation. REDART 120 Neuman 80 Fireclay 60 Ball 40 Total 300% \+ Grog 10% \+ Bar. Carb. 1%

Description: New info You might want to check out this version of June Perry Red using Frit 3134 and stains, as its UMF is just slightly better than the traditional June Perry base recipe, moving it out on the Stull map from just slightly into potential crazing or underfired territory into glossy territory! https://glazy.org/recipes/83334 . I have not yet had a chance to compare that recipe using stains, using the traditional tin and chrome for red, and using copper for June Perry Aquamarine. While adding copper to glazes that craze quite often stops the crazing, and I haven’t heard any complaints about this recipe crazing so far, I know it can be a problem with the June Perry Red and June Perry Purple. It is possible that this recipe might in general make a slightly more durable glaze. But I don’t know yet if it affects the gorgeous turquoise color so I will hopefully be able to do some side by side tests with the new recipe, as well as pictures comparing this JP Aquamarine recipe with Grolleg and EPK. If I find that this new version of JP Red looks just as good with copper as the Gerstley Borate recipe, I will post a second version (unless one of you tests it and gets to it first, which is no skin off my nose!) - but if it doesn’t look good with the copper I will post the photos and not publish a second recipe. A variation of June Perry Red from John Britt’s The Complete Guide to Mid-Range Glazes, sub 1.3% black copper oxide instead of chromium, no tin. Get a beautiful, intense turquoise color, that is consistent and breaks on the rims or high points, usually breaks white or grey. Created by Karuna Douglas (first two photos are from her shared on Facebook, permission from her to post the recipe and use her pictures on Glazy after she asked me to post this recipe here as she does not wish to have a Glazy account at this time). It is unclear if Karuna uses Halloysite for kaolin in all her glazes including this one, or not, as she did not mention anything about a specific kaolin with this recipe but someone who is in this group thinks she may have mentioned using Halloysite in glazes in other posts, which I could not find, so if this doesn’t turn out the right color for you I would try using Halloysite in a small 100 g test batch and see if it makes a difference, or if you don’t have access to Halloysite whatever better quality, lower titanium porcelain kaolin you have access to, for me that would be Grolleg. Please comment and post pictures and please mention which kaolin you use, while I don’t have good pictures (really bad lighting) my first attempt using EPK was pretty close in color to these pictures, although I will post a picture when I have a chance to try the recipe with Grolleg to see if the kaolin makes much difference (I don’t have access to Halloysite, but with blue green colors it is usually having too much titanium in the clay that effects color more so than how much iron is in the kaolin). Please post pictures and comment just in general if you use this glaze! She specified that she didn’t use bentonite, so I didn’t put that in the recipe though it is in John Britt’s book with the June Perry Red, so use it if you want to, but there is plenty of clay and gerstley borate to keep this glaze in suspension without the bentonite.
