Name: Mason Color Works White Underglaze Base Recalculated Version
Atmospheres: Oxidation; Reduction; Neutral; Salt & Soda; Wood; Raku
Description: I was irritated by the original that was posted not adding up to 100, as many older recipes are and also some recalculations were done including an ingredient that should have been separate. So I simply recalculated the dry materials to 100 to make weighing out batches easier for myself, although did not double the amount of stain as the amount of stain will vary completely depending on the color of stain used and the brand. If I could I would have put 10-80 for the stain. Do not use antifreeze for this recipe, it is in Vince Pitelka’s original recipe if you look at the link for it, he developed it during a time when propylene glycol was harder to find on it’s own, now you can easily and cheaply buy food grade propylene glycol on the internet and at health food stores etc The amount of stain is not fixed at 40, I wish I could put in a range in the recipe. Like adjusting the amount of propylene glycol, every stain will need a different amount. Different brands, different colors, how intense or dark or light you want the color to be, it is possible if you do a line blend to get 20 or 30 or more different shades and even colors from one stain depending on how much you use. Test Test Test! Just like with glazes to test tiles and with stains for underglazes it is especially helpful to do line blends with different percentages of stains, you will be able to find the right amount to put in the recipe and also identify other shades you might want to use. And just to reiterate, do not under any circumstances use antifreeze. Propylene glycol is available (food safe) on Amazon and in health food stores and grocery stores, and it is more concentrated and much safer than antifreeze!!! For all of Vince Pitelka's Handouts, please visit: https://www.vincepitelka.com/handoutsinformation/ One very useful recipe on his website is for Mason Underglaze, which actually includes three recipes: CMC solution (great on its own as a glaze additive to slow drying and improve brushability), Underglaze Liquid (which can be used with any underglaze to greatly improve brushability), and finally the Mason Underglaze recipe itself. ## Mason Underglaze Recipe https://www.vincepitelka.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/Mason-Underglaze-Recipe.pdf This recipe for an opaque white underglaze base comes from the Mason Color Works of Liverpool, Ohio, manufacturers of Mason ceramic stains. It’s been in use for decades, and seems to give good results for underglaze brushwork. Like most commercial underglazes, it is not appropriate for trailing or other thick-application techniques. The underglaze has two parts, liquid and dry, and the liquid is also made up of a recipe within a recipe. #### Dry Materials See recipe below. You can batch it as little or as much as you want depending on how many different underglaze colors you plan on using. The stain amount is 0-40, most stains are added about 3% for dark colors and 10-15% for lighter colors or red, pink, and oranges. Determine what percent you need and calculate how much that would be in relation to the parts per 100 in the recipe x batch size and you will get how many grams you need to add Wait to add the stain after the dry recipe below has been mixed with the underglaze liquid. ####Add Underglaze Liquid -- 75 (think of it like adding water to dry mixes of glaze, some people just add 100 grams of water to 100 grams of dry glaze materials for every glaze when doing initial testing. Here, you are adding 75 parts to the 100 parts of dry materials, although it is recommended to start by adding 3/4 this amount first, see what the consistency is like, and decide if you need the full amount or even more to have a brushing consistency you like). ####To make the underglaze liquid, combine: Propylene glycol (food grade) ------ 2 parts (adjust for thickness you prefer) Water ----------------------- 2 parts CMC Liquid --------------- 1 parts To make CMC liquid, stir 30 grams of dry CMC in 1 quart or 1 liter hot water and let it sit for 2 days. Stir well before use. I add about 0.2% the weight of the CMC of copper carbonate to keep the CMC liquid from rotting and ruining the underglazes! This is a small enough amount that it will not flux the recipe nor change the color, and toxicology at this low of an amount is a nonissue. The CMC gum and propylene glycol in this mixture make it thicker and smoother than a slip containing only water, giving a smoother brushing consistency especially when applying underglaze to dry greenware or bisqueware. You will likely end up adjusting the amount of CMC and the amount of propylene glycol with the water in order to get the brushing consistency you prefer. ####When making this recipe: Dry-mix all the dry ingredients, add about 3/4 of the underglaze liquid and blend thoroughly, and then blend in more underglaze liquid a little at a time as needed until you achieve the desired brushing consistency. You may not need the full amount of underglaze liquid. After the dry ingredients and the underglaze liquid have been blended add the stain. Vary the amount of stain for a darker or lighter color, and of course if you add a significant amount of stain you will need to add additional water to adjust the consistency of the final mix.

Name: Bleeding Blue
Description: A rutile blue on top of a copper red. When applied thickly, you get a dark, intense blue with spots of red that "bleed" through. I've also considered naming this recipe "I-Can't-Believe-it's-not-Cobalt Blue". This glaze's color is pretty dependent on the firing pattern, and will probably look different if you try it. As a rule of thumb, decreasing the amount of barium used will turn this glaze into a pale rutile blue with no "bleeding" effect, and increasing the barium will turn it into a dark reddish-blue and eventually a dark copper red. Chromatically, there's a lot going on in this glaze. On the surface, there's a floating rutile blue, and underneath you have a copper red that makes this glaze darker and occasionally bleeds through. The tin in this glaze is not an opacifier, and is there to develop the copper red underneath--if you take out the copper but leave the tin, the whole thing turns an opaque white. As mentioned before, tweaking the barium is the easiest way to control the color. HCP's Erie Blue uses Strontium, and while this has the advantage of being safer to work with, Strontium seems to be runnier than Barium and doesn't create as intense blues with my school's firing schedule as Barium. And this variant looks closer to HCP's original pictures than when I tried using the original recipe? Revision of HCP's Erie Blue, using 6g Barium instead of the original's 6.6g Strontium.

Name: Coleman Space Dust
Description: This glaze is pretty much Coleman Tea Dust but I have adjusted down the silica and alumina to the frit limit. That is the lower limit where you cannot decrease silica and alumina anymore using potash feldspar and have to use a frit instead. The inspiration being Ben Owens work with Tea Dust glazes, e.g. https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/54dbcae7e4b0a4fe55c907d0/1425064435638-16PI3YZH1HQLSTJSUKU3/Teadust+Detail.jpg The relatively low viscosity of the glaze makes for larger and more isolated crystals. The key to getting the halos around the supposed pyroxene crystals is to incorporate a long cooling cycle. I am using the follow firing schedule: 220 C/h to 980 C 165 C/h to 1120 C 65 C/h to 1265 C hold 20 minutes drop to 1220 C hold 30 minutes 165 C/h to 950 C hold 30 minutes 165 C/h to 925 C hold 180 minutes 15 C/h to 890 C hold 60 minutes This somewhat complicated schedule is an adaptation of Carol Marians firing schedule, found here https://carol.knighten.org/2022-GlazeTests/2022-05-07-pursuit-of-tenmoku/ I am guessing, without any evidence, that a simpler schedule that holds 4-5 hours at 1700 F or 925 C would yield about the same results. If you were to fire the glaze in a more conventional cone 10 program you get the large isolated crystals but you don't get the halos around them. If you cannot get hold of Kalifältspat NGP you can try any other potash feldspar. For your convenience here is a chemical equivalent, being reasonably close to the original analysis, using Custer Feldspar: Custer Feldspar 38.19 Wollastonite 23.05 Silica 12.96 Red Iron Oxide 10.99 Talc 8.73 EP Kaolin 6.09 Note that I have omitted Bentonite since this version contains some plastic clay. The original version however have no such plastic clay and thus need some Bentonite to be at all workable. This version is lacking a bit of potassium but it should be fairly easy to get closer to my analysis using an on-line calculator such as: https://blobsallad.se/glazecalculator/solverwp.html or https://glaze.warewolves.ca/

Don't ask me to explain how it works, Kaolins formula are very very close and the granulometries are the same? Thickness seems to be important to get both colors not too thin not too thick, I fired it at cone 8-9 I am also puzzled by the color, using chrome at 1% (should be green) and cobalt 0.4% plus titanium at 6% (should be green again) why these colors appeared? I would have never tried this, thank you Serene for sharing this surprising recipe. There is still a lot to do with this new recipe, please share your experiences. Never forget "Prêt à l'emploi dans son seau, un émail n'est qu'un violon dans sa boite" Daniel de Montmollin.

Description: I just altered this floating blue and swapped out some materials. Wether you call it Substitutes or should I consider it a new recipe maybe ? Comment on opinions I ges. It’s nearly a new recipe This is all the info that came with it which I didn’t follow exactly But close. Was a medium fast fire up to cone 5 to 5.5 tho. Keep items away from hot spots because it will effect it and blemish the finish easily This glaze is brown or pond scum green when applied thinly so needs to be fairly thick. Will be a nice bright blue when the glaze thickness is correct and darker Blue on iron rick bodies. Also don't fire too hot, the included firing scheduled should get you to ^5.5 also works best with Specific Gravity of about 148. Setting viscosity with a Ford cup will save you countless hours of testing and this method will help you get the right thickness on the pot. Viscosity should be about 20-22 seconds using the Ford cup. This glaze works much better if dipped rather than poured. This is because a consistent thickness is a key to repeatable results along with not firing too hot. Start with a single dip of 5-7 seconds followed by a second dip on the top 1/4 to 1/3 of the form. Use cookies and test first because it may run onto shelves until you get it dialed in. Tony Hansen has a great article on using a Ford cup on his Digitalfire site. Here's the link https://digitalfire.com/glossary/viscosity Best to fire to cone 5 or 5.5 with a 15 min hold then drop 100 degrees for 45 minutes. See the firing schedule below. How to mix: Add about 78% water. This should bring you to a Specific Gravity of about 148.5 Check Specific Gravity - should be 148.5 or thereabouts. Glaze works best for me at 148 - 150. Check and Set Viscosity with a #4 Ford cup to about 20-22 seconds. Chances are you'll need to flocculate or deflocculate the glaze to get it to 20-22 seconds. This link will take you to an article by Pete Pinnell that does a great job of explaining how to get a glaze to a properly flocculated state. Give is a quick read, I'm sure you'll find it worthwhile. http://www.claytimes.com/articles/glazeadjusting.html You'll know you've got the right thickness when a 5-second dip gives you about 1mm or just less than the thickness of a dime. I got my Ford cup on Amazon, here is the link: https://www.amazon.com/TCP-Thickness-Viscosity-Measuring-Viscosimeter/dp/B00IL7DVNW/ref=sr11?dchild=1&keywords=Ford+%234+Cup&qid=1587238297&s=automotive&sr=1-1

Name: Li Floating Blue
Description: I liked the looks of Joe Thompson's (@oldforgecreations) "OldForge Floating Blue" (https://glazy.org/recipes/77013). It reminds me of Amaco Potter's Choice Sapphire Float, which is a commercial glaze I like. I'm just a hobby potter with a full-time job as a chemist, elsewhere; so when I had some time this weekend for some glaze trials, I wanted to try OldForge Floating Blue. I didn't have any SrCO3 (nor any SrO). I also don't have any whiting, but I ususally substitute wollastonite and adjust that quantity and the SiO2 quantity accordingly. I was not motivated enough to go to the local Clayworks supply store to purchase some SrCO3, either. However, I had some Li2CO3. I substituted one third the quantity of Old Forge's SrCO3 with LiCO3. I only had one afternoon for this, thus I did not set up an experimental design and mix differing quantities of Li2CO3 to evaluate effects of varying Li2CO3 content. So, I made an educated guess at one third the SrCO3 quantity as a SWAG trial, substituting Li2CO3. Procedure: I was a bit concerned about the partial solubility of the Li2CO3. Given I'm using 1% by mass of Li2CO3, a potentially significant amount of this strong flux would be in solution - the first dip of the tile would mean less percentage of that flux in the visible glaze matrix. To compensate for that concern, I glazed tiles with four, three, and two dips of glaze to compare. I glazed a fourth tile with two dips, then held the tile horizontally and poured the third layer of glaze over that tile to see what effect, if any, would result. I did not sieve this test batch. I added one milliliter of water (municipal tap water) for each gram of total dry solids. I did not measure the specific gravity. I blended with an immersion blender. The mix was a bit on the thick side; but given my concern about the partial solubility of Li2CO3, I did not want to use more water than necessary. Firing schedule: I fired with a slowed-down rate - 100°F/hr - of heating on both the upside and downside of the firing schedule between 1050°F and 1150°F to mitigate quartz inversion expansion/contraction. I fired to 2100°F, then slowed down to a rate of 108°F/hr up to cone 6 (2232°F) with no hold, dropped 100°F and held for 10 minutes. Conclusions: Based on the results (please see posted pictures), I do not see a significant difference between three and four dips other than the expected muted texture of the tile. The tiles with three and four dips demonstrate an attractive phase separation effect. One can also observe the lack of sieving but to me, it's an interesting look. Two dips was satisfactory. I do not notice as obvious a phase separation effect, without magnification, as I see with more dips, but the glaze flowed nicely, pooling at texture. Upon magnification, one can observe the phase separation in the tile with two dips; thus my concern about the partial solubility of Li2CO3 was not an issue with this formulation. The tile with two dips and an orthogonal pour over the two dips suggests one can affect the the look of the 'float' by varying application direction. I will be using this glaze again. I tried some layering, but I only observed a sliver of the base glaze because I dipped a bit deep for this top layer. Next time I try layering this glaze on top, I'll not dip it so deeply. I did not post pictures of the tiles with layering as I am not pleased with the trials of the base glazes I used. But, the Li Floating Blue layer was pleasing. Changed status back to testing - doing acid and base tests because of possible durability issues

Name: Selva / Jungle
Description: •Spanish (English version below) El libro de Daniel de Montmollin, " Pratique des émaux de grès", edición 2020, me resulta algo desconcertante, ya que pone la sílice en el axis vertical y la alúmina en el horizontal. Una tontería de mi parte, pero estoy acostumbrada a que sea al revés. El libro en sí es una joya para descubrir con atención y dedicación. Hacia el final hay un pequeño apéndice de Patrick Buté a respecto de esmaltes "bleus de fer" (azules de hierro) con ejemplos de fórmulas molares y muestras basadas en el diagrama 25 (R2O:RO = 0.30:0.70). Elegí uno de ellos y le agregué boro suficiente para cono 6. Una vez calculado, veo que está muy cercano, químicamente, de varios otras recetas basadas en el Bleu de Fer de Jean -Pierre Prieto. Mis resultados son... ponele que "prometen"... a futuro. Por ahora es verdoso con ciertos dejos azules, amarillentos y marrones. Como la luz cayendo sobre el follaje... Consejo de aplicación: carga muuuuy gruesa desarrolla las diferentes tonalidades. Con carga apenas gruesa un marrón común, sin demasiado interés (probar primero sobre teselas) A seguir.... Tal cual sugiere Marina V. Kurtz entre los comentarios, probaré agregar más sodio, cambiar la frita.... • English Daniel de Montmollin's book, "Pratique des émaux de grès", 2020 edition, is somewhat disconcerting to me, since Silica is on the vertical axis and Alumina on the horizontal one. Not a real problem, but I'm used to the other way. The book itself is a jewel to discover with care and dedication. Towards the end there is a small appendix by Patrick Buté regarding "Bleus de Fer" (iron blue) glazes with different molar formulas and samples based on diagram 25 (R2O:RO = 0.30:0.70). I chose one of them and added enough boron to fire it at cone 6/7. Once calculated, I see that it is very close, chemically, to several other recipes based on Jean-Pierre Prieto's Bleu de Fer. My results are... "promising"... in the future. My test tile is greenish with blue, yellowish and brown hints. Like the light falling through the jungle... Note that the glaze must be veeeeeeeery thick to show the different color shades. With a barely thick load, a common brown, without much interest (try first on tiles) To follow.... As Marina V. Kurtz suggests in the comments, I'll try adding more sodium, changing the frit to get, maybe, a "Bleu de Fer"

Name: Tom Turner Oxblood for cone 7
Description: The silicon carbide needs to be as fine as possible - at least 800 grit, which is what I used. In order for this carbide reduction to work, you must follow this firing program: Stage 1. 240c per hour to 940c - hold 1 hour Stage 2. 240c per hour to 1240 - hold 10 minutes This will bring the glaze to a hot Δ7. Most Δ6 clay bodies will have no problem getting that hot, but always test if you are not sure. Strike firing: firing this glaze again at Δ014 can bring out more red from the thinner spots, which I have done with my test tiles. Here is some of Tom Turner's research, including the Δ9 firing schedule that he uses: https://tomturnerporcelain.glazy.org/downloads/CopperRed35DE.pdf

Description: • Promedio de 7 bases mates probadas en noviembre 2022: 250256, 250312, 258634, 255130, 257252, 269156, 271336 Parece una buena base para tener en cuenta, con algunos cambios. El pequeño porcentaje de zinc le otorga cierta elasticidad que impide los casos severos de saltado presente en varias otras bases mates. Suelo colocar demasiada carga en mis teselas de muestra, lo cual destaca tanto lo negativo de estos esmaltes (saltado, burbujas, etc...) como ciertos hermosos efectos imposibles de ver con una carga "juiciosa" (colores diferentes, cristales de superficie, oilspot, separación de fases...) Test ácido: luego de 3 días parcialmente sumergidos en vinagre, tan sólo la muestra 321 muestra un leve cambio de coloración. En el resto de las teselas no se aprecian cambios de colr o textura. • Average of 7 matte bases tested in November 2022: 250256, 250312, 258634, 255130, 257252, 269156, 271336. It looks like a good base to consider, with a few changes. The small percentage of zinc gives it a certain elasticity that prevents the shivering present in many other matte glazes. I tend to apply the glazes too thick over my test tiles, which highlights both the downsides of these glazes (shivering, bubbles, etc...) and some beautiful effects impossible to see with a "judicious" thickness (different colors, surface crystals, oilspot, phase separation...) Acidic test: after 3 days partially submerged in vinegar, only tile 321 shows a slight change in color. The rest passed the test without any visible change.

I imagine it would be much whiter (slightly creamy white) and may not have the blue tint from the titanium+iron Test Update (Dec 19 2023): I mixed a confirmation batch to make sure the glaze works reliably from the recipe and I didn't get the same result! It is still nice but not what I wanted, dang it. LATER EDIT to the above edit - I am pretty sure that I added a little more (3%?) frit 3134 to my first batch and forgot to make a note of it. Hence the difference with the confirmation batch (less flowing). If interested in trying this glaze, I would try it as listed below and with the extra frit to see what works for you.

Name: Hamish's Yellow
Description: This glaze has a lovely silky satiny feel. It is a solid reliable yellow glaze that does not run unless very thick. It requires salt or soda to go yellow although does not need much. I have fired this glaze in the middle of the kiln where very little soda hit it to good effect. When it gets a lot of soda those areas go a typical white/grey/blueish tone. You can clearly see this one one of the side handles teapots in the pictures here. You can substitute any other granite of feldspar or neph sye for the Devil's Playground Granite I use from Western Utah. The bone ash is not strictly necessary but terns the flecks in the glaze redder as opposed to brown (makes the glaze warmer). I have also had good results with only using 5% bone ash. You can also use 10% zircopax rather than 15% if you like (I find the zircopax helps make the glaze solid and not run). Very similar results in terms of color. When this glaze is thin it goes more towards reddish brown: see the underside of one of the teapot lids pictured here. This yellow glaze will be warmer buttery color if you reduce the kiln and a paler more canary like yellow if you oxidise it. Excess of soda also makes the color a bit brighter/paler/whiter. You can also adapt the color of this glaze by adding iron and/or rutile. I have some examples of test tiles doing this on my blog here: https://www.hamishjacksonpottery.com/blog/2022/10/18/devils-playground-granite-glaze-tests-round-4-pictures-and-notes Slow cooling the kiln will make this glaze even more silky, satiny and buttery feeling. Any questions don't hesitate to reach out to me. I love talking about glazes! You can email me through my website: https://www.hamishjacksonpottery.com/ Or send me a message on instagram: @hamish.jackson.pottery

In my tests it works well at ∆10. - This glaze developed a glossy surface when allowed to cool naturally in my little test kiln. That firing plummeted from a peak temperature of 2350°F to 1584°F (1250°C to 860°C) in just an hour. Be advised, that is too fast for this glaze! Then again, that's probably too fast for almost any glaze. - When given more time, the glaze develops a lovely smooth matte texture. I've seen nice matte surfaces: - When naturally cooled in the large gas-fired fiber kiln during a ∆10 firing with heavy reduction at The Potter's Studio in Berkeley, CA, which took 12 hours to fall from peak temperature to 800°F. - In my small electric test kiln fired to ∆10 oxidation, with a 7hr controlled cool from 2350°F down to 1650°F.

Description: Slip Colors from Ceramic Oxides Tan/Gray - - - - - - - - - - 5% Rutile Light Green - - - - - - - - 1% Chrome Oxide Medium Green - - - - - - 4% Chrome Oxide Dark Green - - - - - - - - - 7% Chrome Oxide Light Blue-Green - - - - - 1% Chrome Oxide, 1/2% Cobalt Carbonate Dark Blue-Green - - - - - 4% Chrome Oxide, 3% Cobalt Carbonate Sky-Blue - - - - - - - - - - 1/2% Cobalt Carbonate Medium Blue - - - - - - - - 2% Cobalt Carbonate Dark Blue - - - - - - - - - - 5% Cobalt Carbonate Light Brown - - - - - - - - 3% Red Iron Oxide Medium Brown - - - - - - 6% Red Iron Oxide Dark Brown - - - - - - - - 9% Red Iron Oxide Black - - - - - - - - - - - - - 8% Red Iron Oxide, 5% Manganese Dioxide, 5% Cobalt Carbonate Saturated Iron - - - - - - 25% Red Iron Oxide (thin applications only – see below) The saturated iron slip is specifically intended for thin applications on greenware where you want the iron color to come through the glaze. A good example is on white shinos, where this iron slip will come through and create a red-brown or brown color. Also, when you want to achieve brush-painted iron brown marks or banding on any glaze, you are often better off doing the brushwork with the saturated iron slip on greenware rather than with an iron oxide patina over the raw glaze coating. When painted underglaze on bisqueware, brushed iron oxide can cause serious glaze crawling. Overglaze, the fresh iron marks are so easily smeared before firing. Using the saturated iron slip on greenware eliminates both problems

Description: Marc's Clear with only 18% Silica, + 2% additional Ferro Frit 3134, +2% bentonite, +40 g of (30g/liter CMC gum solution) in 300g batch Fired at cone 6 with a slow cool I am trying to find a cone 6 oxidation clear to replace Amaco HF-9. HF-9 is a fantastic clear, but it has gotten very expensive, and isn't always available. We use clear brushed over Lois' illustrations on Standard Clay 112. Her illustrations are done with Mason stain colored slips and mason stain colored underglazes. Many of the clears I have tried, although well behaved, are too cloudy even when thinly brushed. This adapted version of Marc's clear is the closest to being right. It seems that very fine bubbles are possibly causing the difference in clarity. When viewed with a 20x loupe, there is no other noticeable difference. The test tiles are from the same batch bisqued at cone 06, our standard bisque temp. Does anyone have any suggestions on how to get rid of these tiny bubbles? Or is there anything in this recipe that might be working as an opacifier? The recipe was well mixed and used 2 days after it was made, mixing well before any application. I cannot bisque hotter, as that would effect other parts of the illustration process, and the HF9 works fine on this bisque. I am considering upping the Boron level by increasing the percentage of Ferro Frit 3134 in the next version. This version does not run, so I think I can make it more fluid without causing problems. thanks

Name: Bertie Ash Glaze
Description: This is a recipe adapted from Bailey's Red, as found in High Fire Glazes by John Britt. Recently my dog had to be put down very suddenly. He was an incredibly important animal for me and my family and to honour his memory and to have a way to more permanently memorialise him, I decided to develop a glaze using his cremated remains. Both human and animal ashes are predominantly calcium phosphate. this is commercially available as bone ash - cremated and finely ground cow bones, and is most commonly used to make bone china. Through my research I discovered that Persimmon/Kaki/Tomato reds traditionally use bone ash in combination with lithium carbonate in high iron glazes to facilitate iron crystallisation during the cooling process. These can give russet to bright red, and suited my desire to find a glaze close in colour to Bertie. I ground his ashes in a pestle and mortar to 200 mesh and replaced the bone ash in the Bailey's Red recipe with this. The result from cone 10 reduction (R1) is a glossy, russet glaze with bright red crystals dispersed with light gold flecking. In oxidation the glaze is darker, much more russet with some light red flecking - not what I was aiming for personally but still perfectly valid.

Description: My 5th revision on a silicon carbide red that started from Tony Hansen's G3806E. Color is similar to V4.1. The base is fluid enough for reds yet has high viscosity and surface tension from high MgO, which I think is the key for a good copper red that doesn't run. This has a moderate expansion, but sometimes crazes on frost^6. Thick application or applying on sharp contours will likely see crawling. Credits to William Chau's posts on copper reds and Tony Hansen's documentation on fluid bases with his G3806 line. Random thoughts: This approximate UMF seems to be approaching the limit on being able to lower it's expansion while keeping it fluid without serious change. More MgO will likely push it to being matte, although if it's fritted it could possibly be pushed more. Alumina and Silica likely can't be pushed too much further without increasing the boron to keep fluidity, but excessive boron negatively affects the color from my testing. Dropping KNaO some more could be worth looking into. Next steps are to look into higher boron bases, with the next test at 0.3 molar as 0.6 was a failure once colorant was added. Changes that were made from V4.1: tin reduced slightly, silica increased slightly, and KNaO lowered, Changes made to the original G3806E base: lithium removed for cost, added some neph sye, and moved more MgO to frit 3249 Silicon carbide mesh is 1000

The idea is to allow the clay particles to fully hydrate and then add the next smaller particles and finally the larger particles, so clay will be fully moist when bagged. Mixed on the wet side for a years use (at least that is the idea). possible issues- bentonite low quantity and switched XX Sagger to OM4 from #27 recipe. Deleted 1% talc too, since I'm out and cannot buy Texas talk any longer. Lack of red color my be due to heavy reduction at end of firing which changes RIO to a brown form. Also, kiln cooled quickly due to use of metal dampers. Titania is 3 times as high as #30 flashing body, so this may cause lack of red color as well. Not sure, but I think firing is most likely culprit.

Some posts I did about my development of the glaze: - the base glaze - using different stains It's important to include the zircopax when using stain or you'll get no or barely any colour. I have been mostly testing with orange stains, as requested by the glaze's namesake. I tested with - Chrysanthos Ultra Orange - Potters Intense Orange from Walkers Ceramics - Pottery Supplies Orange - Potters Red and Yellow from Walkers Ceramics mixed together The first 2 give a strong colour with 3 stain, and could be dialed back to 1 or 1.5 for a pastel colour. The other 2 combo needs about 7 even with the zircopax to give an equivalent colour, but the softer shades can be nice. The examples here with the red/yellow combo all have less than the recommended amount of zirocpax, but are about the same as the Pottery Supplies stain when it is included.

Name: Aubergine Purple
Description: Why aren't there more manganese purple glazes on glazy? They seem to be really simple to make if you follow these rules: 1) minimize boron and possibly magnesium (turns Manganese brown) 2) Keep sodium, potassium, and lithium in high amounts. 3) Barium, strontium, and calcium helps. R20 > 3, RO < 7. 4) Cobalt oxide must be present. The minimum seems to be just under 0.2% 5) Oxidation only. During a raku experiment, a reduced glaze went brown. 6) Sources disagree, but I found that keeping manganese at/under 3% helps. At low-fire temperatures, you can increase manganese to at least 4%.

Name: Mason Color Works White Underglaze Base (SBR)
Description: One of the most useful and reliable sources both then and now is Vince Pitelka's website. There he shares his knowledge on all aspects of the studio, from making your own tools to loading & firing kilns. For all of Vince Pitelka's Handouts, please visit: https://www.vincepitelka.com/handoutsinformation/ One very useful recipe on his website is for Mason Underglaze, which actually includes three recipes: CMC solution (great on its own as a glaze additive to slow drying and improve brushability), Underglaze Liquid (which can be used with any underglaze to greatly improve brushability), and finally the Mason Underglaze recipe itself. If you do any underglaze decoration, even just to sign your name, One note: I used 100% Pure Vegetable Glycerin in place of the food grade anti-freeze which may contain other additives. ## Mason Underglaze Recipe https://www.vincepitelka.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/Mason-Underglaze-Recipe.pdf This recipe for an opaque white underglaze base comes from the Mason Color Works of Liverpool, Ohio, manufacturers of Mason ceramic stains. It’s been in use for decades, and seems to give good results for underglaze brushwork. Like most commercial underglazes, it is not appropriate for trailing or other thick-application techniques. #### Dry Materials F-4 Soda Spar -------------- 20 Kaolin ----------------------- 10 Ball Clay --------------------- 5 3124 Frit ---------------------10 Zircopax --------------------- 5 (or any other zircon opacifier) Total Dry Materials ------- 50 Add Underglaze Liquid -- 75 For colors other than white, add: Ceramic stain -------------- 40 Add the stain after everything else is combined, including the underglaze liquid. Vary the amount of stain for a darker or lighter color, and of course if you add a significant amount of stain you will need to add additional water to adjust the consistency of the final mix. To make the underglaze liquid, combine: Food Grade Glycerin ------ 2 parts. I used food grade glycerin Water ----------------------- 2 parts CMC Liquid ------- -------- 1 parts To make CMC liquid, stir 30 grams of dry CMC in 1 qt. hot water and let it sit for 2 days. The CMC gum and food grade glycerin in this mixture make it thicker and smoother than a slip containing only water, giving a smoother brushing consistency especially when applying underglaze to dry greenware or bisqueware. When making this recipe: Dry-mix all the dry ingredients, add about 3/4 of the underglaze liquid and blend thoroughly, and then blend in more underglaze liquid a little at a time as needed until you achieve the desired brushing consistency. You may not need the full amount of underglaze liquid. Clarification This recipe can be a bit confusing. When a recipe just provides numbers without specifying the weighing increments, the increments can be whatever you wish – grams, ounces, pounds, etc. For the sake of accuracy when mixing glazes or slips, we generally use grams. With any recipe, there is always the question of what factor to multiply the base recipe by in order to get a certain amount of final product. For example, glaze recipes are almost always given in a form where the dry raw materials for the glaze base add up to 100, plus the modifiers, colorants, etc. In a recipe that contains only dry materials, we know from experience that a batch of 12,000 grams of dry material will fill a five-gallon bucket to the rim once combined with water. But this recipe includes underglaze liquid added by weight, and that does confuse matters Since the instructions tell us to make a quart of CMC liquid, a logical starting point is to figure out the whole recipe based on using that full quart of CMC liquid in the underglaze liquid, adjusting all the other amounts proportionally. As explained below, by doing this we end up needing a little over 3000 grams of dry materials, and the recipe produces about a gallon and a half of underglaze base. Here’s how we figured that. Combining one quart of CMC liquid with two quarts of water and two quarts of non-toxic antifreeze as per the recipe gives five quarts of underglaze liquid. A quart of water weighs 946 grams. Multiply that times five (five quarts) to get 4730 grams of underglaze liquid. The recipe specifies 75 measuring units of underglaze liquid, and if we divide 4730 by 75 we get 63.07, rounded off to 63. Thus if we use the whole five quarts of underglaze liquid, in order to get the correct proportional amounts of dry materials we multiply each amount by 63, which gives a total dry materials weight of 3150 grams. Based on these calculations, our recipe is: F-4 spar ----------------- 20x63 = 1260 grams Kaolin -------------------- 10x63 = 630 grams Ball Clay ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams 3124 frit ------------------ 10x63 = 630 grams Zircopax ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams Total weight of dry materials -- 3150 grams Underglaze liquid ------ 75x63 = 4725 grams Total weight of batch ------------ 7875 grams Since 12,000 grams of dry glaze materials yields a full five-gallon bucket of glaze, we can extrapolate and estimate that since the dry materials weigh 3180 grams (including the CMC gum), this recipe should make about six quarts, which is a lot of underglaze base. If you want more or less underglaze base, just proportionally adjust the number of grams of everything, and adjust the quantity of CMC liquid and underglaze liquid that you prepare.

Description: I dip for 10 seconds, on the outside and 5 on the inside (for a little extra variation) for this cup. 130% water is a lot… but I like time to think about the dip, I find it easier to be consistent with the dips, and I find it easier to mix, sieve and remix the slurry. Name: Titanium dioxide in crater glazes (mini study)
Description: The base recipe is the Volcanic dolomite recipe from Linda Bloomfield’s “Special Effects Glazes” book. I wanted to run a little study on the effect of titanium dioxide on crater glazes as the theory is that it helps with increasing the size of the craters. This glaze without titanium is slightly under-fired at cone 6 with a 20min hold (some of the bubbles don't pop), so my thesis was that adding titanium may help the process. This is a simple line test: I added 2% to each test tile so that the first test tile has 2% titanium, the next has 4%, the next has 6%, and so on. The highest amount was 12% in total. This is a preliminary finding - more research should be done - but it does seem like titanium dioxide helps with the crater development. Since it's also an opacifier, it also gives an interesting color effect. Let me know if you do more experiments!

Description: See also 446307 A modification of the recipe in 'Glazes for Australian Potters'. The original #53 contained no Magnesium Carbonate and increased Frit 3134 (60%) Most test tile samples were at about 1.3 sg, but it was not very fluid, so the glaze was applied (dipped) more thickly than probably desirable. Probably should use sg 1.4 to 1.5 and deflocculate to increase fluidity. Approx. mass/sq cm of applied wet gaze is listed for some of the test tiles. Notes from others: Cone 01 – 8 Oxidisation modified version See notes: https://www.australianceramics.com/2016/07/26/surface-therapy-3-glazes-for-functional-ware Tin oxide– 10 parts, has a whitening effect. Nice on terra cotta (cone 01 – 5/6) delivers a smooth opaque glaze, breaking to tan where applied thinly Original recipe does not have magnesium carbonate. Can be fired to cone 8, producing a higher gloss and slightly pearly whiteness. Sometime blistering can occur.at cone 8 1 part RIO makes the glaze a cream colour, but with a tan break on the edges. This break is due to the magnesium carbonate which is also responsible for crawling if the glaze is applied too thickly at the lower temp. Useful colourants: copper (light green) 1-3parts; chrome (green) 0.2-1 part; cobalt (dark blues) 1-3 parts.

The thinner you apply the glaze, the less bubbles will be visible. I would recommend to use it on clay bodies without grog so 1 coat is sufficient to make a smooth surface but it will still turn out good with more coats. This recipe was the result of a research project focused on optimizing clarity and minimizing bubbles in a mid range glaze for use on red and white clay. Of the hundreds of test tiles that I made researching existing recipes and testing modifications, this was the best one. It still has some more room for improvement but I'm at a standstill with my current understanding of glaze chemistry. If you use this glaze PLEASE SHARE PICTURES! I would love to see how people use it and If you have any comments or suggestions about the recipe as well, please let me know. I'm always wanting to learn more.

Name: Southern Song Dynasty Celadon - Longquan Glazes II
Description: Taken from Nigel Wood's Chinese Glazes Chemical analysis found on Table 27 in Chapter 4, Page 78 Converted recipe can be found on page 269 I used Mahavir Potash Feldspar and English China Clay/Grolleg without changing the proportions. Very nice, icy blue typical of Song Dynasty Celadons, especially when thick. Cooler firings yield an icy blue, with slight opacity when thick and no movement. Medium heat firings yield the same bright icy blue as cooler firings, but with more visible microbubbles and more translucency even where thick. Hotter firings result in a slightly darkened gray-blue with high translucence even when thick, and more visibility of variations in thickness. Poor reduction results in a transparent gray glaze with yellow undertones. Push through 100-Mesh sieve while mixing to prevent iron speckling.
Ingredients: Potash Feldspar 34.5; Silica 30; Kaolin 18; Whiting 15; Red Iron Oxide 0.5; Bone Ash 0.3

Name: Northern Song Dynasty Celadon - Longquan Glazes II

I used Mahavir Potash and English Grolleg specifically, without changing any proportions. The Manganese Dioxide is 325 mesh. Color came to be a very nice jade green, typical of classic Chinese Celadons. Poor reduction results in a transparent yellowish glaze. Cooler firing yields a bright satin-finish green with tiny bubbles, and occasionally, light brown flecks. No movement or variation. Medium firing yields a more true, classic celadon green with tiny suspended bubbles and a semi-glossy, waxy 'fat' surface. Very slight movement/variation. Hotter firings result in a deeper gray-green with visible microbubbles and a glassier appearance. Sometimes moves slightly, and inconsistencies in thickness may become more apparent. Push through 100-Mesh sieve while mixing to prevent iron speckling. Underglaze comes out nice and crisp from what I've seen. Tests done on Coleman Porcelain from Aardvark Clay Co.

Name: Jingdezhen Peach Bloom Copper-Lime Pigment c. 1956
Description: This is not a glaze in itself, but rather a pigment used in tandem with a clear glaze. This recipe was found in Nigel Wood's Chinese Glazes book on page 183 (Chemical analysis). The table on this page is labeled Table 73, but the actual recipe on page 271 is labeled as Table 74. As the title suggests, this was used in Jingdezhen potteries as of 1956. It's absolutely beautiful but requires good reduction to get the ripening peach-like red or pink blushing with green splotches. I apply this glaze the way the book outlines how the Chinese potters applied it. They sprayed a clear coat onto a piece, followed by a sprayed coat of the pigment, and topped off with a second spray application of clear, sandwiching the pigment. Any stable clear glaze should work. I've tried Simon's Clear and G1947U Digitalfire Clear with good results from both. Thicker application leads to more concentration of green, becoming metallic after a certain point. Poor reduction/oxidation yields a variegated dark green glaze with streaks of golden yellow. The potash used in my tests is Mahavir.

Name: Jingdezhen Copper-Lime Underglaze Pigment c. 1882
Description: 5/23/25 - I was rereading the background information on this recipe and found I had erroneously labeled it as a Peach Bloom pigment. This is actually listed in Nigel Wood's Chinese Glazes book as a copper-lime pigment for Chinese underglaze reds. However, it is somewhat similar to the pigment used for the Peach Bloom effect, and as you can see, yields similar real world results. Below is the amended information as of this update. This recipe is the 2nd of the two copper-lime pigments on page 183, Table 73 of Nigel Wood's Chinese Glazes has the chemical analysis, while page 271, Table 74 has the converted recipe with modern materials. As the title states, this was used in Jingdezhen porcelain workshops up until at least 1882, to achieve underglaze copper reds. Requires good reduction and seems to like hotter parts of the kiln. Results in a beautiful deep blush red with streams of green and gold, resembling the authentic Chinese examples. Poor reduction/oxidation results in a deep green glaze with streams of gold. Runs a bit and becomes very metallic if applied too thick. Too thin of an application will cause fading from the small amounts of copper volatizing off the piece. I used Mahavir Potash without changing any proportions

It seems to break blue instead of the classic white over sharp contours, however this may be due to uneven reduction of the copper than a feature of the glaze itself. Name: Hindle's Lithium Alkali 1
Description: This is one of a series of glaze bases I formulated to have high amounts of alkali fluxes: lithium, sodium, and/or potassium. This particular one is high in lithium. This particular base glaze brings out some stunning colors especially with copper, chrome, and cobalt, but unfortunately often comes with glaze defects. There are two issues: 1) The glaze chips off of rims and edges of any larger pieces I've tried to use it on. It seems like shivering, but I'm kind of surprised that a glaze could both shiver and craze. 2) With the addition of copper carbonate, the glaze is getting some nasty bubbles on the exterior walls of my pieces. I assume this may be because of overfiring and/or because of the high levels of lithium carbonate, but I'm not sure why it would only be an issue when I add copper and not an issue when I add something like chrome. Anyone have tips on how to tweak the formula to minimize defects without losing the color response? My first thought is that I could increase potassium and sodium levels while decreasing lithium. I included photos of both defects. Let me know what you think!

Name: Pinnell Strontium Matte with colorants
Description: Original base recipe was from John Britt's Midrange Glazes, with 5% TiO2 included. Mixed to S.G. =1.45 it can be sprayed or applied by pouring or dipping. On Highwater's Hestia body and fired in electric kiln to Cone 6, the base glaze was a matte white with shades of VERY pale pink. On Standard 240, it is a plain white with crystals. ### Spray Trials A small test pot was glazed with the basic mix using spraying rather than dipping, then fired to Cone 6. In spray application tests it behaved very nicely. It makes a smooth (if fragile) glaze coat. Additional layers adhered to each other well even when the underlayer had dried. Feathering and overlapping were easy to do with spraying. Note added 6/13/25: The main challenge when spraying is to make sure to build up a sufficiently thick coat to match what would be applied by dipping. PSM behaves differently when sprayed too thinly. A thin coat of spray is not going to give the same effect as a longer dipped coat. Example 1: Antique bronze when sprayed as a thin coat and fired c7R did not form the same smooth dark bronze as the dipped sample. Instead it went nearly black, and did not form a smooth surface. Example 2: a thin sprayed base layer in c7R still formed the stony pale gray base, but lightly oversprayed accents of 5% RIO did not form the red and black markings of a dipped test tile. Need a much thicker coat to get that effect. Only got a slight amount of darkening of base layer. Attractive still, but not as dramatic as expected. ### Reduction Firing This glaze works well in reduction but I have not tested it as thoroughly. Check photos for the subset of reduction tests I have done so far. ### Color Trials Colorants were added to small test batches of 50mL or 100mL each. Colorant test tiles were dipped for 3, 5, or 15 sec. in glaze then fired to electric Cone 6. I have not tested it but I expect you can eliminate the TiO2 and get a more semi-clear base that will not dilute out cobalt-based stains or oxides. Summer 2024 Trials What I found to be good choices on Hestia in Cone 6 oxidation: 1. 0.5% cobalt carbonate (matte medium blue) 2. 5% copper carbonate (copper patina with limited texture) 3. 8% rutile (a matte cream or buff forming a very smooth visual surface) 4. 8% rutile + 5% copper carbonate. This is a VERY nice mix of patina and texture; this is the classic antique bronze combination). In c7 reduction, it is darker but still VERY nice mix of antique bronze with blackish-green. 5. 1% Mason Canary Yellow is a textured neutral gray. 5% in oxidation is textured yellow-green. 7. 5% red iron oxide. In oxidation it is a textured reddish earth brown. A great combo of color and visual texture. In c7 REDUCTION develops metallic purples with speckles of brick red; a great combo of color and visual texture. These were less appealing combinations (but might be what someone else needs/wants): 1. 1% cobalt carbonate (too dark and flat blue) 2. 8% rutile + 1% copper carbonate (a flat, texture-free pale olive green) 3. 1% Mason Black 6600 (turned more blue to dark gray than black) 4. 5% Mason Black 6600 (a very flat matte blue-black) 5. 1% red iron oxide (turned gray, with less texture than 1% yellow Mason stain) March 2025 Trials Test in Cone 6 reduction, 10-30 second dips on Zam Superbody: PSM only - very nice stony white and gray PSM antique bronze - even darker but still nice PSM + 5% red iron oxide - speckled purple black and iron red August 2025 Trials Completed a 20-colorant, 2-level glaze trial comparing a larger number of colorants, and comparing Hestia and Standard 240/Stella clay bodies. At c6 oxidation, colorants and slips that worked well were: Italian umber, red ochre, yellow ochre, rutile Copper carbonate, red iron oxide, cobalt carbonate, chromium oxide, titanium dioxide, nickel oxide, Mason black What did not work well: Ravenscrag slip, crocus martis, French umber, Italian umber, French burnt umber, Alberta slip, Mason yellow, Zircopax, zinc oxide, manganese dioxide. ### Production Glazing Notes 2025 1. PSM+ 1.5% chromium oxide did not form a variegated surface like the test tile. Was smooth green-black instead. Color and finish both are nice, but no texture. May be due to a contaminated batch of chromium oxide used for test tile mixes. DO NOT use in a shared kiln; chromium volatilizes and stains nearby pieces. 2. PSM+3% nickel oxide worked very nicely on a larger production pot. Mix of burnt umber yellow-brown with metallic flecks. 3. PSM base overlaid with a mix of 2.5% TiO2 and 5% rutile did not show much color, and bubbled badly. Seems PSM does not like to be overlaid, and should be dipped or sprayed. 4. PSM antique bronze (copper + rutile) turns dark black-green where application is thin, and verdigris green in thicker areas. Does not work particularly well when poured. Better when sprayed or dipped, to keep coat more even. 5. This is more a HUNCH than empirical, but PSM may not like to be layered because it is formulated as a dipping glaze. This could explain #3 above.

Description: After 20+ tests of different kiln washes, I finally found the perfect one. It still doesn't flake or craze after 10 firings (from C08 to C11). Chemically Reduced Copper Reds In Oxidation. https://tomturnerporcelain.glazy.org/downloads/CopperRed35DE.pdf 3. I use KT-Kast kaolin instead of EPK since it's the whitest burning kaolin I have access to. Crystalline glazes seem to respond best over porcelain. I use a handbuilding stoneware (Mexican grey stoneware mixed with some gritty red Zacatecas clay) with a thick coating of porcelain slip (40 KT-Kast kaolin, 20 nepheline syenite, 15 soda feldspar, 20 silica, 5 Frit 3134, 5 bentonite). Still working out some minor pinholing, though I believe it's an issue with the slip and not the glaze.

Name: Ru ware
Other Names: Ru, Blue Celadon. Running Silica Satin
Description: (Revision #2 w/ 3/4 calcined Grolleg) This glaze is based on Derek Au's analysis From Nigel Wood's Chinese Glazes, The Stonewares of North China, Table 46 Compositions of Ru ware glazes, p. 127 This is the Ru Glaze with no bentonite and 3/4 of the glaze utilizing calcined Grolleg. Glaze was still cracked with application, so more calcined Grolleg was added to prevent this, but the cracks were only smaller and glaze adhered a little better. Application was thick on both pieces, but with thick application at cone 11 the pool of glaze was milky blue with swirls of clear/milky blue mixed in both cup bottom and inner plate. Interesting effect. Good glaze just a little too hot. Will keep trying. At cone 8-9 this glaze is satin and light blue. At cone 11 this image shows the pooling which is sometimes a running matte with streaks of clear deep blue. I like the glaze better at cone 8-9. Ru and Chai glazes have been crawling since day one. I have calcined 3/4 the kaolin to cone 04. Next firing will see if it works. I now have a 2 part theory I'm checking on. I have been applying the glaze very thick to cone 08 bisque with hope of a thick application, which has worked, but with lots of thick cracks and some peeling. Glaze was fragile when touched and squares have fallen off. My guess is this is happening in the quick fired kiln we do (cone 10-12 in 12-14hrs) and the glaze doesn't flow enough to cover the large gaps of glaze. So.... Part1: I have done a test of thinning the glaze to milk/cream consistency. I raw glazed 7 different cups with different glazes that all have kaolin % over 10%. The thinner glazes I double dunked on the outside. then let dry. Next I'm going to bisque them to cone 08 as usual. Then I will re-glaze an additional layer on top of bisqued glaze. Part2: The crawling may be due to bisque firing not allowing all the paper and other combustibles to burn out or maybe combustibles are creating a layer sealing the bisque that doesn't allow the glaze to adhere. Either way, I am going to hold the bisque at 1000 degrees F for 1hr to allow all the combustibles to burn out. Part3: Bisque with hold for 1hr at 1000 degrees F and hold for 3hrs at 1500 degrees F did not change tendency to crawl. All samples crawled including sample of small cup that was glazed green, bisqued to cone 08 and then glazed again thick and fired to cone 9 in wood kiln. All samples in last firing crawled on all clay bodies, so last change to stop crawling is thin application and calcining more Grolleg. (Glomax contains too much TiO to use as substitute, which will change blue color). At cone 12 (no image) surface when glossy with running matte streaks, but barely crawled on small sample. Note: Bisque to 1000 degrees F stopped crawling in most samples, though some still crawled. So lower bisque temp helped. I have switched to calcining more grolleg. This should solve issue. Calcined grolleg added to reduce crawling. slightly more whiting and silica added to counter act calcined addition. Should stop crawling and allow same blue color. When fired hot this is a running silica satin glaze. Beautiful pooling, but may not be good food glaze when fired to cone 12. testing is needed on thick pools of glaze. Chunks in glaze show it needs to be sieved. Probably chunks of calcined Grolleg. All pieces except 4 small bowls crawled. It turns out neither part of my 2 part theory were correct. I now believe the beginning of the firing climbing in temperature too quickly is causing the crawling. This explains how there were some glaze revision samples in each firing that didn't crawl (they were out of the path of the early flame). As I am firing in a shared kiln, this may be out of my ability to slow down. Hopefully, I can find some other kilns to try this glaze in that I know will fire slow at the beginning. If you will post images of wood kiln fired glaze tests with slow firing up to sinter temp that could prove this new theory.

Name: Tom Brady White
Description: This orange glaze is made with 5% Mason Stain 6027 Tangerine. I had a glaze early in my career that I made as a liner white at cone 6. It was white, glossy, high in calcium and would work great with all colorants and Mason Stains. I didn't want to make another glaze called Liner White in our studio so I called my glaze TB White - as in toilet bowl white because the opacifier is superpax and that is a harsher white than the more expensive tin oxide. I did not view the name toilet bowl white as offensive. I view the glazes on toilet bowls as extremely durable as they last forever and put up with lots of abuse in the form of harsh cleaners. One of my students heard us refer to this glaze as TB White and he said "Oh, is that Tom Brady White?" Naturally I thought that was hilarious and a more memorable name for this glaze, so now this glaze is called Tom Brady White in our studio. As you can see from all of the line blends, this glaze plays nice with a wide variety of colorants. One of the things we discovered about this glaze is that if you get enough titanium in it, you can get some nice mottling. So my next line blend with it will be with 1% cobalt carbonate in it with 4.5% titanium dioxide at one end of the blend and rutile at the other.

My hypothesis was that there were discrepancies in batches of raw materials that was throwing off the chemistry. However, after retesting the original recipe and even altering with a diferrent feldspathic material and even different flint mesh sizes, the original chemistry was affirmed and is accurate. Findings: - The original recipe's chemistry is consistent. I found no considerable differences in the original recipe from four months ago and today's test results. - Clay body has some impact. The darker or more tinted the claybody, the more blue this glaze picks up. I'm thinking this is an iron issue. That said, even on white stoneware, the glaze remains red. - Lighting matters. When I look at this glaze in my garage overhead florescents, it looks a bit more muddied. Bringing it into natural light, it color corrects to the actual red color. - Firing Cycles matter- slow cooling will absolutely cloud this glaze. It will encourage more phase separation. I fire in an L & L test kiln before taking test tiles to my studio and firing in a large Skutt barrell kiln. - Application matters. If you're getting phase separation, try a thinner application. If you're still having issues, adding 2-3% Zircopax can help to opacify the color and build a more consitent color with a thinner coat.

Name: White Engobe Recipe
Description: This is white because of the 10% Zircopax. Increase that 20% for maximum white. The black version of this is changing out ziropax for approx. 10-15% Mason stain 6600 This recipe has been tuned to have about the same fired shrinkage as Plainsman M390, Coffee Clay and M340 at cone 6 (we measure this at 6.7% dry-to-fired shrinkage using the SHAB test). We also confirmed fired-shrinkage-match using the EBCT test). If the body you use has between 6.5 and 7.0 fired shrinkage, this should work. Do not ignore this detail. If you apply this as an engobe (e.g. by dipping leather-hard functional pieces), and it is not firing-shrinkage-compatible with the body, it could eventually flake off during use. The color is whiter than previous trials (because of the zircopax), but some might prefer a little blue stain to brighten the color. We used 0.2% Mason 6336 with good success, other stains we tried agglomerated and caused specking). As will other engobes we recommend mixing in a kitchen blender, it is an ideal way to get the lumps out and thoroughly wet all particle surfaces. A thixotropic dipping slurry is needed and we have found it is possible to create a deflocculated one using 1000 powder, 780g water, 3g Darvan. This produces a specific gravity of 1.55. If it is too viscous add more Darvan, too fluid add a tiny amount of Epsom salts to bring it back to a creamy texture. A brushing version can also be made, see the notes for the L3954F black engobe. Other Comments: Brush on version: 75g gum solution, 280 grams of water, 500 grams of powder recipe (makes approximately 1 pint) A good mixer is needed to mix in the last of the powder. (Let it soak over night to break up all the lumps) This produces a consistency that is very brushable. --- 5000 gram powder 390 ml of water 20 grams of darvan no. 7 produces less than 2 gallons having a specific gravity of 1.55 (100:78:0.4) If you find after a day, it is a bit too fluid add a tiny amount of epsom salts to bring it back to a creamy texture. You can start with 15 darvan to play it on the safe side. :) ----- I ran some tests using Robin's Egg Mason Blue stain (6376) in increments of .1, .3, .5, .75, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, & 6 percent. 1% Robin's Egg Blue makes the slip seem a bit whiter and leans towards a cool tone. 5% and 6% gives a nice Robin's Egg blue, I don't believe you would need any more stain to this slip to achieve a deeper colour. I glazed this with a translucent semi-matte glaze.

Name: "Revised" Hansen Clear
Description: Original recipe 'Hansen Clear' occasionally had issues with cloudiness. Trying to rewrite to be clearer. ORIGINAL RECIPE: - custer feldspar 20 - wollastonite 20 - silica 20 - kaolin 20 - frit 3134 20 - bentonite 2 Swapped the custer feldspar for soda feldspar/minspar 200 because it has it has less alumina which could in turn increase transparency. Microcrystalline growth is more likely with custer feldspar (due to primarily containing potassium vs sodium), which increases the likelihood of cloudiness and little bubbles. Minspar 200 should melt clearer than the original custer feldspar, and lowering the frit will hopefully prevent over melting. MUST keep this recipe at a milky consistency and MUST apply even 3 coats or spray for best results. Working on tweaking the recipe to work better with a thicker application. Additionally, in theory, minspar 200 should roughly cost the same amount or be cheaper. Also, since the frit is the most expensive thing in this recipe, lowering it will also save a few pennies. Please view my page for two updated clears which have better results with both thin and thick applications. Leaving this one up for people to reference of what NOT to do/to learn from! :)

Description: Bill van Gilder email: Here’s a cone 6 glaze share for those of you who mix your own glazes…Amber Gold. I’ve liked and used this glaze for years. I like it’s color and it’s pooling and flow qualities – yet it doesn’t flow and run excessively which, of course, can be problematic. And it’s a simple four-part recipe containing materials that are typically found in everybody’s glaze lab. ​As shown in the photo, this amber colored glaze is at its best over textured surfaces and whiteish clays. It’s kind of root beer colored over iron bearing clays. And I’ve never seen it craze/crackle or pinhole on any smooth clay body – light or dark. I do believe the four combined base materials could be colored using oxides other than the r/i/oxide as listed below, but I haven’t gone that route yet. Cobalt carbonate for a transparent and pooling blue? Hmmm…. ​I fire all my cone 6 glazes in an electric kiln using a SLOW glaze firing program with no ramps or holds going up or coming down. I let each kiln load cool at its own pace and open them at 200 degrees F. ​I can’t give you an application thickness number via a hydrometer for this glaze – because I don’t use one. They’re too variable in my opinion. So, the wet glaze thickness is best described as ‘slightly thicker than whole milk but not as thick as cream’. ​And a mixing note… if after sieving, I discover that I’ve unintentionally mixed my glaze batch too thin and watery, I dilute (fingertip stirred) 1 tablespoon of Epsom salt crystals into 3 tablespoons of warm-to-hot water in a small cup. This now slightly syrupy liquid is poured into my too-thin glaze batch and left to sit for 5 minutes. The glaze batch is then stirred up blending the Epsom salts mixture into the liquid mix. I repeat this process if the glaze batch is still too thin. To get a 1000-gram liquid glaze batch amount, move each decimal point to the right one decimal. Multiply the gram numbers by 5 to get a 5000 gram/2- ½ gallons of wet glaze. Or multiply the numbers by 10 to get a 10,000 gram/5 gallon liquid batch.

Name: Kelp, Dawn & Dusk - Tea Dust Variations
Description: This recipe was a miraculous find as it was the first test that was successful using Aardvark Charcoal Clay after testing for 2 years. I have the RIO listed in this recipe because it was the original version I tested (from Temmoku Basic (Line 5) recipe here on Glazy). Subsequent versions with Rutile and Copper Carb came later. The three variations I have had success with: Kelp (+10 Red Iron Oxide) (only the Kelp version uses RIO) Dusk (+6 Rutile - pinkish) Dawn (+6 Rutile/1 Copper Carb - bluish) The quirks: Dusk version can get crepey if it's on too thick and Kelp and Dawn can run if on too thick. Try not to dip for longer than 2 counts. Also I use the trusty "if I can see my veins on the back of my hand it's good" method for glaze thickness when mixing up a batch. Basically, a consistancy of crepe batter is what I shoot for. I recently overshot with water on a batch of Dawn and 2 tsp of dissolved Epsom Salts was a great quick fix. Name: Comfort
Description: 1. Appearance A semi-matte glaze. The colour is between light brown and yellow sand with dark almost black dots and brown sprinkles. # 2. Touch The surface feels nice and gives a comfortable grip. One can feel texture from the dots. # 3. Food safety not investigated # 4. Remarks The glaze was sifted only once at 100 mesh. I suppose it will be a good glaze for vessels. =========== # A. Continuation ### A.1. On food safety #### 2025-04-12: I'm certainly not about to confirm food safety. But I have half immersed a piece in vinegar essence (24.9%) overnight (15 hours, room temperature) and couldn't tell the difference with the naked eye. So I decided to burn more samples and take proper before/after pictures. #### 2025-05-27: I exposed one piece to acid (20% vinegar essence, pH3) and one to a base (2% soda, pH13). 50ml each Both pieces approximate 9cm². Both 24h at room temperature. I could not find a change of texture or colour. A tried to apply test stripes (Fe, Cd, Pb, Zn, Cu, Ni) that were meant for drinking water. They went false positive on lead (>500mg/L Pb - even when only "wild" ingredient, ash, did not expose any Pb under RWM/EDX) in acid. Ni went false positive in base. It did not (not only) relate to pH, because the results stayed unchanged after balancing to pH7. Thus I still have a good "feeling" but no certainty.

Name: Happy Flux
Description: Some Glazy members have shown interest in a glaze similar to Honey Flux (AMACO). Inspired by Derek Au's recipe (Butterscotch +4 TiO2 +4 Rutile, 126958), I created "Happy Flux." My reason for not copying Derek's recipe was to simply reduce the cost of the glaze. After reviewing the SDS sheet, I found that Honey Flux contains silica, whiting, dolomite, neph sy, rutile, and zinc. I swapped neph sy to minspar to reduce COE. I chose titanium over rutile to make it whiter. I assumed Gillespie Borate was part of the composition since there would be no boron present otherwise. As Gillespie Borate isn't required to be listed on the SDS sheet, I included it in my formula. (In contrast, frit must be listed on the SDS sheet according to the internet.) This glaze is fairly unremarkable on its own but becomes more intriguing when layered. For example, I found it particularly interesting when layered with Selsor Chun. If you’d like to make it whiter and creamier, consider adding more zinc.

Name: OldForge FreedomFive Oil Spot
Description: This is one of a selection of straightforward recipes that use the same 5 base ingredients, to give an easy starting point to buying ingredients and mixing glazes: https://www.oldforgecreations.co.uk/blog/freedomfive-glazes-getting-started-with-mixing-glazes Oil Spot glazes have a lot of Red Iron Oxide in them, which releases its oxygen as gas during the firing and causes the glaze to bubble up and mix. This is less obvious on its own, especially with a recipe like this that has less variation within the base glaze, but it becomes very obvious with a contrasting opaque cover glaze. The base will bubble up through it and produce spots. The Red Iron Oxide is also helping the glaze melt sufficiently and balancing out the fluxes, so this glaze requires it to work. Other colourants can be used in combination though, adding 1% Cobalt and/or 1% Chromium will give a black base. The Glossy Base with 10% Zirconium makes a good cover glaze.

Name: Blue to green crackle
Description: Using Jake Brand's burnt honey crackle recipe, I just swapped most of the iron oxide for a small amount of copper carbonate to get a light blue crackle. I kept 0.1% RIO in an attempt to stop the green being too 'coppery' and aim for the reduced iron celadon look. It came out very different than I expected but still great. Probably needed more RIO to temper the colour as I expected. TEST 1: Hot cone 6 electric on Audrey Blackburn porcelain slip. Beautiful ice blue crackle with just a hint of green! I expected a more copper green. This was a bit of a surprise. Applied over a porcelain slip on iron stoneware clay. The high tension of the glaze is pulling the slip off at the rim, so best not to apply over slip - or it will need to adhere very strongly. TEST 2 on a white clay - much more green. Still a very nice crackle glaze. It seems the clay makes all the difference to the colour. Audrey Blackburn porcelain gave the blue. It may be the titanium content of the clay, per a John Britt article on celadons I read. But I don't know if that applies to copper.

Name: Korean Style Celadon
Other Names: blue/green celadon, pumice celadon, Pete's pumice celadon
Description: (Revision #3 switched to G200 & calcined 1/2 Grolleg) This is a revised recipe of an 80/20 pumice/wollastonite Korean style celadon from Pete Pinnell. I have added clay to the mix to create a better application. Before it was like brushing sand, so Grolleg was added. Must be applied thick for blue color. Apply on high silica clay body to reduce crazing. Fired below 1230 degrees may make a running matte glaze due to high pumice, but has not been tested. Last revision showed beautiful clear blue in drips and areas not hit with wood ash. Pumice was reduced and silica added to encourage this blue color, though iron percentage stayed the same as last revision. This test worked as strong baby blue with small bubbles creating almost a Kuan glaze. The crazing was large cracks here and there, very limited. Where really think- glaze still ran, but I think this is the color I want. Will try firing again. At cone 11-12 in salt/wood firing still blue, but more of a grey/blue. It ran significantly in this firing. Looks good, but is crawling. Maybe half of kaolin should be calcined. 1/2 kaolin calcined to remove crawling issue. Switched to G200 as Custer is gone. Kept same silica/alumina ratio and same flux ratio. It is now believed, too fast of temp climb early in firing is causing the crawling. Glaze cracks and falls off clay body when flame hits it. Last firing was super fast at the beginning which suggests this is why certain firings have more crawling than others.
Ingredients: Volcanic Ash (NM) 42; Wollastonite 24; Silica 13; G-200 EU Feldspar 9; Calcined Grolleg Kaolin 6; Grolleg Kaolin 4; Magnesium carbonate 2

Name: Dan's Snowdrift
Description: Aiming for a white crackle, I adjusted a base for a crackle glaze (Burnt Honey Crackle) and used titanium and bone ash as the colorants. It turned out not to be visibly a crazing glaze, I assume because of the bone ash. CTE is still very high. And I have seen crackles with bone ash in, so I'm not sure what happened. Description: Glaze mixture matrix The test cylinders were glazed as follows: 1. Large areas were dipped in one of the glazes listed horizontally (H1 to H12). 2. Reading example M1 - A52as - A131a: Base glaze A52as, top glaze A131a and liner A67a, A52o, A124a, A72a (from top to bottom). Horizontal (used as base glaze) H1 A55j - H2 A67a - H3 A83g - H4 A94a - H5 A55h - H6 A124a - H7 A55k - H8 A66i - H9 A52as - H10 A85b - H11 A28a - H12 A43a Vertical (applied as a top glaze on the upper edge above the base glaze) V1 A104e - V2 A104f - V3 A131a - V4 A132a - V5 A126a - V6 A124a - V7 A52as - V8 A28a - V9 A91a - V10 A65a Liner (as a thick liner - with thickener - applied as a horizontal circle) L1 A67a - L2 A52o - L3 A124a - L4 A72a The liners A67a, A52o and A124a. work well A72a tend not to. The base glazes A83g, A94a, A55h, and A28a run too much and are therefore unsuitable. Flux A132a flows too much and is only usable as a glaze and via A43a. Will test cobalt free black mason stain to see if this surface issue can be resolved with clear. I use 8% additional Ultrox to make a great white underglaze. I did this by lowering the elements that have a higher expansion rate, which then have a higher chance of creating the crazing effect. AKA lower the expansion by increasing SiO2 and Al2O3, and reducing Na and Ca. calculated based off of 182 Standard dry mix clay body. I have found this glaze works wonderfully on various porcelain bodies, so they original recipe may be perfect for you! The crazing is beautiful on the 182 body, just non-functional, thus the revisions. But it's pretty well worth it. Most stunning on darker clay bodies because of the breaking. The Copper Sea version of this glaze is pretty popular in my area in Southeast Michigan. Have seen it used at a few of the community and university studios around here, but there is nothing similar to it on glazy. If anyone knows the origin - I'd love to know! I want to say someone subbed the tin for titanium once and got a similar and cheaper result. Please post pics if you try it out! Or maybe I'll have time to get to it soon. I love the opaqueness of this glaze and how it breaks on the clay bodies. It's a solid base recipe to mess around with colorants. This is is the white version of my other glaze Copper Sea, which has RIO and Copper Carb to make a seafoam green. You can see that recipe here - https://glazy.org/recipes/81407 - No changes significant changes in the glaze look going from Gerstley to Gillespie Borate. - Sometimes I'll throw the .75 RIO from the Copper Sea recipe just for fun. Makes it a little less of an intense bright white. - We have also made this glaze with OLD spodumene that I got from someone closing their studio. It's prob from the 90s, but she wasn't sure how old it was. The OLD spodumene makes this glaze a perfect and beautiful dirty white. Breaks a little more brown and shows the speckles from Standard 553 and Laguna Speckle Brown sooooo well. It's extremely good. I assume the spodumene had more contaminants in the 90s or something like that. But damn we're gonna be sad when it's gone. Pictures are the glaze with NEW spodumene to avoid confusion.

Description: Introduction I used Digital fires G1947U as base for this. http://digitalfire.com/4sight/recipes/cone10glossytransparentbase40.html # AI transparency I found the original receipt from tinkering with AI. I found some pictures of dichroic glass art and wanted to kind of transfer it to a glaze recipe. So, as a newbie, I have to confess: This trial is a fully blind shot. ## Prompt "I would like to create a glaze for high-firing stoneware at 1250°C ± 30°C. The glaze should be stable, it should be predominantly transparent and have a dichroic effect between deep dark lilac and intense royal blue. It should be applied in a medium-thick layer. I would like this glaze to have irregular structures or streaks or other organic-looking irregularities. It should not run off, it should bond well to a stoneware clay and it should either have a real chance of being food-safe or be able to be coated in the same firing with a transparent glaze labeled as food-compatible without this running off. Please provide me with an example composition, describe the effects and give the ingredients with their respective molecular formula." # Observation ## Mixing Initially I mixed the dry recipe with 120% water (including 6% of something called "Stellmittel"). This is what I had used successfully in my previous recipes. That turned out far to thin. Even the 80% are quite thin. At least it feels suitable for pouring but not for brushing. Also the suspension settles quite fast. I will have it fired to see what happens... But my next approach will be about 30% water and 20% Stellmittel. ## Repair No running. 1 brush stroke: to thin. 2 brush stroke appears to me to be perfect.

Description: Soft, satin matte glaze. The titanium is what is giving this glaze its speckled crystallization. By definition, all matte glazes are crystalline glazes. A thicker application causes smaller crystals whereas a thinner coat causes more crystals with greater variation in size. Thinner allows for more of the clay body to show through. This glaze does show texture. Thinner= better crystallization overall. This is a stable glaze at a hot cone six. I glaze directly up to the foot with no movement observed. Natural cooling. Firing/Slow Cooling Notes: The test images shown represent results from a natural / relatively quick kiln cooling cycle. Slow cooling, controlled cooling, or extended cooling soaks will substantially alter the appearance of this glaze. Slower cooling promotes increased crystallization and phase separation within the glaze melt, which may significantly change: Color and hue Surface texture and gloss Mottling and variegation Opacity and depth Crystal development and visual movement Results under slow-cool conditions may look dramatically different from the images shown. Always test with your specific firing schedule, clay body, and kiln behavior before production use.

Description: From Bill Van Gilder's share email: This glaze has had various names over the years: from Wyman’s White (Bill Wyman) to Cynthia’s White and Mamo which, I believe, was much used by Val Cushing and the clay students at Alfred University back in the day. Currently for me, I use it sparingly - something to neutralize and quietly balance the more colorful glazes that might go on a single pot. Note here that I very rarely apply only one dipped or sprayed glaze on a pot. Applying two or more complimentary glazes is typical for my kitchen and tableware. But obviously the two pots shown above are an exception to my rule with Mamo applied solo. And here's that recipe: Mamo - ^9-10 reduction Potash feldspar (200mesh Custer or G-200 EU) 5 lb. Ball clay (Tenn. #10 or OM-4) 2 lb. Dolomite 2 lb. Whiting 8 oz. Tin oxide 8 oz. Sieve batch 80 mesh twice. It fires well from a cool ^9 to a hot ^11. At ^11 of course, you'll see more sheen or gloss and lots more breaking action. The clay body it's applied over matters too: iron bearing brown stoneware = cream colors with speckles… white or light-colored clays = soft-toned whites. Both are acceptable in my view. When overlapped or double dipped a much whiter opaque color is the result. And I’ve never seen this glaze craze, shell or crawl. Adding colored oxides to the recipe is something I've never explored. But with such a simple base recipe I think the potential for creating some soft-toned glaze colors is a good possibility. I've also never tried to adjust this Mamo recipe for cone 6 temperatures. Possibly one of our fellow weekly e-mail readers can reconfigure the recipe to fire at ^6? On another note: I've often been asked to share the recipe for the Blue Ash Glaze I use a lot. So, as a believer that not much in this clay world of ours is sacred, in next week's Emails for Potters I'll share that ^9-10 Blue Ash Glaze recipe along with some details about how I mix and use it. But that's next week. For now, you ^9-10 gas reduction folks… give this simple Mamo glaze a try! ​
