While this requires more rigorous testing, it currently has an absorption rate of .87%. I rolled out a 5\8" slab and cut off a 10" strip. After a cone 02 bisque firing it is 8.5". After a cone 04 glaze firing, it remains unchanged. Total shrinkage is 15%. How does this throw? It's extremely smooth. Holds its shape nicely, though so far I've only thrown 1lb balls. It does feel soft like porcelain. This clay body recipe is one that I prompted ChatGPT to formulate using the charts on glazy.org. My prompt was for a lowfire (cone 02) clay body that was porcelain-like with a water absorption rate of less than 1%. Name: Crackle 9#
Description: A dense and deep network of cracks emerged, with a glacial and poetic appearance. The glaze was nearly transparent, with striking visual depth, and despite concerns about running, it remained stable, even, and clean. After the firing, I chose to emphasize the crackle pattern by applying black ink and gently wiping the surface. The ink settled into the cracks, creating a dramatic contrast between the transparent layer and the fractured lines, making the pattern especially clear and present. What stood out this time, unlike in previous tests—was the presence of especially delicate cracks. They were so subtle that in the flat test tile, I decided not to apply ink, in order to preserve the natural, fragile beauty of the glaze as it was. The final result: a transparent glaze with a quiet, frozen quality, reminiscent of a winter lake at the edge of the world. A restrained material experience, yet rich in depth.

Name: Yongle Reign (AD 1402-1424) Copper Red
Description: Taken from Nigel Wood's Chinese Glazes Chemical analysis found on Table 70 in Chapter 9, Page 178 Converted recipe can be found on page 271 I used Mahavir Potash Feldspar and English Grolleg specifically, without changing any proportions. This glaze is the direct predecessor of the renowned yet rare copper red masterpieces created under the Xuande Emperor's reign (AD 1425-1435) of the Ming Dynasty. Like its successor, this glaze is supposed to be a vibrant, cherry red that breaks clear over rims and texture, all while being stiff and not running off pots like those of the following Qing dynasty. 12/13/25 My result thus far has yielded a livery pink, and I need to figure out what's causing the lack of color development. Despite this, this is one of the best results I've had so far, considering previous tests often have yielded me little to no color. This glaze also crazes ever so slightly on Coleman Porcelain, though copper reds have been known to craze in general. I'm considering firing my next test tiles in small saggars in the future just as the Ming and Qing's contemporaneous examples were to see if this helps. It may also need a unique firing schedule. Tips: -Sieve twice through a 100-mesh sieve to prevent iron speckling in the fired glaze -Glaze your pieces slightly thick for the best color development. I personally do a single 4-second dip for all of my celadons, and other glazes, and get uniform and vibrant results.

Prima driehoek Met een paar mooie combinaties, mn: CD, DE, BD en AD, oftewel alle combinaties met 0,5% cobaltcarbonaat! During the course I learnt that wasn't true, and during the Labs I developed this gloss base with Strontium as the AE flux. Without the Rutile it's a fairly boring clear gloss. With the rutile and most other colourants it becomes something far more interesting. All tests shown include the rutile along with the named colourants. The Manganese Dioxide is 325 mesh. This glaze comes out a soft yellow-olive green, likely due to the higher iron content that is present in a lot of the Yuan Dynasty era glazes coming out of Longquan. The surface is semi-glossy though not fully Satin. Tips: - Sieve twice through a 100-mesh sieve to prevent iron speckling in the fired glaze - Glaze your pieces slightly thick for the best color development. I personally do a single 4-second dip for all of my celadons and get uniform and vibrant results.

Name: Lithium Barium Crystaline Matte
Description: I am a sculptor using this on objects that will not contact food. As such I am assuming this is not a food safe glaze. In order to achieve the characteristic matte-ness in this glaze, controlled cooling is necessary. The glaze is runny (a feature rather than a bug). I like to fire this to cone 02, but could go a couple cones higher (runnier) or lower (less runny) and still be very matte (because the matte-ness is the result of crystallization in cooling). A thick application helps develop matte-ness. I am using the following firing schedule: 1: 250°F/hr to 250°F 2: 350°F/hr to 1000°F 3: 300°F/hr to 1800°F 4: 150°F/hr to 2048°F, hold 10–15 min 5: (cooling) 100°F/hr to 1600°F
Ingredients: Petalite 40; Silica 20; Lithium Carbonate 12; Barium Carbonate 6; Wollastonite 6; Ferro Frit 3195 5; Custer Feldspar 3; EP Kaolin 3; G-200 Feldspar 3; Bentonite 2

Name: Copper Red V7
Description: This was my best result from testing 6 base variations on my previous copper red v6. This version swaps wollastonite for whiting and lowering the amount of frit while adjusting everything else to keep the same R2O:RO. I still believe there's room for improvement and have 2 more base variations to test in a couple months. Background on the glaze itself comes from digitalfire's posts on Fusion Frit FZ-16 and it's impressive melting, and that it could be used for an amazing base glaze. When I found out we had an equivalent Ferro frit on hand, I spent my last semester testing it. My tests moving forward will swap over to FZ-16 instead of 3824. UMF wise, I started from Tony Hansen's G3903 and adjusted from there. Results so far have been very promising. One thing that has perplexed me for awhile is that results tend to be brighter when fired in a gas oxidation firing, and I've seen this happen throughout all my SiC testing on every base tried so far, but our gas firings are also inconsistent. My leading theory on it is that the slow cooling times give the glaze time to oxidize more, resulting in a thinner, brighter layer of red. Now that I've dialed in my electric firings I'll be looking into test slow cools to see how it affects color response. My tests for this base have only been at cone 5 1/2, so cone 6 still needs to be tested alongside slow cooling. The cone 5 1/2 firing schedule used was an attempt to match the gas kiln in our studio and is as follows: 108F/h to 250 1 hour hold 250F/h to 950 no hold 108F/h to 1150 no hold 170F/h to 2150 no hold 108F/h to 2210 no hold Flocculation is a must for this base, it takes to it very well with a saturated epsom salt solution otherwise it will settle very quickly. I did not see any noticeable thickening over time like I did with copper red V2-5. As you can see, I managed to get the recipe to straddle the line between semi-matte and matte, so I'm not sure if I achieved a true matte? I did try to look up some sources of alumina I could add but it seemed to be only the refractory clay that would do that. And I was hesitant to lower the silica much more because I was worried the glaze wouldn't move at all. Name: Deliveroo Turquoise (Revision 1)
Description: Yellow Celadon (Glazy #95303) as the starting recipe, which I amended to use my available materials to create Deliveroo Turquoise #643557. This is a revision of the latter recipe. I created this glaze for the 2023 Level 5 glaze chemistry course with Otago Polytechnic. I was attempting to make a glaze that mimicked the Deliveroo branding colors for some exhibition pieces. I had problems with the glaze developing an orange peel texture when applied to the piece (either brushed or dipped), not matter if it was thick and or thin. (It also crazed quite some time after -- maybe up to a year?) This Revision 1 attempts to rectify the orange peel texture and possibly also the crazing (though only time will tell on that one). It's a task required for 2025 Level 6 glaze chemistry course with Otago Polytechnic. I changed the original Frit 3134 to Frit 3249 since it’s recommended to help reduce crazing — my secondary issue — and also with melting at lower temperatures. (I don’t have Frit 3195, which is also recommended by DigitalFire for better melting.) I used the up and down arrows to lower the boron in the original recipe in an effort to lower the LOI (Loss on Ignition) and reduce the aluminum oxide (Al2O3). I did this until the recipe came in line with the original Yellow Celadon. What I did to attempt a fix: - I changed the original Frit 3134 to Frit 3249 since it’s recommended to help reduce crazing — my secondary issue — and also with melting at lower temperatures. (I don’t have Frit 3195, which is also recommended by DigitalFire for better melting.) - I used the up and down arrows to lower the boron in the original recipe in an effort to lower the LOI (Loss on Ignition) and reduce the aluminum oxide (Al2O3). I did this until the recipe came in line with the original Yellow Celadon. - I added 2% Zircopax since it’s a fining agent. - I used the same clay as before because that seemed sensible – I don’t want to add too many variables. - I'll dip and brush the glaze on different test tiles and aim for a thin rather than thick application: 3 sec. dip and 2-3 layer brush (depending on who the glaze looks). - I'll test the specific gravity and aim for 1.4 to 1.5 (as suggested by Glazy). - I’ll add a 10 minute hold at top temperature (a general recommendation I found written in my kiln manual). As above, I don’t want to mess with too much because it will add too many variables to the test. Research sources: DigitalFire, Ceramic Arts Network, The Little Pot Company The original recipe was: 44.2 ----- Minspar 200 19.4 ----- Wollastonite 15.2 ----- EPK 12.1 ----- Ferro Frit 3134 07.6 ----- Silica 01.5 ----- Dolomite Add: 1% copper carb (01.0) 2% bentonite (02.0) I ground the copper carb in a mortar and double sieved the glaze to try to refine the chunky copper carb.
Ingredients: Minspar 200 46.4; Wollastonite 20.4; Ferro Frit 3249 12.4; EP Kaolin 10.9; Silica 8; Dolomite 1.9; Bentonite 2 (additional); Zircopax 2 (additional); Copper Carbonate 1 (additional)

Name: Black-Blue Trailing Slip for Bisque Cone 6 Revision (NZDAD L6 2025 Studio Research Assessment) (Hiratsu Feldspar version)
Description: My attempt at amending this trailing slip for bisque from Cone 10 to Cone 6. I pretty much reversed the feldspar and the refractory clay in an attempt the reduce the melting temperature and get a stiff, dry slip. I aimed for a very low R₂O and a high RO ratio. I was nervous that the dot LEFT the Stull Chart but read online that's normal for slips? This version has 7% black iron oxide and 1% cobalt oxide to try to create a black-blue slip -- mostly black with a touch of blue. I based the ratios on this Ceramic Arts Network article: https://ceramicartsnetwork.org/daily/article/All-You-Ever-Wanted-to-Know-About-Cobalt-But-Were-Afraid-to-Ask. I dropped them a little bit lower for testing. I removed the Zircopax, too, since it whitens the glaze. In this version, I replaced the Custer Feldspar (discontinued) with Hiratsu Feldspar from Japan (another potash feldspar) at a 1-to-1 replacement: https://digitalfire.com/material/hiratsu+feldspar. This feldspar isn't listed in the Glazy inventory, so I just listed it as Potash Feldspar in the recipe. --- Thanks to Suzie Lindsay, Jack Troy, and Linda McFarling for sharing the original Cone 10 recipe!

Name: UG v10.2 FZ-16 (SiC reduction base)
Description: Overall this is a failed test, but figured I'd publish this in case anyone finds it useful. This is better than v10.1 and close to being what I was aiming for, but was a bit too stiff still to heal the surface. Test tiles are a bit darker than what the photos show. Revision of the zinc fritted fluid melt base that I started using in Copper Red v6 and v7. This revision increases R2O to 0.3:0.7 while maintaining expansion, and targets a UMF closer to Tony Hansen's G3903. Previous tests were made using Ferro frit 3824, but this switches over to the nearly equivalent Fusion frit FZ-16 due to it actually being available. Colorant additions tested for each variation were done with two tiles, one with a single 10 second dip and one with a 6 second full dip with a 6 second half dip. The variants tested were as follows: With 0.50% copper carbonate and 0.30% silicon carbide (1000 mesh): - Tin at 1%, 0.75%, 0.50%, 0.25% - Red iron oxide at 1%, 0.75%, 0.50%, 0.25% - Tin/RIO at 0.50/0.25, 0.50/0.50, 0.25/0.50 With 0.30% silicon carbide (1000 mesh): - Red iron oxide at 1%, 0.75%, 0.50%, 0.25% - Just the base All test were 80% water and first immersion blended with just the base and 0.30% silicon carbide, sieved at 120 mesh, then remaining colorants were added, immersion blended, and sieved again at 120 mesh. All variants were measured out to 100 ml then flocculated with 6.75 ml of saturated epsom salt solution. Application properties after flocculation were ok, but probably needs more epsom salt solution. Silicon carbide mesh was 1000 Spanish red iron oxide was used if it matters Fusion frit FZ-16 is only available through direct sales as far as I'm aware, and requires a minimum quantity of 50 lb, with shipping costing about as much as the material to have it shipped to California
Ingredients: Nepheline Syenite 25; Silica 25; Fusion Frit FZ-16 20; Grolleg Kaolin 15.5; Dolomite 8; Wollastonite 6.5; Silicon carbide 0.3 (additional)

Name: UG v10.1 FZ-16 (SiC reduction base)
Description: Overall this is a failed test, but figured I'd publish this in case anyone finds it useful. Revision of the zinc fritted fluid melt base that I started using in Copper Red v6 and v7. This revision removes wollastonite/whiting, increases R2O to 0.3:0.7 while maintaining expansion, and targets a similar UMF of Tony Hansen's G3903 where possible. Previous tests were made using Ferro frit 3824, but this switches over to the nearly equivalent Fusion frit FZ-16 due to it actually being available. Colorant additions tested for each variation were done with two tiles, one with a single 10 second dip and one with a 6 second full dip with a 6 second half dip. The variants tested were as follows: With 0.50% copper carbonate and 0.30% silicon carbide (1000 mesh): - Tin at 1%, 0.75%, 0.50%, 0.25% - Red iron oxide at 1%, 0.75%, 0.50%, 0.25% - Tin/RIO at 0.50/0.25, 0.50/0.50, 0.25/0.50 With 0.30% silicon carbide (1000 mesh): - Red iron oxide at 1%, 0.75%, 0.50%, 0.25% - Just the base All test were 80% water and first immersion blended with just the base and 0.30% silicon carbide, sieved at 120 mesh, then remaining colorants were added, immersion blended, and sieved again at 120 mesh. All variants were measured out to 100 ml then flocculated with 6.75 ml of saturated epsom salt solution, and rested for 3 days. Application properties after flocculation were great and had no suspension issues. Silicon carbide mesh was 1000 Spanish red iron oxide was used if it matters Fusion frit FZ-16 is only available through direct sales as far as I'm aware, and requires a minimum quantity of 50 lb, with shipping costing about as much as the material to have it shipped to California

Potentially the addition of gum or a suspension agent could help alleviate some of the settling but not all. Thickness of application will determine the surface quality of the craters in this glaze. You can dip or brush this glaze on in my experience thus far. WARNING WITH CRATER GLAZES! They do melt and bubble in a large volume. SO DO NOT PLACE things glazed with this close together or near other items in the kiln. It expands about an inch or more from the pot and has the potential to essentially reach out and attach to neighboring pots. These ARE NOT useable for FOOD SURFACES, the glaze is brittle and will rub off. This is a decorative glaze and is non-functional.

But I wanted to see what other colors I could get with this and keep that breaking brown variable quality. I'm noticing that the original recipe with the copper carb is the one that does this the best - so it's almost certainly a quality of the copper carb itself. But hey maybe we can figure it out. I originally tested with the titanium, but changing the other colorants. Taking away the copper carb definitely changed the way the glaze melted because those tests were super matte verging on the texture of the clay. Name: Aquamarine
Description: The recipe began from a desire to create an aquamarine glaze inspired by the natural gemstone, with its wide range of blue and turquoise tones, from pale sky blue through greenish blue like seawater, all the way to deep ocean blue, with a glossy, glass like surface. The results are quite successful to my taste, especially when fired with a slow cooling cycle, even though I was hoping for more crystal development. With the current recipe I will continue testing different oxide color combinations, and in the next version I plan to reduce the R2O and RO fluxes in order to increase the saturation and strength of the glass forming oxides.

Name: matte crystalline (Copy)
Description: Part of my search for special crystal-effect glazes involves developing a matte crystal glaze based on a zinc and barium combination. So far the tests have been only partially successful, but this recipe feels like it is starting to approach the surface I am looking for. The texture is still a bit too dry for my taste, so I plan to refine it, hoping this will also encourage more visible crystal formation. At the same time, this test produced an interesting glaze with the addition of one gram of iron oxide, so I am planning to try it again with a slow-cool firing schedule and possibly with additional colorant oxides.
Ingredients: Barium Carbonate 43; Nepheline Syenite 25; Zinc Oxide 19; Frit 6004 6; Lithium Carbonate 4; Kaolin 3

Name: CAC Turquoise
Description: Beautiful semi matte to smooth matte glaze. Barium Carbonate is toxic, substituting Strontium Carbonate does not work as well. Always use a mask when mixing and rubber gloves when glazing. After mixing let stand 24 hrs then sieve through 80 mesh twice then through 100 mesh twice, stir thoroughly between each sieve. Then while glazing, stir, stir stir. This glaze likes cone 9 the best and as much reduction as you dare. It will run if it is to thick. I was told the glaze had been tested and does not leach barium or copper. I tested a cone 8 oxidization test tile for 90 hours in white vinegar and noticed no color leaching or surface degradation. See photos. I make no claim that this glaze does not leach barium or copper, use at your own discretion. I am currently testing a Strontium version of this glaze.
Ingredients: Nepheline Syenite 48.1; Barium Carbonate 37.3; Silica 7.5; Kentucky OM #4 Ball Clay 7.1; Rutile 5 (additional); Bentonite 4 (additional); Copper Carbonate 2 (additional)

No crazing visible on B17 c stoneware when fired to a cone 7-8 DEV NOTES: found that 50211 (v1) was just on the edge of crazing WOL version had slightly raised silica and no craze visible stain version 504633 blended to 9.43 sial (507059) - seemed stable through out Therefore to make the V2 brushing we added more silica, increasing the SIAL and lowering the calculated thermal expansion 300g BATCH for a full (enough) 400ml container

Name: Copper Red V7
Description: This was my best result from testing 6 base variations on my previous copper red v6. This version swaps wollastonite for whiting and lowering the amount of frit while adjusting everything else to keep the same R2O:RO. I still believe there's room for improvement and have 2 more base variations to test in a couple months. Background on the glaze itself comes from digitalfire's posts on Fusion Frit FZ-16 and it's impressive melting, and that it could be used for an amazing base glaze. When I found out we had an equivalent Ferro frit on hand, I spent my last semester testing it. My tests moving forward will swap over to FZ-16 instead of 3824. UMF wise, I started from Tony Hansen's G3903 and adjusted from there. Results so far have been very promising. One thing that has perplexed me for awhile is that results tend to be brighter when fired in a gas oxidation firing, and I've seen this happen throughout all my SiC testing on every base tried so far, but our gas firings are also inconsistent. My leading theory on it is that the slow cooling times give the glaze time to oxidize more, resulting in a thinner, brighter layer of red. Now that I've dialed in my electric firings I'll be looking into test slow cools to see how it affects color response. My tests for this base have only been at cone 5 1/2, so cone 6 still needs to be tested alongside slow cooling. The cone 5 1/2 firing schedule used was an attempt to match the gas kiln in our studio and is as follows: 108F/h to 250 1 hour hold 250F/h to 950 no hold 108F/h to 1150 no hold 170F/h to 2150 no hold 108F/h to 2210 no hold Flocculation is a must for this base, it takes to it very well with a saturated epsom salt solution otherwise it will settle very quickly. I did not see any noticeable thickening over time like I did with copper red V2-5. Tests were immersion blended and sieved twice at 120 mesh with the base, blended and sieved once with red iron oxide+SiC, blended and sieved once with copper carb and tin oxide. 1000 mesh silicon carbide Spanish red iron oxide was used if it matters

Mis resultados son... ponele que "prometen"... a futuro. Por ahora es verdoso con ciertos dejos azules, amarillentos y marrones. Como la luz cayendo sobre el follaje... Consejo de aplicación: carga muuuuy gruesa desarrolla las diferentes tonalidades. Con carga apenas gruesa un marrón común, sin demasiado interés (probar primero sobre teselas) A seguir.... Tal cual sugiere Marina V. Kurtz entre los comentarios, probaré agregar más sodio, cambiar la frita.... • English Daniel de Montmollin's book, "Pratique des émaux de grès", 2020 edition, is somewhat disconcerting to me, since Silica is on the vertical axis and Alumina on the horizontal one. Not a real problem, but I'm used to the other way. The book itself is a jewel to discover with care and dedication. Towards the end there is a small appendix by Patrick Buté regarding "Bleus de Fer" (iron blue) glazes with different molar formulas and samples based on diagram 25 (R2O:RO = 0.30:0.70). I chose one of them and added enough boron to fire it at cone 6/7. Once calculated, I see that it is very close, chemically, to several other recipes based on Jean-Pierre Prieto's Bleu de Fer. My results are... "promising"... in the future. My test tile is greenish with blue, yellowish and brown hints. Like the light falling through the jungle... Note that the glaze must be veeeeeeeery thick to show the different color shades. With a barely thick load, a common brown, without much interest (try first on tiles) To follow.... As Marina V. Kurtz suggests in the comments, I'll try adding more sodium, changing the frit to get, maybe, a "Bleu de Fer"

Name: OG Turquoise (whiting only)
Description: ###Rebecca's Notes### I am working on creating my own version of Dave's Turquoise with ingredients available to me. I did a series of tests where I subbed with either Mahavir or Neph Sye instead of Custer, Subbed EPK for tile #6 Kaolin, and Sub Gillespie instead of Gerstley. The UMF works out quite close, but the boron is 0.01 lower in mine and I didn't worry about trace minerals. I called the Mahavir version OG turquoise and the Neph Sye version ODG Turquoise. Name: Matt's Nuka
Description: Nuka recipe from Tim's recipe that was created based on a Hamada Shoji Nuka glaze with Japanese materials. This recipe may be way too refractory to melt in a 12-14hr cone 10 firing. I had to burn my own rice husk to get ash. mixed wood ash is mostly pine. Rice husks were burnt in bonfire for 1hr within a steel paint can. Once cool, ash was ground for 30sec in mortar & pestle. Ash was black carbon colored and same size as original husks when burned. Once ground, it looked like expresso grounds. Glaze itself was thick and looked like fur once dry on bisqued ware. 2 samples pictured were fired with wood in an 11hr fast fire. Kiln cooled very fast as well. Glaze stuck to bisque and did not flake off during drive to kiln.
Ingredients: Rice Husk Ash 34; Mixed wood ash 33; Silica 20; Grolleg Kaolin 13

Name: S072 ochsenblutrot strontium-6%
Description: nach ca. 45 jahren wieder eine versuchsreihe mit strontiumcarbonat in einer kupferrot- (sang de boeuf, ochsenblut-) glasur gestartet. 6% SrO, 10% SrO, 14% SrO. mein eindruck: srco₃ stabilisiert die glasur – das kupfer verteilt sich gleichmäßiger, das rot wirkt intensiver und dampft weniger stark auf benachbarte stücke ab. nachteil: bei höherem sro-anteil bildet sich auf der glasuroberfläche eine „apfelsinenschalenhaut“ mit kleinen pickeln. der teilweise ersatz von cao durch sro erhöht die temperaturstabilität der glasur und verstärkt die rubinrote farbwirkung.

Name: S072 ochsenblutrot strontiumcarbonat 10%
Description: CaO menge belassen, und 10 % SrO zugeführt, temperatur stabilität der glasur und die rubinrote farbwirkung erhöht. kegel 10. mittig eine messerspitze W4 (lavendelasche-glasur) geträufelt. ergab interessante verläufe an vertikalen flächen. nach dieser 10 %-tigen SrO probe kommt eine probe mit 14% SrO. dieses dunkle rubinrot stell ich mir auf einem hochwandigen porzellanscherben gut vor.

However in the original glaze it tended to over nucleate unless applied very thick. Therefore I continued by doing a line test with increased boron levels up to +0.075. This one gave me the best result in crystals while still being somewhat stable on the pot. Make no mistake though, with increased boron and such low alumina this will run easily so be very mindful of application thickness. You might also want to experiment with firing schedules. See how crystallization changes with fast cools, slow cools and holds. I would not apply this on any food surface. While I am unconcerned with any of the materials this is not a durable glaze for food surfaces. The zinc and calcium form a bristol reaction. For some reason a bristol reaction combined with copper is very detrimental to glaze durability. I have tested this with a gloss meter. Named after my mother, it was her favourite and she is now resting in it.

Name: purple dusk (modified)
Description: Stain is MS 6097 red. Currently trying to fix the microbubbles without getting rid of the phase separation. It is proving more difficult than expected. As it stands, the current recipe is based off of variant #11. All tiles have been fired to cone 5 in an electric test kiln. Here is the full list of variations: 1. Whiting instead of wollastonite in the base. No zinc, and 3% zircopax. 2. 2% zircopax, no zinc. 3. 3% zircopax, no zinc. 4. 4% zircopax, no zinc. 5. 5% zircopax, no zinc. 6. 6% zircopax, no zinc. 7. 5% zircopax, 5% titanium, no zinc. 8. 2% zircopax, 2% zinc. 9. 2% zircopax, 3.5% zinc 10. 2% zircopax, 5% zinc. 11. 3.5% zinc and zircopax 12. 5% zinc and zircopax 13. 3.5% zinc, 5% zircopax 14. 3% zinc and zircopax, 25% silica. 15. 3% zinc and zircopax, 45% G-200. Overall, the best glass is on test 7, followed by tests 5,6,11, and 12. Those four are all about the same, with very slight bubbling. 7 has practically no bubbles. Unfortunately, the phase separation is best on tiles 8-10 and 13, which all have seriously visible bubbles. Tiles 11 and 12 have the best overall finish, based on smoothness and phase separation. It seems like the glaze needs at least 3-5% zircopax for a stable finish, but once you get over 4%, the color really starts to suffer. Adding zinc in a similar amount as the zircopax seems to work well, but the perfect ratio has yet to be found. UPDATE: After running tests 16-18, I have discovered the perfect ratio! !!!!16: 5% zinc, 3% zircopax. This is the one. Stunning and perfect and beautiful.!!!! 17: 3.5% zinc and zircopax, with 4% rutile added. Decent color but has almost no mottling. 18: 3.5% zinc and zircopax, with 0.3% cobalt instead of 0.2. Overall, not much of a difference.

Description: Part of an exploration plotting the Bud Powell base across a spread of points on the Stull map. This is the bottom right corner. I was hoping to see more phase separation effects but its a pretty solid semi-opaque semi-gloss that doesn't craze on my porcelain. I need to test more to explore potential fuming from copper and chrome which may have caused pinks in the titanium dioxide and rutile tiles. Good colorant combs: Chrome - 0.6-1.0% (good earthy arts & crafts green) Manganese diox - 3-5% (dusty pink mauve) Copper Carb - 0.25-1.0% (Pale blue to seafoam) Copper Carb - 5-9% (deep rich green with black crystals) Red Iron Oxide - 6-7% (variegated glossy tan) Rutile - 3-5% (pale pink with some variegation) Rutile 9-15% - (sandy yellow tan) Cobalts seemed pretty bland and boring. Stains did not work well.

Name: 0. Base Septiembre, set fundente /September Base, flux set
Description: Spanish (english below) Siempre me produjeron curiosidad los morados/púrpuras oscuros de manganeso. Encontré algunas guías en libros y glazy: baja alúmina, bajo boro, dióxido de manganeso en torno a 3%, óx de cobalto entre 0.10 y 0.20%. Muchos citaban que el uso de estroncio colaboraba y también había menciones al bario. Algunos se inclinaban por bases bien alcalinas (K, Na, Li) y otros por bases con predominancia de alcalino-térreos (Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) Decidí probar con este set fundente, haciendo una "grilla de Currie" a medida: subir la alúmina de a 0.5 en la UMF y la sílice lo suficiente para llegar a las relaciones SiO2:Al2O3 de 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, y 15 (ver diagrama). Cometí varios errores: las teselas verticales no eran blancas. Me equivoqué de frasco y, en vez de óxido, usé carbonato de cobalto. Olvidé usar el mixer para mezclar las muestras y sólo usé el tamiz: se notan manchones de cobalto en los esmaltes. El morado oscuro está allí pero va a precisar ajuste. Como curiosidad aparte, a veces la teoría y la práctica se dan la mano: las teselas 5 y 10 son mates y las teselas 4, 9 y 14 parecen infracocidas. 😊 English I've always been fascinated by dark purple manganese glazes. I found some guidelines in books and here, on Glazy: low alumina, low boron, around 3% manganese dioxide, and 0.10-0.20% cobalt oxide. Many sources mentioned that strontium helps, and some also mentioned barium. Some recommended alkaline bases (K, Na, Li), while others suggested alkaline-earth bases (Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba). I decided to test this flux set, creating a modified "Currie grid": increasing alumina by 0.5 in the UMF and enough silica to achieve SiO2:Al2O3 ratios of 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, and 15 (see diagram). I made a few mistakes: the vertical test tiles weren't white, I grabbed the wrong jar and used cobalt carbonate instead of oxide, and I skipped mixing the samples with a mixer, only sieving: you can see cobalt spots in the glazes. The dark purple is there, but it will need some fine-tuning. On a side note, theory and practice sometimes align: tiles 5 and 10 are matte, while tiles 4, 9, and 14 look like they're underfired. 😊
Ingredients: Spodumene (Crecer) 2024 26; Nefelina Sienita - 2024/ Crecer 26; Strontium Carbonate 20; Whiting 2024 (Crecer) 20; Frita 174 - 2024/Crecer 8; Manganese Dioxide 2.8 (additional); Cobalt Carbonate 0.15 (additional)

Description: This glaze recipe is not mine. It was given to me by Tony Hansen (the creator of digital fire) - This glaze has been in my books for ages. Along my glaze making journey I have found many different variations of it; Mainly because Kona Feldspar and gerstly borate is either impossible or difficult to come by. This has resulted in many substitution recipes which are not the original. I did not want the original to be lost to time and adaptation and I don't see it on glazy, So I will hold it's memory here. It's truly my favorite glaze. Long lasting and a true potters red. Tips about this glaze : 1. Gerstly borate makes it very thick so it generally needs a little more water than a common glaze recipe. The gravity is best around 1.25 - 1.3. 2 Iron sources are, in my experience, getting low quality. Try yellow or black iron oxide as a substitute. 3 The amount of boron in this glaze is insane and its ratios are super off. 4 the amount of water you put in is vital. Too much and it'll run or be too thick, too little and the red will often turn into a bluish tint. "No wonder it turned red with almost no metal flux. Look at how they abused boron so long ago!"

Name: S 128 kuan KO-E F1C-1 R
Description: Starke Reduktion nötig, um einen intensiven jadegrünen Seladon-Effekt zu erzielen – je dicker der Glasurauftrag, desto kräftiger und wasserartiger das Grün. Für das beste Ergebnis die Glasur 2–4-mal auf die knochentrockene Oberfläche tauchen. Ein Fingerwisch am lederharten Scherben darf kein Glasurmehl mehr lösen. 2–3 mm Glasurschicht intensivieren die Farbtiefe. Ein dicker Scherben hilft Bodenrisse durch Spannung zu vermeiden; alternativ kann Gegenglasieren der Unterseite Abhilfe schaffen. Starke Reduktion beginnt idealerweise bereits zwischen 800°C und 900°C – Timing und Intensität der Reduktion sind entscheidend für Farbwirkung und Klarheit. Die Glasur und ihr grüner Farbton reagieren empfindlich auf Unter- oder Überfeuerung: zu niedrige Temperaturen ergaben Fettiges Seidenmatt Grün, zu hohe Temperaturen ergeben ein klares Jade Grün. Eine Variante mit schwarzem Eisenoxid zeigte bei besonders dicker Auftragung Blasenbildung – unklar, ob dies ursächlich war. ist noch zu testen.

Name: S126 KCC II A1 (Schreiner Alexasche)
Description: nicht höher als kegel 9 brennen. starke reduktion ab ca. 800 °c. rezept auch mit vielen anderen eisenhaltigen holzaschen getestet → alle mit zufriedenstellendem ergebnis. wichtig: aschen gut waschen, sehr viel haftmittel (z. b. relatin) verwenden und in mehreren schichten auf knochentrockener glasur auftragen. craquelé-bildung hängt stark von der tonsorte ab → entweder schuppen-craquelé oder feines haar-craquelé. Do not fire higher than cone 9. Strong reduction from approx. 800 °C. Recipe also tested with many other iron-containing wood ashes → all with satisfactory results. Important: wash the ash thoroughly, use a generous amount of adhesive (e.g. Relatin) and apply in several layers to bone-dry glaze. Craquel´e formation depends heavily on the type of clay → either flake craquelè or fine hairline craquelè. ( "scaly crackle" or "scaly crackle glaze.")

Name: [1] K3 Titanium Cerium
Description: This glaze is developed in the K3 Glaze research project of Jeannine Vrins. The aim is to look for the lowest melting temperature, low amounts of colourants and frits and a low ecological impact. The Kaolin in this glaze is a Polwhite from Imerys and has a low Alumina content and a higher KNa content than other kaolins. If you use another kaolin I suggest to find the right temperature which will be a bit higher than the 1180°C I fired these to a well molten surface. Another way to lower your temperature is to use a finer grained silica. My firing schedule: 150°C/h to 1080°, 60°C/h to 1180°C, 10' soaking time and 200°C/h cooling to 950°C. I add 80% of water with some deflocculant, bentonite and cmc in it, a rheological mixture which makes it brushable and suspended. On a tile of 10 square centimetres I use 10 grams of glaze. Test and experiment with this recipe before you put it on your work! I suspect you will have different results because you use different sources for your raw materials, a different kiln, different claybody, and a different artistic hand. I would be very happy if you add your pictures under mine in this K3 glaze library. The K3 Glaze library is part of my PhD research at PXL-MAD Hasselt. Thank you to Anton Reijnders to support me with all his knowledge (his new book will be published 9/2026). And a big thank you to Derek Au to support the ceramic community with this glaze database.
Ingredients: Krijt (CLPRT 23 XRF) 33.3; Kwarts (CLPRT 23 XRF) 33.3; Kaolien (CLPRT 23 XRF) 33.3; Titanium Dioxide TiDi (CLPRT-XRF23) 10 (additional); Cerium oxide 2 (additional)

Name: [63] K432 Chroom Tin
Description: This glaze is developed in the K3 Glaze research project of Jeannine Vrins. The aim is to look for the lowest melting temperature, low amounts of colourants and frits and a low ecological impact. The Kaolin in this glaze is a Polwhite from Imerys and has a low Alumina content and a higher KNa content than other kaolins. If you use another kaolin I suggest to find the right temperature which will be a bit higher than the 1180°C I fired these to a well molten surface. Another way to lower your temperature is to use a finer grained silica. My firing schedule: 150°C/h to 1080°, 60°C/h to 1180°C, 10' soaking time and 200°C/h cooling to 950°C. I add 80% of water with some deflocculant, bentonite and cmc in it, a rheological mixture which makes it brushable and suspended. On a tile of 10 square centimetres I use 10 grams of glaze. Test and experiment with this recipe before you put it on your work! I suspect you will have different results because you use different sources for your raw materials, a different kiln, different claybody, and a different artistic hand. I would be very happy if you add your pictures under mine in this K3 glaze library. The K3 Glaze library is part of my PhD research at PXL-MAD Hasselt. The Kaolin in this glaze is a Polwhite from Imerys and has a low Alumina content and a higher KNa content than other kaolins. If you use another kaolin I suggest to find the right temperature which will be a bit higher than the 1180°C I fired these to a well molten surface. Another way to lower your temperature is to use a finer grained silica. My firing schedule: 150°C/h to 1080°, 60°C/h to 1180°C, 10' soaking time and 200°C/h cooling to 950°C. I add 80% of water with some deflocculant, bentonite and cmc in it, a rheological mixture which makes it brushable and suspended. On a tile of 10 square centimetres I use 10 grams of glaze. Test and experiment with this recipe before you put it on your work! I suspect you will have different results because you use different sources for your raw materials, a different kiln, different claybody, and a different artistic hand. Name: [131] K3 Koper Kobalt
Description: This glaze is developed in the K3 Glaze research project of Jeannine Vrins. The aim is to look for the lowest melting temperature, low amounts of colourants and frits and a low ecological impact. The Kaolin in this glaze is a Polwhite from Imerys and has a low Alumina content and a higher KNa content than other kaolins. If you use another kaolin I suggest to find the right temperature which will be a bit higher than the 1180°C I fired these to a well molten surface. Another way to lower your temperature is to use a finer grained silica. My firing schedule: 150°C/h to 1080°, 60°C/h to 1180°C, 10' soaking time and 200°C/h cooling to 950°C. I add 80% of water with some deflocculant, bentonite and cmc in it, a rheological mixture which makes it brushable and suspended. On a tile of 10 square centimetres I use 10 grams of glaze. Test and experiment with this recipe before you put it on your work! I suspect you will have different results because you use different sources for your raw materials, a different kiln, different claybody, and a different artistic hand. I would be very happy if you add your pictures under mine in this K3 glaze library. The K3 Glaze library is part of my PhD research at PXL-MAD Hasselt. The Kaolin in this glaze is a Polwhite from Imerys and has a low Alumina content and a higher KNa content than other kaolins. If you use another kaolin I suggest to find the right temperature which will be a bit higher than the 1180°C I fired these to a well molten surface. Another way to lower your temperature is to use a finer grained silica. My firing schedule: 150°C/h to 1080°, 60°C/h to 1180°C, 10' soaking time and 200°C/h cooling to 950°C. I add 80% of water with some deflocculant, bentonite and cmc in it, a rheological mixture which makes it brushable and suspended. On a tile of 10 square centimetres I use 10 grams of glaze. Test and experiment with this recipe before you put it on your work! I suspect you will have different results because you use different sources for your raw materials, a different kiln, different claybody, and a different artistic hand. The aim is to look for the lowest melting temperature, low amounts of colourants and frits and a low ecological impact. The Kaolin in this glaze is a Polwhite from Imerys and has a low Alumina content and a higher KNa content than other kaolins. If you use another kaolin I suggest to find the right temperature which will be a bit higher than the 1180°C I fired these to a well molten surface. Another way to lower your temperature is to use a finer grained silica. My firing schedule: 150°C/h to 1080°, 60°C/h to 1180°C, 10' soaking time and 200°C/h cooling to 950°C. I add 80% of water with some deflocculant, bentonite and cmc in it, a rheological mixture which makes it brushable and suspended. On a tile of 10 square centimetres I use 10 grams of glaze. Test and experiment with this recipe before you put it on your work! I suspect you will have different results because you use different sources for your raw materials, a different kiln, different claybody, and a different artistic hand. I would be very happy if you add your pictures under mine in this K3 glaze library. The K3 Glaze library is part of my PhD research at PXL-MAD Hasselt. Thank you to Anton Reijnders to support me with all his knowledge (his new book will be published 9/2026). And a big thank you to Derek Au to support the ceramic community with this glaze database.
Ingredients: Kaolien (CLPRT 23 XRF) 38; Kwarts (CLPRT 23 XRF) 35; Krijt (CLPRT 23 XRF) 15; FR 3221 CLPRT 8; Tin Oxide 5 (additional); Zircoon Silicaat (CLPRT XRF 23) 5 (additional); Chrome Oxide 0.04 (additional)

The aim is to look for the lowest melting temperature, low amounts of colourants and frits and a low ecological impact. The Kaolin in this glaze is a Polwhite from Imerys and has a low Alumina content and a higher KNa content than other kaolins. If you use another kaolin I suggest to find the right temperature which will be a bit higher than the 1180°C I fired these to a well molten surface. Another way to lower your temperature is to use a finer grained silica. My firing schedule: 150°C/h to 1080°, 60°C/h to 1180°C, 10' soaking time and 200°C/h cooling to 950°C. Name: Stroke & Coat Base with zirconium
Description: My community studio basically drinks Stroke and Coats by Mayco.. we do a lot of paint nights and kid stuff, so they're perfect. They don't move, they behave like fired on tempera paint, and they self glaze. You can use them from 05 to 6 with no color changes. S&C are billed as "wonderglaze", they're a really strange thing. Mix the recipe and then add the cmc afterwards to make it brushable (or not). Flocculate however you want. I don't really ever touch bentonite anymore unless i'm making a mud mask. Note about CMC - if you are mixing it from powder, use hot water, let it stand for a few minutes, and before you mix it up add .02 copper to it (way less than a pinch) to keep it from rotting over the long term. Note about Zircopax, from TH: Suppliers of encapsulated stains recommend a zircon addition, but are often unclear about why. Here is the reason, it is a "fining agent". If you are using this as a lowfire glaze, the zircopax isn't as big a deal. It really counts when you get to cone 6 temps, then it keeps the stain from gassing out, which you definitely have to worry about in quantities more than 8%.

(with Neph Sy and colorant cobalt) Test results: I dipped the tiles 3 times into the glaze in overlapping layers. To show this test tile I used the original recipe with Neph Sy. Reason is that I can't find the exct composition of slate. Only a general descriptin. See below! I have already a glaze containing shale and have plenty of shale powder on stock. -- Without colarant : On the white clay body it's a smooth surface without crazing. First glaze layer fits well. On the second and third layer the glaze shows pinholes and runs. Same result on the Southern Ice Porcelain body. Glaze seems to run a little bit more. For Slate/Shale I have found this description on a internet website for roofers: This is only a general description. Mineral Composition: 30-60% sericite, a fine-grained light mica (muscovite), important for the cleavage and smooth workability of the slate. 10-30% chlorite, also important for the cleavage and color of the slate. These two components are so-called foliated silicates, i.e., minerals that are arranged in very fine, plate-like layers. 20-40% quartz, which gives the slate strength and hardness. 0-5% calcite or other carbonates 0-3% other minerals such as feldspar, rutile, ores, and coal, some of which also give the slate its characteristic color.

Name: Kohiki/Mishima/Hakeme Slip

Description: Mix to a yogurt consistency, very thick. Apply to a slab, allow the slab to set to leather hard. During the drying process, you can alter the cracking with brush strokes. Use a heat gun to dry the slip surface out. When the slip has dried out (should look matte) cast the slab repeatedly on the table, stretching and thinning the slab and causing the slip to fracture and tessellate. From studying Akira State's work, it appears that if slip is applied unevenly the thin parts will dry and crack more than the thick parts. If the slip is too wet, the cracks won't happen. If the slab is too dry, the slab will tear apart. Bending a slab slightly and checking to see if the slip cracks is a good way to check. This will look best on dark clay. Fired in reduction it looks nice and toasty! Also works as hakeme and mishima.

Name: Rutty Butty
Description: Glossy Transparent Glaze can be made as a dipping glaze using just water, or as a brushing glaze. Name: Radiant Ash; Unicorn Cream
Other Names: Radiant Ash Var. W/Bi/Sn/Mn; W/Bi/Sn/Mn Ash crystal 10.28
Description: an off-white base with rainbow iridescent macros making use your yard scrap. this one seems to be slightly dichroic. cooler, pale purple hues poke out more in sunlight where a warmer yellow/beige takes hold under florescent lights. unbothered rainbow macros slay regardless almost like oil to water when playing with other glazes. strong rivulet reaction during overlaps or this one will crawl/gravitate towards & over other glazes during the firing with minimal mixing interface. great effect to implement if that's your thing does well under a variety of ramp hold temps, but prefers less time on the upper end and more around the Fe crystalizing range, at least from my experience. would imagine this doing well in 5-6 range given amount of B present but i don't fire anything below ^8 light will shine through if your porcelain is thin enough for those considering the potential note on ingredients: wood ash is mixed yard brush [mostly hickory/maple/evergreen & shrub] sieved dry with fine wire strainer until a fine powder/sediment remains. amount weighed out and added to mix, unwashed, AFTER everything else in recipe has been sieved 2x 100-mesh personally hate sieving spodumene so i throw that in with the wood ash when weighing out. the gelling effect of unwashed wood ash mixes with the soapy effect of spodumene and the glaze becomes more manageable after sitting for like an hour. a dash of prepared peptapon 9 [in very small amounts helps counteract intensity of foaminess from ash & spond. while unifying everything] is always helpful for any crystalline recipe, just ease up on additives when working with ash [very potent gelling effect] this is my standard practice with any ash recipe. consistency is key with glazing
Ingredients: Silica 28; Zinc Oxide 20; Spodumene 16; Ferro Frit 3134 12; Fusion Frit 644 10; Wood ash 6; Barium Carbonate 4; Dolomite 4; Tungsten Trioxide 6 (additional); Bismuth oxide 4 (additional); Rutile 2 (additional); Manganese Dioxide 1 (additional); Tin Oxide 1 (additional)

Name: [412] K3 alternatief 3 Tin Chroom
Description: This glaze is developed in the K3 Glaze research project of Jeannine Vrins. The aim is to look for the lowest melting temperature, low amounts of colourants and frits and a low ecological impact. The Kaolin in this glaze is a Polwhite from Imerys and has a low Alumina content and a higher KNa content than other kaolins. If you use another kaolin I suggest to find the right temperature which will be a bit higher than the 1180°C I fired these to a well molten surface. Another way to lower your temperature is to use a finer grained silica. My firing schedule: 150°C/h to 1080°, 60°C/h to 1180°C, 10' soaking time and 200°C/h cooling to 950°C. I add 80% of water with some deflocculant, bentonite and cmc in it, a rheological mixture which makes it brushable and suspended. On a tile of 10 square centimetres I use 10 grams of glaze. Test and experiment with this recipe before you put it on your work! I suspect you will have different results because you use different sources for your raw materials, a different kiln, different claybody, and a different artistic hand. I would be very happy if you add your pictures under mine in this K3 glaze library. The K3 Glaze library is part of my PhD research at PXL-MAD Hasselt. Thank you to Anton Reijnders to support me with all his knowledge (his new book will be published 9/2026). And a big thank you to Derek Au to support the ceramic community with this glaze database.
Ingredients: Kaolien (CLPRT 23 XRF) 39; Kwarts (CLPRT 23 XRF) 36; Krijt (CLPRT 23 XRF) 16; Tin Oxide 10 (additional); Chrome Oxide 0.3 (additional)

Name: Rock
Description: This glaze was made by accident in a limit test, but it's sorta nifty! In reduction it creates a texture exactly like fake rocks, and in oxidation it creates craters. It's very stiff and should be applied on the thicker side for the dramatic effect. I used 330 grams of water for a 500 gram dry mix, about 66g wet/100g dry and it was just thick enough. I'll be testing alternate carbonates to see how their bubbling changes the color and texture, since grey is meh. Interestingly enough, the reduction firing of this glaze seems to have a fully resolved glossy inner layer, and anywhere clay is exposed was already from dipping quickly in such a thick mix. While I certainly need to look and test more, this is potentially 'functional' if not for looking and feeling like a rock.
Ingredients: Silica 50; Ferro Frit 3195 40; EP Kaolin 10; Rutile 4; Bentonite 2; Manganese Dioxide 2; Cobalt Carbonate 0.5

Name: Blueberry Mush (V1)
Description: An interesting spider web of semi-opaque matte blue over a translucent green which turns black where it gathers. I was aiming to create a glaze 'in the spirit, no, the very essence of a blueberry'. A bit melty, apply thin as the carbonates become very bubbly and grey otherwise. It fails in oxidation and is just sort of a blue-grey. I'm working on color adjustments, thickness, and how to address the off-gassing of the carbonates. The effect came from a color run I did on the base glaze where I noticed the floating effect and became interested - I believe that the boron and calcium lent by the frit is what's doing it, as other floating blue glazes rely on similar levels of silica/boron/calcium.
Ingredients: Ferro Frit 3195 80; EP Kaolin 20; Rutile 4 (additional); Bentonite 2 (additional); Manganese Dioxide 2 (additional); Cobalt Carbonate 0.5 (additional)

Name: Satin Matte Clear* (material substitions)
Description: I have made material substitutions for the UK and have had great success over Amaco velvet underglazes, at Cone 6. SG1.4. Below notes from original creator: This is based on a glaze I’ve been using for years. I’d love to give credit where it is due but the original is a recipe that’s been floating around for ages and I don’t know its origin. I’ve been removing opacifiers and colourants from various satin matte glazes searching for the one that makes the best satin clear for over underglaze illustrations. I think it’s sad that so many illustrators feel like they have to leave underglazed surfaces raw in order to avoid ruining their work because gloss clears wash out colour or feel cheap and plasticky and satin clears are foggy. This one has never failed me! Of course it’s a great matte base so you can add an opacifier or some colourants to it as well. Works well with no special firing, however the factory setting “fast fire” on many kilns will yield a somewhat shinier surface. If using pre-set firings, stick with medium or slow. If custom programming, you can ramp up fast to save time and slow through the peak to allow this glaze to come out more matte. I make it in small batches with CMC gum to allow for painting. If I made it as a large batch dipping glaze I would give it a specific gravity of 1.50 and adjust from there.

Name: Aventurine
Description: Aventurine is a type of quartz, molten silica that crystallized and solidified during cooling. It contains metallic particles in the form of flat platelets, which create a characteristic sparkling effect as light reflects off the metal crystals. The stone is identified by its metallic sheen and can appear in a range of colors such as green, red, brown, black, and even blue. In ceramics, the term aventurine refers to an iron rich glaze in which iron particles crystallize during cooling. Like any crystal, they reflect light and create a sense of sparkle, although in this case the crystals are relatively small. This is a very fluid glaze with a high flux content, and due to the low amount of clay and free quartz in the recipe, it scratches easily and is considered more prone to wear. For some time now, I have been researching aventurine glazes. The starting point was a beautiful natural stone, with depth, shine, and sparkle that are hard to ignore. From there, curiosity emerged about how to translate a geological material into a ceramic language, and how to imitate in a glaze not only the color, but also the behavior and the tactile quality of the stone. The experiments move between different versions using iron oxide and additional oxides, searching for that delicate moment when the glaze melts, responds to heat, and reorganizes itself during cooling. In the kiln, subtle differences appear viscosity, sparkle, and depth that tell a story of chemistry, time, and temperature. It is a slow research process, full of experiments, mistakes, and surprises.
Ingredients: Barium Carbonate 38; Ferro Frit 3110 37; Magnesium carbonate 7; Silica 6; Lithium Carbonate 5; Frit 6004 4; Kaolin 3; Bentonite 2; Rutile 15 (additional)

Potentially the addition of gum or a suspension agent could help alleviate some of the settling but not all. They do melt and bubble in a large volume. SO DO NOT PLACE things glazed with this close together or near other items in the kiln. It expands about an inch or more from the pot and has the potential to essentially reach out and attach to neighboring pots. These ARE NOT useable for FOOD SURFACES, the glaze is brittle and will rub off. This is a decorative glaze and is non-functional."

Name: Satin Matte Clear* (5:1) add silica
Description: This is based on a glaze I’ve been using for years. I’d love to give credit where it is due but the original is a recipe that’s been floating around for ages and I don’t know its origin. I’ve been removing opacifiers and colourants from various satin matte glazes searching for the one that makes the best satin clear for over underglaze illustrations. I think it’s sad that so many illustrators feel like they have to leave underglazed surfaces raw in order to avoid ruining their work because gloss clears wash out colour or feel cheap and plasticky and satin clears are foggy. This one has never failed me! Of course it’s a great matte base so you can add an opacifier or some colourants to it as well. Works well with no special firing, however the factory setting “fast fire” on many kilns will yield a somewhat shinier surface. If using pre-set firings, stick with medium or slow. If custom programming, you can ramp up fast to save time and slow through the peak to allow this glaze to come out more matte. I make it in small batches with CMC gum to allow for painting. If I made it as a large batch dipping glaze I would give it a specific gravity of 1.50 and adjust from there.
Ingredients: Kaolin 104.4; Standard borax frit 77.4; Whiting 64.8; Silica 53.4; Bentonite 3 (additional)

Name: Basic Lincoln 60
Atmospheres: Oxidation; Neutral; Reduction; Salt & Soda; Wood
Description: This clay came from needing a cheap but workable throwing body for general use while I build a portfolio of work. After getting clay from many of the mines in california and running various tests I found that lincoln 60 on its own was the right combination of cheap, long term available, consistent, and workable. The other clays I worked with were Amador, Green Stripe, Ione Kaolin, C-Red, Gauge Red, Carbondale Red, and Lincoln 8. I've tried three way combinations of many of these clays and found lincoln 60 with any of the reds to produce a superior throwing body than the lincoln clay on its own. Ideally, I would like to try a blend of Lincoln 60, Tile 6, and Gauge/Carbondale Red, but the reds in California are inconsistently available. Most of these are very usable on their own with the exception of ione kaolin, which I found to perform poorly for throwing and had some strange thixotropic issues. A triaxial blend of lincoln 60, g200eu, silica, and wollastonite was performed at cone 10 to assess the vitrification of the finished clay body. The table of results is in the images associated with this body and show that you can fully substitute the 5% wollastonite with silica and almost certainly stay below 0.5% absorption.
Ingredients: Lincoln 60 85; G200 EU 10; Vansil W-30 Wollastonite 5

Name: Pussy Willow Mist
Description: This recipe came from a search to make the perfect soft and snowy ice fog haze glaze for pussy willow impressions in dark clay. Could it be simplified? Probably. But it works well and I'm going to a take a break before I try to fix what isn't broken. From my testing, going to 100% frit and no gerstley tends to kill the optical blues and increases enclosed visible bubbling in the glaze body. If you are looking for something similar that still breaks but more cream toned and opaque, up the colourants.

Name: dupe 22 CLEAR
Description: Made specifically to fit Armadillo Clay's Cinco Blanco (fired to a hot cone 6) and Armadillo's Cone 5 Porcelain (fired to a hot cone 6). Commercial gloss clears don't seem to fit these clays, and result in crazing. This glaze does not craze on these clays if fired to a cone 6.5, even when applied thick. Dolomite provides magnesium (low expansion) and a lack of Neph Sye means a reduction in sodium and potassium (both high expansion). No zinc, so it should provide minimal interaction with stains and underglazes, but testing is always recommended. It does interact with Mason stain 6006 Deep Crimson, 6381 Blackberry Wine, and possibly others. If you want to use it as a gloss base and add encapsulated stain, you'll need to also add 6-8% zircopax (or spectralux or equivalent) to keep the glaze from dissolving the encapsulation and causing bubbles. Alternatively, John Britt's "Robust E" also fits these clays, but contains 2% zinc, which interacts with some stains and underglazes. Apply thin. 7500 Grams dry + 7500 grams water = 2.5+ gallons

Name: Chappell Floating Blue, Blue Hare
Description: Source/Alternate names: James Chappell The Potters Complete Book of Clay and Glazes Source/Alternate names: same oxides as Slate Blue With Green Specks, similar to Blue Jean Blue and Cobbled Floating Blue Notes: Candice Roeder: a deep blue-brown background of great depth with lighter mottled blues that seem to float on the surface of the background glaze. with more of the lighter mottled blues where the application is thickest. Watch thickness near the bottom of the pot. It fires best on the light side of cone 6 (standard cone just bending), seems to get greener and more fluid the higher you go. Cone 5 works well, too. The book says to weigh the ingredients very carefully, use distilled water or water that is known to have a low mineral content. Mix then add the CMC solution. The book warns that the glaze is fickle, and recommends against firing this glaze in the same kiln with glazes that contain copper, chrome, nickel or manganese. Mineral content of the water is an important factor. I have noticed an adverse effect as the author noted, and now fire an entire kiln load of this glaze. Notes: Martha Muzychka: not what I expected, mostly green with a few spots of blue. On black stoneware clay, it gives an unusual cloudy effect. Notes: Ivy Glasgow: a popular and beautiful (when done right) glaze. The original Floating Blue pigments have been tested and found to be food safe. When floating blue works, it is lovely. Key seems to be firing to no more than Cone 5-1/2 and cooling quickly. Notes: James Chappell: the colours seem to float on a surface of a darker background of great depth, reminiscent of a deep pool of water. Its colour and opacity vary greatly with thickness so it highlights irregularities in the surface. Phase separation in the translucent matrix makes the colour swirl as small rivulets of more fluid glass flow around more viscous phases. Titanium crystals in the matrix make it sparkle. Calcium-borate boron-blue crystals grow on the surface. Bubbles of escaping gases create pools of lighter coloured glass surrounded by darker rings. Small black speckles are produced by unground particles of iron. Use distilled or low mineral water, force all material through an 80 mesh screen, stir thoroughly before and during use to prevent settling out of the iron content, apply the thickness of a dime, fire to cone 6 oxidation exactly, and cool normally. Do not substitute any other chemicals for those given, it is a fickle glaze. It depends on the Gerstley borate to suspend it. Notes: I substitute Cobalt Carb 2.0. What caught my eye, was the description of it as slate blue, which doesn't fit my results. So, I picked up the original recipe, and it differs from the one Sharon posted. You might try this version in your tests. It is called Floating Blue...from James Chappell's book, Clay and Glazes. This glaze produces a deep blue-brown background of great depth with lighter mottled blues that seem to float on the surface of the background glaze. The glaze has more of the lighter mottled blues where the application is thickest. Watch thickness near the bottom of the pot. The C.M.C. measurement refers to a premixed CMC and water solution. For the Silica, I use 325 mesh Flint. The rutile, is just powdered rutile from the ceramics supply. It fires best on the light side of cone 6 (standard cone just bending), seems to get greener and more fluid the higher you go. Cone 5 works well, too. I do not find a need for bentonite. The book says to weigh the ingredients very carefully, use distilled water or water that is known to have a low mineral content. Mix then add the CMC solution. Sieve two or three times through a 60 to 80 mesh sieve to thoroughly disperse the cobalt, iron, and rutile. The book warns that the glaze is fickle, and recommends against firing this glaze in the same kiln with glazes that contain copper, chrome, nickel or manganese. Mineral content of the water is an important factor. I have noticed an adverse effect as the author noted, and now fire an entire kiln load of this glaze. The glaze should be stirred occasionally during application because the iron has a tendency to settle. Chappell's Suggested variations: Stipple on additional glaze with brush or apply with sponge for an even more mottled effect. Or: lightly sponge a thin wash of 3 grams of chrome oxide to 100 grams of water plus a tablespoon of CMC over the top to produce a floating blue glaze with subtle green tints. Or: Over the glaze, sponge lightly with a rutile wash consisting of 2 grams rutile per 100g of water for a floating blue glaze with slightly tan crystalline tints on the surface. submitted by: Candice Roeder source for original recipe: James Chappell
Ingredients: NKO Nepheline Syenite 47.3; Gerstley Borate 27; NKO Kwarts 20.3; NKO Kaolien v2 5.4; Rutile 4 (additional); Bentonite 2 (additional); Red Iron Oxide 2 (additional); Cobalt Oxide 1 (additional)

You may find that some stains need more or less for full effect. It's called Zircopax in the recipe, but what I use is actually Superfine Zirconium Opacifier from Keane's, not actually Zircopax brand. Different stains have different strengths. The stains here are Chrysanthos Ultra Stains. Test how much you need of your particular stain to get the colour you want. The titanium seems more opaque on white clay than on black clay. I suspect too that the specific titanium oxide I am using is not as effective as it could be. So I would recommend testing that on your clay with your titanium as well.

Description: This was an off shoot of a glaze called Alabama rain from a John Bitt book. The original glaze did not have the flux ratio I liked and had custer feldspar (which people were looking for a replacement for) so I redeveloped the recipe for some of my students. This glaze is a workhorse glaze; It works well on white, red, and black clays. You can add iron to it to turn it a little grey. It turns into Sea salt type color. . Be warned, This glaze should not form a matt texture, crystals, or turn tan . If it does that probably means you are not firing hot enough. You can see in one test tile that the glaze makes crystals. I can't recall if this is from a small hold att 1600f or if I did not fire it hot enough but this glaze is not supposed to crystalize from the Tidi. If used properly the glaze should turn Zinc pink. Notes: This glaze is great on porcelain, white stoneware, and red clays. It is meant to be a workhorse with good flux ratio and melt at cone 6. Light pink if fired correctly. Can be turned in to a few other glazes if you add a little black iron oxide to it. By adding 1% black iron oxide you can get a great multi color glaze and by adding 3% black iron oxide to the recipe you can get a very good "sea salt" type glaze". (Will put this glaze in another tab) If you do not have Mahavir feldspar you can probably use G-200 feldspar. I have no tested this but I am willing to bet it'll work. This glaze was made public as a gift to my patrons who by vote decided to make it available to the public. If you do not have gerstley borate, You should be able to use Gillespie in a 1:1 . I have not tested this yet although that seems to be the consensus with other recipes I have tried. "How am I gonna balance the flux ratio, it's gatta be higher than this.....maybe..... Put some zinc in that B!t(h? ...... Put some zinc in dat bish!......ZINCINABISH!"

Name: 24k Bright Gold Lustre (11%)
Description: This is a bright gold lustre glaze based on a modern mercaptide system rather than traditional sulphur–resin lustres. The gold source is a gold(I) aryl thiolate, chosen for its clean thermal decomposition and reliable reduction to metallic gold at relatively low temperatures. The organic vehicle uses a high-temperature acrylic polymer system with a small resin component to control film strength, drying behaviour, and edge stability during firing. Micro-additions of metal fluxes are included to promote adhesion, gloss, and even gold deposition. Many of the materials in this recipe will look unfamiliar if you’re used to historic lustres. That’s intentional. This formulation was developed to avoid common problems such as burnishing, purple cast, crawling, and uneven deposition, while keeping firing temperatures low enough for use on most glaze bases. In our testing various cone 6 glazes were used throughout. A UV tracer is included in this formulation to make application more predictable across different substrates. Lustres can easily disappear visually on darker or highly coloured glazes, making it hard to judge coverage while working. Under UV light, this tracer reveals the wet film clearly, allowing you to see exactly where material has been applied and how evenly it’s laid down. An image of the tracer in action is included. Because several components are not self-explanatory from their names alone, a full technical walkthrough is provided here: 👉 https://www.tyndrumpottery.com/gold-lustre-glaze That guide explains: what each component actually does why it was chosen over more traditional options how the gold compound is made and how the system behaves on the bench and in the kiln This recipe is shared openly for educational use, experimentation, and further development. It assumes a basic level of chemical handling competence and is not intended as a beginner lustre.
Ingredients: Toluene 32.33; Isophrone 32.33; Aryl Gold(I) Thiolate 20; Polymer Blend 15; Bismuth Octoate 0.27; Rhodium Octoate 0.07

Name: Jingdezhen Yingqing (Qingbai) Body I
Description: Taken from Nigel Wood's Chinese Glazes Chemical analysis found on Table 14 in Chapter 3, Page 51 According to the text, Yingqing/Qingbai clay bodies were high in iron content as far as porcelains go, at nearly 1%. However, with good reduction, they're meant to be bluish white under the icy iron-blue celadons that coated them, while any unglazed portions reoxidize to a nice rust-orange, making for a beautiful warm/cool contrast while also being superbly translucent. 1/20/26 This clay is not plastic on its own, and is very short and crumbly without the addition of bentonite. I started with 30g of bentonite to my 1000g batch (3%), and this seemed to be a good start. After wedging in the bentonite, throwing on a wheel and hand-forming coils went relatively smoothly, though next batch I will try 4% and go from there. Hopefully this doesn't impact the end whiteness or translucency. Raw clay is very red from the red iron oxide and bisque fires to a nice pale buff-tone. Will test cone 6 shrinkage and cone 10 shrinkage, as well as how a blue celadon and a clear look on it. 2/12/26 The porcelain tiles have all been fired! This clay comes out a cool gray-white and is very vitreous and thus prone to plucking and slumping. Two tiles stuck together but I was able to get them loose with some plucking. The clay almost glazes itself. Excellent translucency at a quarter inch and below. Only minimal orange reoxidation from the iron, am going to tweak this as I really like the orange flashing effect the iron is supposed to give. Takes glazes very well with no crazing on my tests. 5/10/26 Got a full piece out of the kiln, a small bowl. Zero plucking issues when placed on kiln wash. Warps a bit, much like many other porcelains. Superbly translucent where thin. No spotting from the iron and the body is a beautiful sheet-white with some orange oxidizing present where the foot ring and glaze meet. With some minor tweaks, this is an all around a wonderful clay to work with! Dry shrinkage: 4.17% Cone 04 shrinkage: 6.25% Cone 6 shrinkage: 12.5% Cone 10 shrinkage: 12.5% Brand name materials used: Mahavir Potash Feldspar Amtalc C-98 Texas Talc (Discontinued, my local supplier still has reserves on hand) English Grolleg/China Clay

Description: With this recipe i tried to achieve something similar to 'Mary's Error Fake Shino' but with the ingredients that I had to hand. So far i am very happy with how the tests have come out. Fired to Cone 6 on 4 test tiles. No hold or soak on the firing. Each test tiles were on a speckled white clay body (Primo 2502 with speckle) They were dipped for 3,4,5 & 6 seconds. Each dip worked well. I prefer the thinner / 3 second dip. I actually developed this recipe to work on 'Nelson Pottery CB3' clay, but have not yet tested it on that clay. I will add photos soon. Please excuse any mistakes. This is my first glaze and i am by no means an expert.

I used my recycled clay which is a mix of porcelain, stoneware, and my wild clay based clay body.

Name: Kwong All Purpose clay (1)
Description: In the original recipe, the first ingredient was fire clay. After looking up a subsititution i found that grog could be used, not realizing that there was grog already added to the recipe. This created a consistency that felt like it was melting/oobleck-like. Along with this weird consistancy it was very grogy, so difficult to work with to say the least. It fired successfully, creating a red-brown color. I didn't enjoy this clay, but that was purely a user error.
Ingredients: Grog 70; Redart 50; Tile #6 Kaolin 10; Wollastonite 5; Strontium Carbonate 0.5

Name: Brown Stoneware Sumike Takada (2)
Description: This clay was nice to work with; it had a smooth texture and felt workable. The only downside is that it was quite short. I'm sure that with more testing and with letting it sit longer to absorb the water, it would help. It fired to a beautiful earthy brown.
Ingredients: Redart 45; Goldart 41; Tile #6 Kaolin 7; Silica 5; Custer Feldspar 2

Name: Mott's Red Clay (3)
Description: Mott's Red Clay was a clay that, for the most part, made up. I modified and tweaked the recipe "Beck Dark Stoneware." https://glazy.org/recipes/281993 because our glaze kitchen didn't have all that was needed for that particular recipe. I substituted Newman Red Clay for Redart and Kentucky ball clay for Tile 6. Because there was Redart already in the recipe, I met in the middle by upping the amount of Tile 6 and the amount of Redart. This clay threw really well and held its shape well. It fired to a dark earthy brown that I personally wasn't the hugest fan of, but it was a nice classic color.
Ingredients: Redart 45; Tile #6 Kaolin 40; Custer Feldspar 10; Grog 5; Hawthorne Bond 5

Name: Ben Jorden (4)
Description: For this clay body, it was much more crumbly than the previous ones, but after some more water, smoothing, and sitting, it was much easier to cut into and didn't break apart like the other clays. I really loved how this threw it was very smooth and felt structured. It fired to a beautiful earthen red color that I've found difficult to achieve.
Ingredients: Redart 60; Tile #6 Kaolin 15; Goldart 15; Grog 10; Silica 10

Name: Red Ben (5)
Description: This was an extra l clay that I tested out. In our glaze kitchen, we had two mystery "Red Clay." I used the formula of Ben Jordan Redart: 60, Goldart: 15, Tile 6: 15, Silica: 10. I replaced the Redart with Redclay 1. It produced this yellow-brown clay that had a short, in nature, consistency that I believe would be helped if left longer. It threw well, but i wasnt able to salvage a usable piece because I pulled the walls thin. It fired to a light brown, which wasn't bad but just boring for my taste.
Ingredients: Red clay 60; Tile #6 Kaolin 15; Goldart 15; Grog 10; Silica 10

Ingredients: TP 289 - Esmalte brillante Dp colors/2024 100; Zinc Oxide 6; Cobalt Oxide 0.5

Name: Big Ben (6)
Description: This was by far my favorite clay body that I made. It is rich in texture and color. This was also a test from our mystery "Red Clay." I used the formula of Ben Jordan Redart: 60, Goldart: 15, Tile 6: 15, Silica: 10. I replaced the Redart with Redclay 2. When I mixed 200g for the test, it was difficult to mix because there were big chunks of dry material. It threw beautifully with a great deal of structure and smooth pulls that didn't fight me at all. There was some cracking right before the first pull, but that didn't show up anywhere else. When I mixed a big batch of this clay, it mixed and wedged so well that I had no complaints about it. When fired to ^5 It turned this stunning dark, almost completely black, like color. The breaking of the shrinkage ruler was definitely a user error of not letting it dry out properly.
Ingredients: Redart 60; Tile #6 Kaolin 15; Goldart 15; Grog 10; Silica 10

Description: Hopefully the final version of my magnesium matte glaze. Swaps some KNO for lithium to help with the surface tension issues introduced by the magnesium. Benefits from epsom salts if using as a thinner dipping glaze, despite its clay content, due to its lithium content. Lithium is pretty soluble so wait until the water saturates and becomes the typical "foxy" yellow color before trying to add the epsom salts. Next up is color experiments 😎. Note: the lithium may not be strictly necessary and could be substituted with more 3195 if not on hand or too expensive. Just may pinhole more on dark/gassy clays.

Name: Subtle Lumina
Description: A deep glaze with a quiet, organic presence, in grey-green tones with bluish hints and darker areas that emphasize movement across the surface. The texture ranges from smooth to slightly granular, with a subtle sense of micro-crystals that diffuse the light and create a soft, hazy yet lively appearance. In thicker application, the color builds in depth, with darker pooling and occasional signs of movement, while in thinner layers the glaze opens up to a softer, lighter tone. The surface evokes a sense of natural weathering, almost like moss-covered stone or a mineral shaped over time. The glaze is relatively stable, with a slight tendency to move in thicker areas, contributing to its organic and varied character. It is an excellent starting point for exploring additional color variations, as this base responds richly to subtle adjustments and additions.

Name: Trudy’s Red Gold (final-rounded)
Description: Shop glaze created by me for Fired Clay Pottery. Based off a recipe from one of the original owners of Ceramics Canada, Trudy Bond. I had to tweak for shifts in material chemistry over time, and to work around some discontinued materials. This glaze was formulated to work around an existing firing cycle, rather than fine tuning the firing cycle to the recipe. It’s sensitive to silica level changes, flux ratio changes, and while I did try to eliminate the lithium, I found it gives the background colour more of a beer bottle brown tone rather than the reddish tones I wanted. You WILL have to roast off a portion of the Alberta Slip. Glazy doesn’t allow me to show the split in the recipe. How much roasted vs raw you need will vary on your batch size. Plainsman recommends starting with a 50/50 split. I found I need closer to a 2/3 raw, 1/3 roasted for a 20kg batch. Too much roasted and the glaze will hard pan, not enough and it’ll be prone to drying shrinkage that can lead to crawling.
