Name: Spruill EXPERIMENTAL "Straight 6" v1 ???SAME AS MAHAVIR VARIANT???
Description: 6 materials, equal proportions. At C5, with one-one-thousand dip, it looks awesome. Dip line stays put, no ridge, no clay body discoloring at edge. At C6, with two-one-thousand dip, it STILL looks awesome on bare clay body test tiles. However, on a decorated crafted object the 2-second dip demonstrates milkiness relative to dipping tong placement (see following observations), so another test will be performed on a similar object, but limited to a 1-second quick-dip. TEST PANEL 1, cone 5 100ml water volume. "one-one-thousand" dip produces complete, even coverage. Close inspection is very smooth with no pitting or dimpling of any kind. Sheet of glass. This clear glaze is very clear. Starting acid test today, 2026-3-1, Sponge soaked in lemon juice. >>>PASSES ACID TEST. After 24 hours, zero leaching, lustre intact. TEST PANEL 2, cone 6 2000ml water volume (20x quantity factor, so each material weighs 332g). Dissolved Borax (breaking down chunks) in 1000ml hot water 1st, letting it sit until all other 5 dry ingredients were combined, used immersion blender to thoroughly dissolve Borax in water, then added Borax solution to dry mix. Topped up mix with another 1000ml hot water, 50:50 dry to water ratio. FORGOT TO RUN THE WET BATCH THROUGH A ROTARY MILL TO REMOVE ROCKS ...remember that. Did two types of tests: Cone-6-A: Undecorated plain clay body sample tile repetition, and Cone-6-B: "Nut bowl" object made from plain white-clay body with interior underglaze application, and exterior decoration using incised circular pockets with brushed underglaze and incised fluted teardrops brushed with stroke-and-coat. Cone-6-A results Did two-one-thousand dip. At cone 6 results were once again very smooth, with no visible difference between "1-second dip at cone 5" and "2-second dip at cone 6" on test tiles (see side-by-side photos), except that there were very tiny, and very sparse, pits (someone with better vision than I pointed them out, and I could see them when wearing glasses). On close inspection were right on top of grog particles in the tan-spec clay body, but the Brown Bear dark body was 99.9% smooth with very, very sparse pits which is suspected to be a result of my omission of final rotary milling pass to remove rocks. Cone-6-B results Did two-one-thousand dip. - Interior was perfect, unpitted high gloss, no pooling, crazing, shivering, etc. - Exterior exhibited an even, high gloss lustre. Some milkiness occurred below the convex equator on one side opposite of tong-jaw placement. Possible causes being (A) 2-second dip allowed too much glaze adhesion, (B) location of object relative to heating elements in kiln, (C) probably not due to gravity otherwise the milkiness would have been all around the circumference. Area of milkiness is approximately 1/8th total surface area... corresponding to 1/4 of the bottom 1/2 of the object. Finally, there was some gravitational slide coincident with the stroke-and-coat, but this is expected because of the chemical interaction between over- and under-coats. OBSERVATIONS REGARDING POT-LIFE: When left standing in a bucket, the glaze will transform into a weird marshmallow-like wad. Subsequent attempts to dilute simply end up returning to this weird sponge state that is like a bizarre slurry of dense foam. Water apparently reaches a maximum suspension balance with the solids, and excess water floats on top of the sponge. No hard-pan, just a foamy slurry with water floating on top. Variant of "Straight 6" recipe, per veteran suggestion, experimented with reduced Borax. Implementation: Increased Silica by 2%. Decreased Borax by 4%. R2O:RO ratio is 3.0 : 7.00 Silica:Alumina is 9.0. Result: Fail. Cloudiness appears in surface indentations. Conclusion: High Borax is essential.
Ingredients: Tile #6 Kaolin 16.6 (additional); Borax 16.6 (additional); Ferro Frit 3134 16.6 (additional); G-200 Feldspar 16.6 (additional); Silica 16.6 (additional); Wollastonite 16.6 (additional)

Name: Aventurine
Description: This folder documents the development of silica and lithium rich glazes aimed at encouraging the formation of Aventurine type crystals. The inspiration comes from the mineral aventurine, a type of quartz formed from molten silica that crystallized upon cooling. Its structure contains tiny plate like metallic particles that create a characteristic sparkling effect due to light reflection. The experiments in this series explore how chemical composition and firing and cooling conditions influence crystal formation, surface sheen, and visual depth, with the goal of achieving a rich, shimmering effect across a range of colors such as green, red, brown, black, or blue.

Name: Emerald Moss Flow
Description: This folder documents a series of experiments exploring the relationship between boron content in a glaze and the color development of iron. The tests examine how boron influences melting temperature, glaze fluidity, and the way iron expresses itself, from a range of warm browns to attempts at achieving greenish tones. The experiments also focus on the impact of application thickness and firing and cooling conditions on the formation of textures, oil spotting, and phase separation, with the goal of understanding how to guide the system toward greater depth and color variation.

Name: Calcination raw materials
Description: Over the years, I have been calcining kaolin to address issues related to powder absorption. However, I still encounter application problems in the studio, especially with materials such as titanium dioxide, magnesium carbonate, zinc oxide, and of course kaolin. These materials have a high absorption capacity, which requires adding a significant amount of water. This leads to a low specific gravity and results in a glaze layer that is too thin. The initial tests were conducted by comparing identical recipes, where one batch was made with raw materials and the other with the same materials after calcination.

Name: Deep brown Tenmoku - Titanium Dioxide
Description: Notes From Previous Recipe : Last time I got a nice shade, but the texture came out less shiny than I expected, which also means fewer microcrystals. So I researched how I could improve that! The main change I tested was to advance the melting time of the glaze in the firing – to see if that would allow more time for the crystals to develop. I did this by changing the ratio of two main fluxes: Frit 3110 and potassium feldspar. The result? The glaze melted earlier in the firing, and the shine improved. I still haven’t achieved exactly what I’m looking for, but I can see an interesting direction! Updates : I compensated for materials using target solve. Images don't do the glaze justice. I did a 3 day lemon test and noticed some loss of shine at the end of the third day. I may have too been excessive with my leeching tests, I only started ceramics 7 months ago and started making glazes two months ago so let me know. I’d love any tips.
Ingredients: G-200 Feldspar 50; Ferro Frit 3124 17; Talc 13; Wollastonite 13; Silica 4; Bone Ash 1; Lithium Carbonate 1; Red Iron Oxide 14 (additional); Titanium Dioxide 5 (additional); Bentonite 2 (additional)

Name: Parti-colored Floating Blue
Description: Try increasing CMC gum to 0.8% Apply to dime (1.3mm) thickness. Depending on application thickness this glaze can produce four colors: - Light floating blue (thickest) - Dark floating blue - Green - Golden brown (thinnest) I control application thickness by brushing this glaze onto pots. When mixing this glaze put it through a 100-mesh sieve. This glaze is derived from a recipe published on Peter Gregory's blog site https://opopots.blogspot.com/2011/05/tiles-glaze-testing-chun-zinc.html which uses Janet DeBoos' 144 base from "Glazes for Australian Potters" p. 100. This glaze was found during Currie testing of the recipe from Gregory's blog site. To obtain the parti-colored behavior alumina was slightly increased and silica slightly decreased. Additional changes were made to reduce pin-holing. Wollastonite was substituted for part of the whiting to reduce carbon dioxide outgassing. Zinc oxide was also decreased to reduce melt thickness, enabling pinholes to heal with less heatwork. Bentonite and CMC gum were added to make a brushable glaze. This glaze needs to be further revised to eliminate small pin-holing.

The inspiration comes from the mineral aventurine, a type of quartz formed from molten silica that crystallized upon cooling. Its structure contains tiny plate like metallic particles that create a characteristic sparkling effect due to light reflection. Name: Furikake green
Description: Furikake Green is a lush, variegated cone 6 glaze inspired by the layered depth of traditional Spearmint glazes and the saturated mossy character of Spectrum’s Nori Green. Fired hot to cone 6 in oxidation with a fast firing schedule and natural cooling cycle, it develops a richly mottled surface with floating olive, moss, celery, and deep sea-green tones. This glaze looks good on textured surfaces, porcelain, and white stoneware, where its layered depth and subtle crystallization become more pronounced. Surface movement increases with thickness, often producing darker pooling, haloing, and atmospheric variation. Firing: Oxidation, fast-fired to a hot cone 6 with a natural cool. IMPORTANT FIRING WARNING: The test images shown represent results from a natural / relatively quick kiln cooling cycle. Slow cooling, controlled cooling, or extended cooling soaks will substantially alter the appearance of this glaze. Slower cooling promotes increased crystallization and phase separation within the glaze melt, which may significantly change: Color and hue Surface texture and gloss Mottling and variegation Opacity and depth Crystal development and visual movement Results under slow-cool conditions may look dramatically different from the images shown. Always test with your specific firing schedule, clay body, and kiln behavior before production use.

Name: Selsor Chun with 1% tin, Copper carbonate (Aquamarine)
Description: This is my modified version of Ann's recipe at Cone 6 tested only, natural cool, using Minspar, 3% copper carbonate and 5% additional (extra) silica. Test tiles show various amounts of silica added for comparison. https://glazy.org/recipes/436809 75% water SG 1558 Zahn #2, 17 secs The soda feldspar type was not specified. I used Minspar. Copper oxide is a pain to strain, always getting micro clumps. Had to sieve my test batches three times. I converted the copper oxide 2% to copper carbonate by multiplying by a conversion factor of 1.48. So, my 500gm test batch initially called for 2% copper oxide = 10 grams copper oxide. 10gm x1.48 = 14.8 gm copper carbonate. Hence copper carbonate is 2% x 1.48 = 3%. I found in my community kiln, it ran a little bit on my test tile. I added incremental amounts of EPK, but the glaze became transparent and a sick dark pea green color. I added incremental amounts of silica next, knowing I was already close to being underfired. 6% added silica seemed to be the sweet spot without running, without a little bulge at the bottom of the tile, or being underfired. (This recipe is normalized to 5% added silica). 9% silica and I could see some areas of underfired stippling (as Stull says). 12% silica was horribly underfired across the entire tile. 80% water for good application thickness, single dip.
Ingredients: Silica 33.32; Minspar 200 32.39; Ferro Frit 3134 16.2; Whiting 9.52; Dolomite 5.71; Zinc Oxide 2.86; Copper Carbonate 3 (additional); Bentonite 2 (additional); Tin Oxide 1 (additional)

Description: This is a revision of Alberta Slip Rutile plus Cobalt Carb by Studio Stiina https://glazy.org/recipes/121839 Which is a revision (added Cobalt) from Tony Hansen's GA6-C recipe which requires a slow cool. https://digitalfire.com/recipe/ga6-c My results showed severe crawling (as Tony stated), and it would run off any vertical piece even though my little test tile looked perfect. Small bowls were more forgiving. I added 4.5% silica and calcined half my Alberta slip which profoundly improved my results in a cone 6, no slow cool, community kiln. I mostly used Standard Clay 225 and 112. 103% water. I need to make some more and add a little more silica for total of 7% which is this recipe here, normalized to 100%. Large batch testing... If too thick an application, it will develop a few pits on the outside, which is a kiln setting that I can't control, so I need to keep the application thin enough to avoid it. Hence, the water recommendation and a quick dip. This glaze needs to be sieved as the calcined Alberta slip is quite clumpy. A 4" round plastic cleaning brush with a drill attachment is the quickest way to get the job done. Doing by hand took me an hour.... SG: 1.462 to 1.484 Zahn #2 cup: 16 to 17.6 sec

Name: Fire 2
Description: 113g dry material : 100g water; theoretical SG calculated at 1.51. Dry mixed, added water and mixed, let sit 24 hours. Mixed again and sieved with 80 mesh, measured SG at 1.44. Two dips both roughly 2 seconds on a #16 Porcelain tile (#800) fired in a community kiln with natural cool to cone 5 (might be a little hot). Fired May 2, 2026. Original glaze used bone ash with black iron oxide to achieve the kaki (persimmon) glaze effect, with red-orange flecks on a dark background. My substitutions here did not include bone ash, and as expected... this glaze is only a consistently dark, dark, dark red (nearly black). I may attempt to add some Zircopax and see if I can lighten it up, but bone ash (tricalcium phosphate) is likely needed to achieve the desired effect.
Ingredients: Nepheline Syenite 26; Silica 21; Ferro Frit 3195 20; Wollastonite 12; BT2213 Fabi Talc 11; EP Kaolin 10; Black Iron Oxide 12 (additional); Bentonite 1 (additional)

Name: Earth 2B
Description: 113 dry material : 103g water; theoretical SG calculated at 1.5. Dry mixed, added water and mixed, let sit 24 hours. Mixed again and sieved with 80 mesh, measured SG at 1.45. Two dips both roughly 2 seconds on a #16 Porcelain tile (#283) fired in a community kiln with natural cool to cone 5 (might be a little hot). Fired May 2, 2026. This is Gabriel Kline's Spearmint glaze (https://ceramicartsnetwork.org/ceramic-recipes/recipe/spearmint-64cf04cf-ae6d-4650-84b9-fa94b4c2981c), with an addition of 1% manganese. Glaze likely needs a slight reduction in COE to bring it <7.0. Manganese in this version gives yellow colors in the variegation created by the rutile, which can't be seen well in the photo but are there! This glaze has small divots in top of glaze surface that aren't quite pinholes. A slight hold just under peak temp might help encourage a better finish.
Ingredients: EP Kaolin 27; Wollastonite 27; Ferro Frit 3134 22; Silica 19; Nepheline Syenite 4; Rutile 6 (additional); Copper Carbonate 4 (additional); Bentonite 2 (additional); Manganese Dioxide 1 (additional)

Name: Water 2
Description: 107.5 dry materials : 100g water; theoretical SG calculated at 1.5. Dry mixed, added water and mixed, let sit 24 hours. Mixed again and sieved with 80 mesh, measured SG at 1.44. Two dips both roughly 2 seconds on a #16 Porcelain tile (#274) fired in a community kiln with natural cool to cone 5 (might be a little hot). Fired May 2, 2026. A single long dip (3-4 seconds) or a quick double dip is the ticket. Note that I originally input talc as "Talc" material, but I actually used Benwood Talc (Fabi Talc) -- I updated recipe here to reflect. If original recipe was formulated on Amtalc, it could be worth while to re-target based on original recipe... but this glaze looks great here. This recipe is from Mastering Cone 6 Glazes (by John Hesselberth and Ron Roy), and has the G-200 feldspar substituted with Mahavir Potash feldspar. I also added bentonite to improve suspension. The authors rigorously tested this glaze for food safety, and it's a dream!
Ingredients: EP Kaolin 20; Ferro Frit 3134 20; Mahavir Potash Feldspar 20; Silica 18.5; BT2213 Fabi Talc 11.5; Wollastonite 10; Rutile 6 (additional); Bentonite 1 (additional); Cobalt Carbonate 1 (additional); Red Iron Oxide 0.5 (additional)

Chat GPT originally had set 0.8 cobalt carb, I rounded up to 1. This glaze was a bit on the thin side and first dip was 2 seconds, second dip was 4 seconds. Name: Riptide
Description: Riptide captures the shifting color and movement of turbulent coastal water, somewhere between storm surf, deep ocean teal, and midnight blue. This glaze develops a suspended, smoky depth with soft phase separation and subtle tonal layering throughout the melt. Thin areas may break toward cooler green-blue tones, while heavier application produces richer saturation and darker pooling. Riptide performs especially well on porcelain and white stoneware, where its layered depth and subtle visual movement become more pronounced. Firing: Oxidation, fast-fired to a hot cone 6 with a natural cool. IMPORTANT FIRING WARNING: The test images shown represent results from a natural / relatively quick kiln cooling cycle. Slow cooling, controlled cooling, or extended cooling soaks will substantially alter the appearance of this glaze. Slower cooling promotes increased crystallization and phase separation within the glaze melt, which may significantly change: Color and hue Surface texture and gloss Mottling and variegation Opacity and depth Crystal development and visual movement Results under slow-cool conditions may look dramatically different from the images shown. Always test with your specific firing schedule, clay body, and kiln behavior before production use.
Ingredients: Silica 25.56; Ferro Frit 3195 20.63; Mahavir Potash Feldspar 19.92; Whiting 17.43; EP Kaolin 16.46; Rutile 5 (additional); Copper Carbonate 3 (additional); Cobalt Carbonate 2 (additional)

Name: Deep Sea
Description: Deep Sea is a richly atmospheric cone 6 glaze inspired by the shifting color and suspended depth of open ocean water. This glaze develops a luminous field of saturated cobalt, indigo, and violet-blue layered over subtle smoky gray undertones. Depending on thickness and contour, Deep Sea moves between electric ultramarine, stormy navy, and muted midnight blue, with darker pooling in recesses and softer lavender-blue blooms across thinner areas. Deep Sea performs especially well on porcelain and white stoneware, where its layered tonal variation and floating micro-variegation become more pronounced. Texture and carved surfaces encourage darker pooling and increased dimensionality. Firing: Oxidation, fast-fired to a hot cone 6 with a natural cool. IMPORTANT FIRING WARNING: The test images shown represent results from a natural / relatively quick kiln cooling cycle. Name: Verde Cobre with Substitutions
Description: Substitution version of William Chau’s Cobre Verde (https://glazy.org/materials/57824) Note the discolouration from an overnight spa session in cleaning vinegar. I used materials I have on hand, including some that will soon not be available (Mahavir, EPK). I added clay to the recipe for bucket properties, kept the silica:alumina ratio very close, and just had to accept adjustments to the alkaline metal portion due to material source. Kiln firing was a cone-verified perfect cone 6 with a drop and hold schedule based on the digitalfire one. Cooling rate was naturally very slow through the 1000-900 C range, as it was a solidly packed community studio kiln. This was a quick and dirty test for a baseline, not a super precise assay. Additions of cobalt and EPK on the second and third test tiles were done volumetrically: first tile was dipped, 1g of cobalt added, second tile dipped and 5% EPK was added before dipping the third tile. I think I added roughly 80g of water, but it wasn’t precise and I didn’t record specific gravity. No sign of running: any bulges on the test tiles are from application drips.
Ingredients: Silica 35.2; Dolomite 18.4; Ferro Frit 3134 12.7; Mahavir Potash Feldspar 11.3; EP Kaolin 10; Copper Carbonate 6.5; Zinc Oxide 5.8
